summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirchi seed was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, but the High Court in revision held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the lal mirble powder was adulterated. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case where food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy disgusting, decomposed or insectable, it would be deemed to be unfit for human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 2(1)(f). On behalf of respondent it was submitted that in view of the construction that the expression 'insect infested ' includes infestation even by dead insects, the further point to be considered is, whether mere insect infestation without more, would be sufficient to hold the article to be 'adulterated ' within the meaning of section2(1) (f). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law, because the presumption in his case could be drawn against him. The Sessions Judge rejected the evidence on the ground that the lease deeds were not registered and were not admissible in evidence under section 49 of the Registration Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that he was an agricultural agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a "dealer and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub para must be carried to its logical conclusion. [901 C] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , followed. 1.2 It is clear that sub para speaks of storing for sale, as a dealers although the word "as dealer" is not there because storage had reference to "business as a 'dealer and therefore it is easy to see that the evidence which was "brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of witnesses. The Magistrate rejected the testimony on the view that he is the next door neighbour and has a "soft corner for him". [902 D E] Manipur administration vs M/s. Naya Chandra Singh, ; , referred to.

The plaintiff respondent instituted a suit for recovery of possession of the land described in Schedule to the plaint, on the allegation that the defendant was a monthly tenant under the plaintiff at the date when the notice to quit was served upon him. The trial court decreed the suit and the decision was affirmed by the District Judge. On second appeal, the High Court held that the notice was insufficient for the purpose of determining the tenancy. It further held that even though the parties might have intended to create a lease for one year, no operative inase came into existence, the only facts admitted were that the respondent remained in possession of land belonging to the plaintiff with the permission of the Receiver who represented the plaintiff 's estate, and paid rent to the latter. The High Court also held that as the notice served by the plaintiff upon the defendant did not fulfil this requirement, the plain tiff 's suit was bound to fail. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the question whether there was a contract to the contrary in the present case was a registered instrument but ex facie it was not an operative document at all and could not consequently fulfil the requirements of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. Debendra Nath vs Syama Prasanna, 1126 37 282 certain reported cases, such inference has been drawn. One such case had been referred to by this Court in Matilal vs Darjeeling Municipality, (1924) L.R. 58 I.A. 178 and Mati Lal vs Darsole Municipality, A.I.R 1933 Pat. 485, disapproved.

The appellant, a firm, instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the respondents, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati, w/o Shri Pindi Kumar Gulati. During the course of proceedings in the suit, when evidence was being recorded, the plaintiff obtained summons from the court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce in the Court records relating to the Income tax Assessment of the defendants, M.Dagi Rampindi Lal for the assessment years 1964 65 to 1971 72. The Income Tax officer to whom the summons were issued, sent the record in a sealed cover through an Inspector along with a letter dated November 1,1972 claiming that the said record was privileged under Section 137 of the 1961 Act and that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an assessee could be made. The plaintiff also applied for and obtained summons requiring the Incometax Officer to produce the Income 's record relating to M/S Borizeon Industrial Products (P) Ltd., and Bishamber Nath Kaul. That record was also sent by the IncomeTax Officer in a separate sealed cover along with letter dated 11,1972, claiming that it was privileged tinder Section 137 Of the 1961 1961 Act. The Commissioner of Income Tax rejected the application on the ground that the question of privilege as claimed by the assessee was important and likely to arise in the course in the trial of suits in future also, a reference was made by the learned Single Judge to the Full Bench which held that when a party to a proceeding in a Court applies for summoning any documents, records etc. from the income tax authorities, the court may summon the said documents, record etc. summoned for and submit his view to the Court in answer to summons. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that after the repeal of Section 137 by Act V of 1964 there is no longer any impediment left in the way of a civil court to summon the production of documents filed by an assessee during the assessment proceedings before an Income Tax Officer after 1.4.1964 in respect of assessment years, 1964 65 onwards and that the finality attached to an order of the Commissioner with regard to claim of privilege under Section 138(1)(b) has no relationship to the power of the court to summoning that record. For a proper appreciation of the question debated before this court it would be desirable to refer to the relevant provisions of the 1922 Act and 1961 Act, as amended from time to time, and notice the changes brought about in the matter of claim of privileges by the income Tax Department. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Full Bench was right in holding that the omission of Section 138 did not make any difference and that it had taken away for all times the jurisdiction of the courts to call for the record from the Income 8 tax authorities. Those provisions, as already noticed had only put the exercise of that jurisdiction under a cloud and those fetters were coterminous with the life of Section 54 of the Income Act or Section 137 thereof. The finality which has been attached to the order if the Commissioner under Section138(1) (b) of the Act is applicable only in cases where application is made to the Commissioner by a party or any other person for receiving documents or information. It has nothing to do with the powers of the Courts to summon such documents,record etc.

One Mammotty was ill for a long time and was in hospital and he was discharged uncured a month before the execution of the gift deed and remained in his mother 's house afterwards. There were conflicting versions about the nature of the disease and a plea was taken in the case that the gift was made in contemplation of death and was voidable. The trial Judge and the first Appellate Court did not accept it. After the death of Seinaba, the present suit was brought by Kunhamu an eider brother of Mammottty for partition and possession of a 6/16 share of the property which he claimed as an heir under the Muhammadan Law, challenging the gift as invalid. To the suit he joined his two sisters as defendants who submitted were entitled to a 3/16 shares each. He also submitted that the first three defendants were entitled only to the remaining 4/16th share as heirs of Seinsaba. The first three respondents contended that when succession opened out on the death, his widow was entitled to the enhanced share of 1/4 as there was no issue and the remaining 3/4 was divisible between him and his two daughters, Kunhami getting twice as much as each sister, These shares according to him were unaffected by the invalid gift in faVour of Sewab and accepted on her behalf by her mother. This contention was accepted and it was held in this case that all the three courts had held that a gift by the husband to his minor wife to be valid must be accepted on his behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Mohammedan Law. Held, further, that there is good authority for these propositions in the ancient and modern books of Muhammadan law and in decided cases of undoubted authority. In the ancient & modern books the law of gifts attaches great importance to possession or seisin of the properties gifted (Kabz ul Kamil) especially of immovable property. The Hedaya p. 518 quoted from Radd ul Mukhtar, Vol. 4 p. 548, referred to.

The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras, issued on September 30, 1959, directing the respondent to pay the arrears of contributions and audit fee under the Commissioner 's demand notice dated June 25, 1957. The respondents moved another petition in the High Court for an order restraining the Commissioner from enforcing the provisions of the Amending Act 27 of 1954. The High Court upheld the plea on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was Premature, and that audit fee demanded by the Commissioner was without determination under section 76(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Commissioner had not determined the cost of auditing the accounts of the respondent temple and proceeded to observe "It is sufficient to say that the demand made of the petitioners ' temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. 1, 62 8 3 nP towards the audit of its accounts in respect of the year 1963 does not rest upon any determination made under section 77(2). HELD : (i) The Commissioner had no power under section 78(2), to impose a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institutions governed by the provisions Of the Act. [920 C] (ii) Under the Act a fee though levied for rendering services of a particular type is not to be, co related to the services performed for each individual who is intended to obtain the benefit of the services. The co relation must be between the expenses incurred by the authority levying the fee for generally providing the service and the aggregate of the levy from persons who are to be made subject thereto. It is a necessary corollary that under the Act general rules prescribing the levy of fee from religious endowments have to be framed, and not rules governing individual endowments.

The appellant, a contemner under section 19(1) of the , was alleged to have committed contempt of the High Court. The High Court held that no appeal lies to this Court under section19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner for bearing the case piecemeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: An appeal is maintainable as a matter of right from any kind of order made by the High court in the proceeding for contempt. The proceeding is initiated under section 17 by issuance of a notice. Thereafter there may be many interlocutory orders passed in the said proceeding by the trial Court. It could not be the intention of the legislature to provide for an appeal to this court as a matters of right. [512C D] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to. Baradkanta Mishra v Justice Gogatikrunna Mishra; , distinguished. Barodakanta Misra vs JusticeGatikroshna Mishra ; , distinguished and held inapplicable. Bardakanta Das vs Justice S Gatirushna Misra, A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206, distinguished. The order or the decision must be such that it decides some bone of contention raised before the High Courts affecting their right, the mere order issuing the notice is not appealable. [511B C] Bardikanta Mishra V Justice Gitikrushnna Mishra and Anr., ; , followed.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The trial court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone plus a fine of Rs. 500. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. Held, that the word " text " is comprehensive enough to take in the subject as well as the terminology used in a statute. In Craies on Statute Law 3rd Edition, the sama idea is expressed in the following words: at p. 349; Sometimes an Act of Parliament instead of expressly repeating the words of a section contained in a former Act merely refers to it, and by relation its provisions to some new state of things created by the subsequent Act. In such a case the is rule of construction that where a statute is incorporated by reference into a second statute, the repeal of the first statute by a third does not affect the second ". The word " in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another, it amends the subject or proposal of it though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. The language of the said section is sought to be effected on the basis of the words " unless a different intention (1) I.L.R. 1955 Punj. (2) 763 appears The repeal by this Act of any enactment shall not affect any other enactment in which such enactment has been applied, incorporated or referred to".

The appellant was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait, he executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty some time in April 1928 on the basis of which he received advances of money from time to time from the latter. The last entry in the Hatchitita was made in March 1929 and the total amount borrowed up to that date came up to Rs. 3,801. Adwaita Charan Roy died in 1930 and after his death, Satish Chandra Roy became the managing shebait and continued to act as such till his death in 1940. There was an adjustment of accounts between Nanitash and the creditor in whose favour the H 39th was executed, and a sum of Rs. 5,068 having been found due to the 128 creditor, Satish Chander gave him a renewed Hatch for that amount. It appears that while Adwa was still the managing trustee, a suit was instituted by some of his co Shebaits to remove him from his office and pending the hearing of the suit, Ramjanaki Roy, another co Shebait in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Burdwan, being Money Suits Nos. 261 and 262 of 1932, for recovery of the moneys due in respect of the Hathita and the promissory notes mentioned above. Both the suits were decreed on the ground that the appellant was a mere benamidar for her husband Aghore in respect Of the purchase of Ga Schedule properties in court sale, and also that the Kobala executed by the Chakrabortys in favour on July 26, 1940, was a fictitious conveyance made in favour by Aghpur Nath Roy in the name of his wife. The trial judge decided against the appellant and granted their prayers in both the applications. Orders were made for reopening of the decrees and making fresh decrees in their places in accordance with the provisions of the Bengal Money Lenders Act. Direction was also given for restoration of the properties mentioned in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga to the deities under the provision of section 36(2)(c). Against this decision, Oramba Sundari took two appeals to the High Court of Calcutta and the learned Judges who heard the appeals affirmed the decision of the courts below. The questions that fell for consideration were : (i) whether in a proceeding under section 36 of the Act it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decreeholders on record were in fact benamidars for another person; (ii) Whether even if Aghmore was proved to have advanced the money upon which the Chakraborty 's obtained the decrees, in reopening the decrees or in working out the rights of the parties in accordance therewith the provisions Of the Bengal Act the court could treat the Chakraborty as the decree holders alone. For a proper determination of this point it is necessary to examine the scope of section 35 of the said Bengal MoneyLenders Act and the reliefs which the Court is competent to grant in terms of that section.

The respondent company instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent. annum on the ground that it had obtained a decree in favour of the appellant and that the appellant was entitled to execute the decree under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appellant contended that the respondent company could not claim to be transferees of the decree within the meaning of Order XXI Rule 16 of C.P.C., because, as the respondent Company had become entitled by virtue of this document read in the light of section 8, to all the rights and remedies including the right to prosecute the pending suit and to obtain a decree the decree that was ultimately passed by the City Civil Court in favour Of the appellant on the 15th December 1949. Held, that the High Court was wrong in holding that the application for execution filed before the City civil court not mentioned any of these particulars but merely stated that the Court should declare them the assignees of the decrees as the decretal debt along with other debts were transferred by the respondent to the appellant company by the document under consideration and the appellant could not be said to have been a transferee of the suit within the terms of Order 21, rule 1(2)(j) of the C. P.C. The words "decree holder" in section 8 of the , are wide enough to include an assignee of a decree under the decree. The expression "decreeholder" in the Code means a person who has obtained a money decree and includes a person in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder. It is not necessary that the words "where a decree . is transferred by assignment in writing or by operation of law, the transferee may apply for execution of the order to the Court which passed it. The proper meaning of the word "decree" in Order XXI rule 16 must be given to the words used in the section and the words 'decree holder ' must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity might afterwards become entitle to the benefits of the original decree by virtue Of the assignment in his favour. The word "judgment debtor" in order XXI, r. 16 of Civil Proce dure means a decree which is transferred before the transferee can benefit from the provisions of rule 16.

The respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows"WI ' type "T.H., Window" and "Composite Winds" of certain sizes "in accordance with the specifications, designs drawing and instructions in writing referred to in r. 1 hereof and Class 11 of the conditions of contract and with such materials as are provided for by and in all other respects in accordance with such conditions so far as applicable". The respondent submitted its tender on the basis of the current price of mild steel billets fixed by the Government, but not charge for service, was taxable. He accordingly remanded the case with a direction to assess tax on the price for sale of materials only. The Board of Revenue exercising revisional power confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner observing that the contract undertaken by the respondent was not a contract of service and that the amount received by the appellant was not taxable. The High Court held that the contracts between the respondent and the Executive Engineers were a "building contract" and the amount paid by the Respondent was not 'taxable ', but held that there was no stipulation for passing of property in the goods to the factory before actual completion of the erection work; there the contract did not contemplate dissecting the value of the goods supplied and, the value, of work and labour bestowed in the execution of the work. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The object of the respondent ' was to enter into a works contract. That clearly appears from the terms of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work. [510 C] (ii) The service was not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. The contract undertaken was to be executed according to and the specifications given with glass clear words and conditions. There were not two contracts one of sale and another of service. [511 E F] (iii) The primary undertaking of the Respondent ' was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows.

The appellant was charged under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. The prosecution case is that on November 8, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to Ram Avtar and stated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. On November 16, 1967 Shanker Lal handedover the said formal order by which he was agreed, would be sent through Shankar Lal. On December 16,1967 Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report lodged by Shankar Lal in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the F.I.R. The High Court allowed the revision petition and quashed the charges framed against the appellant. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: There was no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. [ 279 B] The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the same nature of thing made no mentioning of the names of Raj k Kumar Agarwal respondent because the case was of the complainant itself that he appeared on scene only prior to the filing of the complaint.

The petitioner, an Allopathic doctor by profession, had himself drafted and filed was originally drafted and was unduly long and repetitive, written submission with the assistance of counsel crystalising the issues for determination by the Court was filed. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 ( 'Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration is run and controlled has also prescribed rules and issued instructions which are not being properly implemented. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railways with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings, increasing human error as a contributing factor to accidents, non allocation of adequate funds for improvements, improper utilisation of the assets and facilities, etc., in the administration at different levels, prevalence and increase of indiscipline, frequency of thefts, robberies and murders of passengers, ineffective checking and supervisory system, want of replacement of equipment and repairs to bridges as also non provision of adequate facilities to passengers. The Joint Director (Safety) has filed a counter affidavit in answer to the Rule on behalf of the respondents. It has been averred that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as the locomotive drivers are concerned there were as many as 14471 of them as on March 1, 1982; unmanning level crosses were provided mostly on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. It had been further pleaded that periodic review is undertaken about manning of unmaned level crossing crossings and opening of new level cross sheets in consultation with appropriate State Governments. Initially it used to be the obligation of the respective State Governments to provide for such level cross ingings at their cost in view of the accepted position that at a level crossing the right of way is of the train in preference to traffic on the road. As that arrangement was not working well, with effect from April 1, 1966, a Railway Safety Work Work Fund has been set up and expenses are being met out of it. From 1978 potentially hazardous unmanred level cross over crossings were provided mainly on roads when the volume is low. The movement of the railways and their functioning in view, the commendable view to accept may be that the rates and fares should cover the total cost of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations, if any. It is of paramount importance that every citizen must get involved in the determination of march to resurrect the society and subordinate his will and passion to the primordial necessity of order in social life. The responsibility cast by the Railway Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It was also the paramount obligation of tho State to ensure availability of situations, circumstances and environments in which every citizen can effectively exercise and enjoy those rights. The right to life has recently been held by this Court to connote not merely animal existence but to have a much wider meaning to include the finer graces of human civilization. If these rights of the citizens are to be ensured, it is undoubtedly the obligation to ensure that every bona fide passenger is a guest of the service.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The applications were dismissed by the Revenue Tribunal on the ground that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41 rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. The appellants contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Act read along with Regulation 19(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Tribunal rejected the applications holding that they had been time barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act makes a decision of the Tribunal in appeal as final and conclusive and not to be questioned in any suit or proceeding in any court, the Tribunal was right in taking the view that the applications were barred by limitation. HELD: The language of Regulation 20 applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a ease where the Appeal has been dismissed for want of prosecution under Regulation 19 (1). [143 E] In the context of section 20 and in view of the express language of section 17(1), it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case when the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer. It is also open to it to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits.

The appellants, two descendants of the first appellant and the second appellant, were the descendants of one Dinanath Sao. The main controversy in the present litigation is whether by the Punch Faisla Award of 1896 an absolute dedication of the village Telibandha was made in favour of the temple either by Dinanath or by his descendants. The two appellants, both descendants of Dinanath, brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent Kamal Narayan, another descendant of Dinnath Sao from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandraji Swamy for the village of Telivancorebandha and for accounts. The appellants contended that the Pun ch Faisira Award was not set aside by the Court and the suit was dismissed as compromised. Held, that the title to the property in dispute could be determined on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and the question whether the dedication made had ceased to be valid by anything which happened afterwards. The fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. On a consideration of the context this Court came to the conclusion that Dhuj Singh had only a life interest in the properties and pointed out that "in cases where the intention of the testator is to grant an absolute estate, an attempt to reduce the powers of the owner by imposing restraint on alienation would certainly be repelled on the ground of repugnancy; but where the restrictions are the primary things which the testator desires and they are consistent with the whole tenor of the will, it is a material circumstance to be relied upon for displacing the presumption of absolute ownership implied in the use of the word "Malik". Surajmani vs Rabi Nath Ojha (1907) L.R. 35 I.A. 76, referred to.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Parishad. There were three charges against the appellants. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the same. The gist of the charge against the appel lant was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associating with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of 'Criminal Contempt '. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The language used by them was unfortunate. Counsel for the appell lant did not justify the language of the Resolution. There is no gainsaying that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. The words used by him were unfortunate. [603C] 2.1 In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the aforesaid observations. [ 603A B] 2:2.3. The appellants did not commit any contempt. They did not do act with decency in regard lo the res pondation. The Chairman of tile Action Committee, described as contemnor No. 1 was actively associated with the making of the resolutions which contained defamatory remarks about their Chief Justice and since they also issued the resolution for publications in newspapers. He was guilty of criminal contempt.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 was entered into a joint Hindu family with the object of partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators. On or about 2nd July 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the said stamp paper was registered by which the abovenamed arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah the district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 8 and he functioned and acted as one of the arbitrators. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge, Hoohghly at Chinsura to return back the award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for registration. On 2nd September 1978 the learned Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the Arbitrators ' application to return the award. In January 1980 the arbitrators ' application was heard and the learned Subordinate Judge ordered return of the award, holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take possession for presenting the same for registration, and that the limitation for the registration of the Award had already expired. The High Court in Civil Rule No. 621 of 1980 set aside the order of the Sub judge holding that the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending was that is to say, from 28th January 1978 to 24th November 1983 the award was in court and this was manifest from the order in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1977. The appellants Nos 1 to 5 filed an application under Section 14 of the Act before the learned sub Judge praying for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in Misc., case No. 74 of 1977 initiated by the appellant No l.

The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" in Kalyan. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting of the premises. The appellant agreed to vacate and the respondent let out to him a portion of his new building which 219 was not riot far from "Fida Ali". The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the grounds inter alia (1) that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises; (2) that section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, did not apply. Held, that the respondent was only seeking to enforce his rights under the statute and the appellant could not be permitted to assert in a Court of justice any right founded upon or growing out of an illegal transaction. The plea of waiver is unsustainable. In the present case the question was not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 Of the Act declares to be illegal. By enforcing the contract the consequence will be the enforcement of an illegality and infraction of a statutory provision which cannot be condoned by any conduct or agreement of parties. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co. ([1945] 1 K.B. 65, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84 and 85, referred to.

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990 whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject, were found tampered with, the marks initially obtained and the marks increased due to tampering, and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardians. The appellant Board 's action was challenged by some of the examinees/parents/guardians before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petitions and directed the Board to take expeditious steps to declare the results of the examination within the specified time. The Board appointed seven enquiry officers to conduct the enquiry. Show cause notices were issued to the students on July 30, 1990 informing them of the nature of tampering, the subjects in which the marks were found tampering with, and the tampered marks initially secured and the mark increased due due to tampered and also stated the proposed punishments, if any, in the inquiry it would he found that the marks are tampered with. The declaration of their results were withheld pending further enquiry and the rest declared on June 30,1990. Several writ petitions were filed in the High Courts against non declaration of the results and the High court directed to take immediate action to declare results of examination within specified time, and to take steps to publish the results within the stipulated time. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Standing Committee did not apply its mind in the proper perspective to the material facts, and that the finding that tampering was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or the guardians to their advantage was based on records, was perverse. On behalf of the respondents it was submitted that the Act empowers the Divisional Board to deal with the use of unfair means at the final examination conducted under the Act, and Regulations; that the Committee did no power to take the impugned decision, etc., without approval of the Divisional Boards, and therefore, the impugned notification was without authority of law. On merits also it was held that the Administrative Judge was not competent to recommend to the Governor or compulsorily retire the District and Sessions Judge and the order of the Government made pursuant thereto was declared illegal. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The examination Committee of the Regional Board itself a statutory body acted on behalf of its Divisional Board and is not a delegate of theDivisional Board. Truely it is regulatory in character and the powers were exercised by the Committee and recommended to the State Govt.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge found the appellants guilty under both heads of charges and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500 each. On appeal by special leave the appellants contended that section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act was inapplicable to the facts. Held: (i) The object of the Act as set out in the preamble is to make more effective provision for the prevention of bribery and corruption. A new offence of Criminal misconduct by a public servant is created by section 5 and under sub section (2), it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine or with both. The offence is of four kinds or categories. Bribery as defined in section 161 of the Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (a). Bribery of the kind specified in section 165, if the offence is habitual and falls within cl. (b) contemplates criminal breach by a Public servant and the wording takes us to section 405 of the Code. It is with cl. 4 that the offences committed in the course of traps are less grave and call only for lenient or nominal sentences. The word "corrupt" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receiver. One may accept money that is offered or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case he obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public Servant. The words "corruption" and " illegal means" find place in section162. Apart from "corvert and illegal means", it has also the words "or by otherwise abusing his positions as a Public Servant". If a man obtains a monetary advantage by the abuse of his position, he will be guilty under sub cl.(d). Sections 161, 162 and 163 refer to a motive or reward for doing or forbearing to do something, showing favour or disfavour to any person, or for inducing such con duct by the exercise of personal influence. It was not necessary for an offence under clause (d) to prove all this. It would be enough if by abusing its position as public servant a man obtained for himself any pecuniary advantage, entirely irrespective of motive or motive or incentive for showing favouror disfavor to any persons, or any person inducing such gratification by the use of his positions. The fact that the offence was committed in course of the traps is less grave, and call Only for lenient and nominal sentences does not make it punishable under cl. 5(d). [188 H; 188 A] (ii)The words " Corrupt or illegal means". find place In section 162 of the Evidence Act may become difficult if intending offenders especially in cases of corruption are not furnished opportunities for the display of their inclinations and activities. Where matters go further and the police authorities themselves supply the money to be paid as a bribe. severe condemnation of the method is merited, as in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh vs The State of Vindhya Pradesh, ; , referred to.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P. against defendant 1, the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor and defendant 2, the surety. Defendant 1 contested the suit inter alia contending that the court had no jurisdiction to hear the suit and he had no knowledge about the suit transaction. The allegation of fraud made against him in the plaint was denied. He also denied his liability for the claim of the Bank as heir and legal representative. Defendant 2, who was surety, opposed the suit on the ground that the Court had no Jurisdiction to hear it and that he had not exercised such care as a prudent man would in the circumstances of the case which resulted in the loss of security, namely, pledged oil tins and, therefore, in view of combined operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the bail bond was discharged. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor pledging oil tinins as and by way of security for the advance and, hence, two securities were offered, namely: pledge of goods; personal guarantee of the surety; and personal guarantee Of the surety, and the personal guarantee. The surety was discharged from his liability as surety if the creditors had put it out of their power to hand over to the surety means of recouping himself by the security given by the principal. Allowing the appeal of the respondent Bank, ^ HELD: 1. Clause 5 of the letter of guarantee under discussion, which is in pari materia with clause 7 of the Letter of Guarantee under discussion held as under: "On behalf of the Respondent Bank reference was made to cl. 5 of exhibit P 4 which has already been quoted. It was contended that on account of this clause in exhibit P4 the appellant had opted out of the benefit of section 141 of Indian Contract. [923D E] 2. Clause 7 provides for non discharge of surety even if the creditor Bank enters into a composition with the principal creditor and that the bail would nonetheless be liable even if it is found that a creditor has taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by the Principal. That doctrine is very clearly expressed in the note in kees vs Barrington 2 White & Tudor 's L.C. 4th Edn. at p. 1002, para 280, p. 52, the statement of law bearing on this point reads as under; "280.Effect of loss of securities.

The appellant was the holder of a "patelki inam" lands situate in what was previously known as the ceded area of Berar. The Inam Commissioner, after seeing from the previous records as to who was in enjoyment granted the mukaddam inam of a bigha and a half from year to year as desired by the mikaddaman. The appellant 's claim with regard to these plots was alternatively placed on a somewhat different footing and he was not entitled to hold the "p Patelki inam". Held, that the grant was not a service grant but no question of a share in the emoluments of the patel 's office arose there. The grant was from yearto year in lieu of patel services and was binding on the jagirdars who agreed to be bound by it. The mere fact that the lands were given by way of emoluments for the pateent Patel 's offices did not make the grant a mere grant of office with emoluments in the shape of Inamlands. The order of the Government excluded the " patelki inams" from the resumption proceedings relating to the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir of Nawabag. The lands were treated as a homogenous unit by the orders passed on August 28, 1922, and the appellant was entitled to his share in them. The fact that in the inam enquiry and the sanad granted to the Inamdar of the Nawabag huq was not an order of descent or the estate was impartible.

The respondents were the descendants of a Hindu family governed by the Mitakshara law. They claimed that they were Hindus residing in Sind, that some four or five hundred years ago they were converted to Islam like the members of another such sect, and that despite their conversion, the Cutchi Memons retained a large part of Hindu Law as their customary law, including its concept& of joint family property, the right of a son by birth in such pro perty and its devolution by survivorship constituted the customary law of Cutchi memons in Madras and Bangalore. The respondents claimed that there was no question of passing of the said properties to them on the death of their father as envisaged by section 3 of the , Act or its being applicable to them or the said property, they having come to them under Hindu Law rule devolution of joint Family Property by survivorship. Their case was that only one third of the properties, that is, the undivided share of their deceased father could be properly said to have passed to them, on his death and to be assessable under the Act. The Deputy Controller rejected these contentions as also the evidence led by the respondents in support thereof and assessed 10 L120 SupCI/72 994 duty at Rs. 2,05,996.41 P on the basis that the entire estate valued by him at Rs 12,23,794 was assessable. The respondent filed two separate appeals both of which were rejected by the Central Board of Revenue by its order dated December 30, 1961 and as aforesaid, at the instance of the respondents referred to the High Court the question whether the said evidence, or the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third or more of the aforesaid estate only concluded the issue before him, viz., that the rules of Hindu law including the rules as to joint family properties and its succession by survivorship constitute the customary Law of Cutch Memons in Bombay and Bangalore, and whether the Khojas were to be considered as orthodox Sunnis or Ismailia Shias. The High Court upheld the respondents ' contentions and answered the question referred to it against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Courts of Madras have adopted a view different from the later trend of opinion in the Bombay High Court. [234 B] (ii) It is not correct to say that the rule of Mahomedan law applicable to the Khoias applied only to matters of inheritance and succession but also in matters of their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship. The question as to which customary law was applicable turns really on the consideration as to (1) [1922] 57 I.A. 237, followed. (iii) It has been held by this Court that the custom of Hindu Mitakshara law applicable only to cases of succession and inheritance as it would apply in the case of an intestate separate Hindu possessed of self acquired property and no more. The concurrent findings of the courts here was that he was not a Bombay Halai Memon but a Porbandar Memon. [235 C] (iv) It cannot be said that the customary rule of Muslim law applicable in all matters relating to Muslims nor did it abrogate the custom and usage in respect of matters other than those specified in section 2 of the Act, and therefore, when a Cutchi could dispose of by a will without the restriction of the one third under the Mahommedan Law, on the one hand, and joint family Property which he could not so dispose of.

The appellants are manufacturers of different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not dispute that the different kinds/categories of fabrics manufactured in their mill are subjected to payment, of excise duties on their removing from the Factory. They filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the validity of the circular. During the pendency of the writ petition in the Delhi high Court, the Central Government by a Notification No. 20/82 C dated 20.2.1982 amended rules 9 and 49 of the Rules. The appellants amended the writ petitions and challenged the constitutional validity of section 5 1 of the Finance Act, 1982 and of the amendments to rules 9 & 49 of Rules. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that no duty of excise can be levied and collected in respect of yarn which is obtained at an intermediate stage and, thereafter, subjected to an integrated process for the manufacture of different fabrics; that in spite of the said decision of the Delhi and High Court, they filed a Writ Petition before the High Court inter alia challenging the vires of section 51 of the Act and of amendments to Rules 9 and 50 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. It is the case of the appellant that no excise duty can be imposed and collected, in respect thereof, of yarn obtained at any intermediate stage, and thereafter subjected to a integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics, will be liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9, and 49; that even assuming that there can be fictional removal as provided in the Explanation to Rules, 9 and rule 49, there cannot be such fictional or deemed removal without the specification of the place where the excisable goods are produced, cured or manufactured, but are used for the purpose manufacture of end product (Varnish) within the factory premises itself, there is no removal within the meaning of rules. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Explanation to Rule 9 and Rule 49 contemplate the collection of duty levied on the production of a commodity at an intermediary stage which again is utilised in such continuous process for manufacture of the end product. [707C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants have challenged rule 9 and Rules 49 as they stood before amendment. The Explanations to Rule 10 and Rule 48 contemplate the recovery of duty from the appellants. [700D] 1:3 It is true that under Rule 9(1) there is a provision for specification by the Collector, but the question is what has to be specified by the collector. It does not require the Collector to specify the place of manufacture and also any premises appurtenant thereto. The words "which may be specified" by the Collec tor in this behalf occurring in Rule 9 (1) of the rules do not qualify the words "any place where they are produced", cured or imported, but relate to or qualify the word "any premises appurtenant therewith". In other words, if the place is not the place when the excisable Goods are produced. cured or any premises ancillary thereto, but also removal within such place or premises for captive consumption or 'home ', as it is called. Thus if a commodity which is manufactured in such place and premises and is used for manufacture or manufacture of another commodity then it will be a case of removal for the purposes of payment of Excise duty.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that Miss Eylene (P.W. 2) used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. She developed illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. In April 1963 Miss E Tara went to Ambala to her maternal aunt, who is employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital, and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. The appellant asked Russel Niel to bring to him Roshan Lal and when he was called, he told that if they wanted to save themselves they should make some settlement with him and demanded a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . But the appellant removed a golden ring from his finger. On the same night the appellant contacted the girl, Miss Eene and asked him to come to the house of N. K. Lal, P.W 11 and stayed there with her sister. The girl was then told that he never asked for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to RusselNathaniel. The accused threatened the girl and his wife to make arrangement for the bringing up of the child. Russel n Neniel replied that if he wanted to meet the appellant they should do some settlement. On being questioned the appellant told the D.S.P. that he had never asked him for bribe, and that money was not paid to them in repayment. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant of the charged under s.5(2), Prevention of corruption Act and section 5 (1)(d) of Prevention of 1947. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel, it cannot be said that the appellant has obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act, or for showing or forbiding to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any son. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. When a public servant is charged under Section 161 Indian penal Code and it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing and procuring an official act. When the public servant charged under S. 161 Indian I.P., it is said that illegal grafication was taking by him, for doing, or procuring an Official act, it is not essential for the court to consider, whether or whether the accused Public servant was incapable of doing any such an official function. [187 E] 3. When an accused is charged with under section 161 I.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He unsuccessfully appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence. The charge framed against him related to the same transaction which stated that the appellant had accepted Rs. 100 by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant. It was urged before the Special Judge as it was contended in the High court that certain statements made by the appellant in cross examination clearly showed that he had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction accorded by him was not a valid one. Held, that the sanction granted in this case was a valid sanction. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King (1948) L.R 75 I.A. 30, referred to. Gokul Chand Dwarkadash Moraraka vs The Queen ([1947] L. R. 75 I A. 30), distinguished. Gokul Chandra Dwarkadassa vs The State of West Bengal ([1950] S.C.R. 869), explained and distinguished. Held further that the sanctioning authority had applied his minds to the fact and circumstances in granting the certificate of fitness, but it was not for him to judge the truth of the allegations made against him by calling for the records of the connected claim cases or other records in connection with the matter from his office. Gokulchandra Dwarkadasi vs The Crown ([1948] L .R 75 1 I. A.30), distinguished and applied.

The appellant landlord was allowed to enjoy the rents and profits of the property for her life time subject to certain charges on account of his two sisters. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of the tenants. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the tenant against the orders of eviction and set aside the orders passed by the appellate authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that a single petition with regard to two different tenancies, though in the same premises one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purpose, was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard tO the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [276 E] 2. When the objection on the score of the landlord being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14 (1) (b) fails the suit must be decreed. It was contended that a tenant with a life interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fide. [277 F G] 3. The right between section K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others is not maintainable because the interest of the remainderman may be prejudiced. [278 D E] 4. When a suit for eviction is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the Act, it is outside the ken of this Act. Even a possible dispute, imaginary or real, between the landlord and the rest man cannot affect adjudication of the claim of the tenant landlord against his tenants under the provisions of the Act. [279 G] 5. The tenancy is one. In the result the appeals are allowed and the order of the High Court as well as that of the appellate Authority are set aside.

The respondent decree holder in the execution proceed ings in this very case between the same parties which came to this Court on an earlier occasion. This very question was raised by the respondent decree holders in the executing proceed ing proceedings in this Court between the parties which took the view that there was a distinction between trees and a grove and grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The position taken by the appellant decree holder then also was that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these are parts of the grove land. [34 C] In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts parts of grovees and groves and grove lands. The proposition is well settled that trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view Of this very legal position it is clear that under the general law, trees, after these clear words of the enactment.

The prosecution case was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju and PW5, both aged about 13 years at the time of occurrence. The trial court on the basis of prosecution evidence found accused No. 1 guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 6 were also convicted for offences under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324, 326 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against accused No 1 was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, it is directed that issue notice limited to the question as to the nature of offence and quantum of sentence. The case of the first appellant, therefore, falls within Section 299 IPC punishable under section 304 Part I IPC. The High Court acquitted accused No 2 and convicted the remaining four only. The appellants were also sentenced for offences punishable under Sections 147, 143, 341 and 323 read with section 149 IPC. On an appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) there was enmity between two groups on account of illicit distillation and suspicion of information being passed on to the Excise officials; (ii) no evidence was led in support of this allegation by the prosecution and no motive for commission of the crime was established at the trial. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The existence of an unlawful assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 I.P.C. [92G] 2.1 In a case like this to determine as to which of the accused is guilty of a particular offence. [93H; 94A] 2:2. The presence of an assembly is necessary postulate, for invoking section 149 I P.C., where the existence of such an unlawful unlawful assembly was not proved, the convic tion with the aid of Section 149 cannot be recorded or sustained. [94B C] 3:3. In a trial court all the six accused were charge sheeted for an offence under Section 307 read with Sec.149 IPC. other charges were also framed against the accused but only with the help of section 149, IPC. After the acquittal of the two accused, could the High court convict appellant No.1 for the substantive offence under section 302 I. P. C. and sentenced them to suffer imprisonment for a period of seven years and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 (five hundred). In default of payment of fine he shall further suffer rigorous imprison ment for a term of three months. Fine if realised shall be paid to the heirs of the deceased.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company, having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of five percent less the Indian tax had to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, it took the same stand. The I.T.O completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For these assessment years 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' plea that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. Its case was that there was 'no actual payment ' of royalty by the I. T.O. completed the assessments for the two assessment year 1969 70 on the ground that it had maintained its accounts as on mercantile basis alone and since no part of the royalty amount has been received by it, and therefore nothing is taxable. For this assessment year 1970 71 (year ending 30.9.1966) and 196869 (year ended 30. 9.1.1969) the assessee filed returns in which it stated that it maintained its account on mercantile system alone and accordingly brought to tax the royalty amounts disclosed. The Income Tax Officer held that it is maintaining its books on mercantile foundation alone and therefore brought to taxation the royalty money amount disclosed. He held that the assessee had not been following any particular method of accounting regularly over the past years. For assessment year 1971 70, however he refused accept the assesses 's plea that the I .T.Os. did never contest its liability to be taxed on the amounts disclosed and further that it has committed a mistake in filing the returns for the assessment year 1968 69 and 196869. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past periods relating to the asses see reveal that the method of accounts was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, the assessee did never dispute its liability on account of commission in the books of the I Company in favour of the assessee by incorporating the figures as per its profit and loss account, that the Indian company was not aware of the fact that the royalty should be assessed to income tax only on its actual receipt under section 5(2)(a) of the Act on the grounds that it maintains its accounts in regard to royalty amount on cash receipt basis. The Tribunal held that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assessment, 1967 68 & 1968 69 it has been maintaining its account books on cash foundation and since the assessee does not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Costventry. The High Court also held that though the Indian Companies made a credit entry in the account of the assesse in its Books, it did not actually received any royalty income in India, that it could not be said that the assesses had received the amount and that the amounts cannot be assessed until they were actually paid over to the non resident Company or dealt with according according to its directions. Dismissing the appeals by the assessee, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal was right in answering the question against the assessee. [102B] 1.2 In the instant case, admittedly, the agreement contemplated royalty amount being remitted in Sterling Currency currency to U.K., but it cannot be said in such a situation that he has not received the income in the India. [103C] C.I.T vs Macnzillan & Co., ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The third accused was acquitted and the fourth accused was convicted. On appeal, the High Court found corroboration in material particulars and against the appellant. Held, that though the conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in materials particulars. The law may be stated in the words of Lord Reading C. J., in R. vs Baskerville, (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, and R. v. Baskaville; , referred to. Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, (1947) L .R. 75 I. A. Mad, 307, distinguished. Bhsuboni Sahu 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction Of the first accused upon which he had been charged. Bhobbubonioni Sahu v The King (1949), L. R. 76 1. A, referred to and distinguished. Held further, that even though the appellant was acquitted on the evidence, his conviction was unsustainable, because, without corroboration of the approver 's story, the conviction was sustainable, as there should be corroboration of his accomplice in material facts and qua each accused. Bhunoni Sahu V. The King ([1949)L.R 76 I A. 324), referred to, Held further that though section 133 of the Evidence Act which provides that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in material details, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the terms of Martin B in Res. vs vs Boyes ([1924] L. A I.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961, the appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. On July 8. 1961, he was charged in the Court of Special Judge for an offence under section 6(2), read with s.5 (1) (d) and section 21 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The case of the prosecution was that the appellant committed these offences by obtaining a sum of Rs. 180/ for Sri A.D. Singh, Executive Engineer (Electrical) from Ramprit Singh, P.W. 2 by resorting to corrupt and illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as public servant. It was alleged that on the morning of July 6, 1961 the Electrical Executive Engineer, Sri A., D. Singh accompanied by his Head Clerk, the Appellant paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhas. Ramput Singh,P.W 2, along with other witnesses proceeded to the appellant 's office and handed over a petition to P. W. 11 Girjanandan Sinha expressing his apprehension that the Executive Engineer or his Head clerk would demand some bribe from him. It is alleged that the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.,W. 19 picked up the currency notes and upon comparison he found them to bear the same serial numbers which had been noted down in the statement exhibit 2. The Deputy Superintendent Of Police, who was then a public officer, accompanied by two witnesses proceeded with the appellant to the office of the Anti Corruption Department at Patna within two days and got the matter settled otherwise they would be put to a big loss. Thereafter P.Ws. 20 and 22 picked up currency notes from the floor below the table and made an attempt to get away but he was taken under arrest and after his person was searched the currency note notes were found lying on the floor near the seat. The appellant dropped the bundle of currency notes on the floors below the Table and made a attempt to secure away but the Deputy superintendent of Police P. Ws. 20, P,W. 16, P 19 and subsequently by the Inspector Shahidhar Putt, P W. 17 picked up a currency note and upon comparing it with the same in the statements exhibit 2, prepared a trap under section 161, Indian Penal code. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 165 (2) of I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal by the appellant, the Patna High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the Special judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that on a plain reading of section 81 of the the Indian Evidence Act, the officers and servants of the Board were deemed to be public servants only when acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the . HELD: (i) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal C.P., and therefore a 'public servant within section 2 of the prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1958. [687 E] (ii) Under this clause the words "corporation engaged in any trade or industry" include a banking, insurance 'or financial corporation, a river valley Corporation and a corporation for supplying power, light or water to the public. It cannot be brought within the scope of acting or purported purporting to do act in pursuant of any provisions of that Act. [688 G] (iii) The word "officer" in the Service or pay or of the Government within the terms of section 21(9), Indian penal Code is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty.

The appellant was tried and convicted under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Jowar (Restrictions on purchases and sale and control of movement) Order 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ . The sentences were directed to run concurrently. On appeal by special leave it was contended that r. 141(2) of Defence of india Rules 1962 is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. Rule 141(1)(ii) of Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964 authorises the Collector to seize stocks but does not enable the Court to forfeit the juar seized from the house of the appellant because, he says that the Maharashtra State Jowarsar (restrictions) Order 1965, it is illegal to maintain the order regarding forfeiture of the juwar seized from his house. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The order of the High Court maintaining the order of forfeiture was allegal and liable to be set aside. On the second point the learned counsel for the appellant contended that rule 141( 2) of 'the Defence of India Rules,1962 is ultra rites because it laid down a Rule of evidence contra to. the law in section 115 of the Evidence Act, that r . 141(ii) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of Indian Rules. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased Kunwar Singh was a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, Brijendra Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. They were proceeding on their bicycles and as they reached a spot near Barhpur Block, Violet was alleged to have shouted "the Vakil has come". Sia Ram and his companions who were hiding behind a Shisham tree came out and confronted Kunwar Singh and his associates. Sia, Ram Chandra and Shri Ram Chandra fired a shot from a point blank range as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down. All the accused thereafter ran away. The deceased Kunwar singh removed Kunwar Singh to a nursing home but the latter succumbed to his injury at 5 p.m. The other lawyer Om Prakash, Om Prakash Pandey, who stated in his evidence that he knew the deceased and was therefore able to identify him. The Sessions Court and the High Court accepted the evidence of Sia as against the appellant. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Si Ram and Violets. It dismissed the appeal filed by the State Government except in regard to Shri Ram whom it convicted under Section 302 read with section 109, and sentenced him to death, and dismissed the Appeal filed by State Government. Allowing the appeals of S, ^ HELD: 1. The question which then arises for consideration is whether the only inference which arises from the fact that violet gave the particular shout is that by so doing, she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh, Section 107 of the Penal Code which defines abetment provides to the extent material that a person abets the doing of a thing who "Intentionally aides, by any act or illegal omission, the doing Of that thing. " Explanation 2 to the section says that "Whoever either prior to or at the time of the commission of an act does anything in order to facilitate, the commission thereof is said to and the doing 'of that act". [626 F] 2. The words of SIA Ram must therefore be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission Of the crime. [627 C] 3.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted all the accused but on appeal by special leave, it was contended that when three of the four named accused were acquitted, they must have taken part in the murder. Held, that the conviction of the appellant was clearly wrong. In the first illustration the court certainly can convict two or more of the named accused if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence. But what is the position if the Court acquits 3 of the 4 accused either because it rejects the prosecution evidence or because it gives the benefit of doubt to the said accused ? Can it hold, in the absence of a charge as well as evidence , that though the three accused are acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointaneously with one of the said named persons ? If the Court could do so, it would be making out a new case for. the prosecution : it would not be deciding contrary to the evidence adduced in the case. Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 848, relied on. Mohan Singha vs State Of Punjab, A.I.R., 1959 S. C. 849 and Mohan Singh V. State of U.P., ; , referred to. Mohan vs State, A, I. R. , distinguished. Mohan singh vs State o/S.

The petitioner, a foreign supplier of MSCR defective sheets or coils, was granted import licence for the supply of MAIR defective sheets and coils on 30th May 1984. The petitioner placed order on M/s Metalic metal Indus tries Pvt. Ltd., Singapore for the supplies of MSCC defective sheets/coils on the 30th July, 1984. It may be mentioned that the rate of duty on the day was 60% + 40% + Rs.650 per M.T. and 10% CV.D. at Rs.325 per M.; addl. duty 45% and C.V. D. at RS.325 p.m. The total duty came to a very large sum of money. The demand, according to the petitioner, was arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional. The instant writ petition was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April,1988 this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective Sheets/coilils" which have arrived at Bombay Port per S.S.SEA. until further orders." The petitioner asserted that he was ever ready and willing, rather was anxious, to get the material on payment of the then prevailing customs duty. However, due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner the petitioner 's, that it to say, by the order of the Income Tax Authorities, the goods could not be released.

The appellant was the Managing Director of a bank. The respondent No. 1 sold the property to respondents Nos. 2 to 4 who were respondents 2 to 8. The sale was confirmed on June 23, 1943, and the purchaser was section N. Borkar, respondent No, 7, now respondent No 1. The question for decision in this appeal was whether the debt of the father was avyavaharika or otherwise. Held, that the liability of the sons to discharge the debts of the respondent No., 1 under Hindu law is not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the whole coparconary estate including the share of the son and it is equally open to his creditors to proceed against it; but this was subject to the sons having a right to challenge the alienation or protest against a creditor proceeding against their shares on proof of illegal or immoral purpose of the debt. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyvavahaayarika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals ". In the present case the payment order was made by the Deputy Registrar on April 21, 1942, and after the order had been sent to the Collector for recovery, the property was attached on April 24, 1942.
