The notice of sale was issued on November 24,1942, and was published under sections 165 and 166 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. The proclamation of sale in respect of the whole bungalow was dated December 12, 1942; it was sold on January 25, 1943. The property put up for sale was plot No. 36 D measuring 6 acres and one Guntha and its value was specified as 13,000 rupees. There was a note added that no guarantee was given of the title of the said respondent or of the validity of any of the rights, charges or interests claimed by third parties. The order confirming the sale also showed that the whole property was sold. It was valued at Rs. 16,000 and there was a mortgage of Rs. 2,000 against it and what was sold and confirmed by this order was the whole house.

The petitioners, who are both guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends. They are alleged to have been engaged in the business of lawyers and who constituted two important parts of society. The question whether a party has the right of cross examination or not shall be decided by the Committee in accordance with section 8 C of the Act. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 In order to avoid any further delay in the proceedings before the Committee consisting of Goswamy and Wadhwa, JJ., constituted by Order dated 23rd February 1988 to enquire into certain incidents which took place on the 15th January, 1988, 2nd January,1988 and 17th February, 1988. [5H; 521A] 1.2 The orders of the Committee directing the filing of complaints and the criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf of the committee should be quashed and the said orders of that Committee and also the criminal proceeding. [525C D] 2.1 The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section 8 B of the Commissions of Inquiry Act, which are issued to be examined at the end of the inquiry. [500D E] 2:2 In the instant case, the petitioners have been alleged to be engaged in business of Advocates and who were both guardians on whom notices under section 13B of the , are issued have to be exammed at the conclusion of the enquiry. The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B of that Act before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined.

The petitioners who were seven in number challenged the Act on the grounds, inter alia, that they were not liable to pay tax under the Act as it was optional and involve payment of tax even when no passengers or goods are transported. Held, that the levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The levy of a lump sum leads to the result that even if passengers or Goods are not transported but the tax is payable, is of any force, because there may be days when the business done might result in tax in excess of the lump sum payable. The word "shall" is ordinarily mandatory, but it is sometimes not so interpreted if the context or the intention otherwise demands. In re Rustom (3) Bom. 396; Jethaji Peraji Firm vs Krishnayya (1929) I.L.R. , and Atma Ram Budhia vs State of Bihar, [1952] 1 S.C.R., 31 Pat 493, relied on. The power to fix lump sum in lieu of tax has been conferred upon Government without guidance, and is therefore unconstitutional. It was not necessary to refer to them beyond Rules 8 and 8 A which have been challenged. Rule 8 prescribes the method of payment of a tax by means of stamps to be affixed to the tickets, and the second proviso is to the following effect: "Provided further that the tax payable under the . Act on fare by the owner of a motor cycle, rickshaw or a motor cab shall be paid to the State Government in lump sum, of which the amount shall be fixed by the State Govt. from time to time by Notification in this behalf." The word 'shall ' is ordinarily directory but it was sometimes not intended so interpreted as to leave the tax untouched by the Rules. The Act and the Rules are further challenged on the ground that they are repugnant to articles 301, 304 and 304 as being a restriction upon inter State trade, commerce and intercourse, to article 19 as involving an unreasonable restriction upon the business of the petitioners, and also to article 14 as discriminating between this mode of transport and the Railways. The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers and goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. No doubt it falls upon persons and goods proceeding to or from an extra State point but it does not cease to be a tax on passengers and Goods. It is limited only to the fare and freight proportionate to the route within the state.

% The appellant company, a private limited Company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry, served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity power, power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week, and the mounting loss. Subsequently negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. Simultaneously, the workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the Appellant pleaded its inability in view of the mountings and falling production for want of raw material and persistent power shedage. The Tin Workers ' Union, Ghaziabad, espoused the cause of such retrenched workmen and ultimately the Government of Uttar Pradesh by its notification dated 9th october 1974 issued in exercise of the power conferred by Section 4 K of the U.P. lndustrial Disputes Act 1947 referred the industrial dispute arising out of retrenchment of 43 workmen between the parties for adjudication to the Labour Court. The appellant contended that the workmen were sought back wages from 1st August, 1974 and the Labour court had directed their reinstatement effective from that date. The Labour Court by its award directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1 st August, 1975 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The Appellant challenged the Award in this appeal. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The relief of reinstatement with continuity in service can be granted where termination of service is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived workman of his earnings. If the workmen are always ready to work but they were kept away on account of invalid act of the employer, there is no justification for not awarding them full back Wages which were very legitimately due to them. A Division Bench of the High Court in Dhari Gram Panchayat vs Safai Kamldar Mandal [1959] Suppl. 2 SCR 136 at 140 held that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief of reinstate must follow, has become final. Under no pretext or guise it could now be re opened. Before dealing with the contentions in this Appeal, it is necessary for this Court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where Awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman) [1959]] Suppl. 1 SCR 136), Management of Paniltole Tea Estate vs The Workmen, ; , Management of Parlakonto Tea Estate v The Workmen; and Management of M/s. Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co operative Society Ltd. vs Labour Court 11, Lucknow & Ors., ; referred to. 1.2. In the instant case, the relief granted by the Labour Judge was justified in awarding full backwages to the workman on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that it was actuated and the reliefs of reinstatement must follow. [567F] 2.1 The view taken therein is correct. The view of gets support from the decision of this court in workman of Calcutta Dock Labour Board & Anr. Employers in relation to Calcutta Dock labour Board & Ors.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the material on record was not sufficient to justify the conviction of the accused appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The confession made by the accused to him must be held inadmissible in evidence. [434 C] (2) It is well established that a magistrate of a higher class is prevented from giving oral evidence of a confession made to him because thereby the safeguards created for the benefit of an accused person by section 164 would be rendered nugatory, it would be an unnatural construction of the section to hold that these safeguards were not thought necessary and could be ignored, where the confession bad been made to a magistrate other than the accused. [427 D E] (3) The fact that the accused alone was with Churi deceased in the house when she was murdered there with the Khokhri and the fact that he had gone to see film show, it will not have taken more than 10 or 437 minutes 'for the accused, to return 'to his house after the film show. [334 C D] (4) The evidence of the approver shows that the appellant was with the deceased at his house on the day of occurrence. Mani Ram (PW 8), who is the uncle (1 A.I.R. 1966 A.P. 131) and Bhagat Ram school teacher (PW 16). Ac cording to Bhagat Ram, he saw the accused and the deceased together at their house on that evening and with which the injuries on the body of the deceased according to Dr. Gupta could have been caused. Besides that it is established by the evidence of Girju PW 1 that the appell lant suspected the fidelity of Churiuri deceased and believed that Joginder had been born to her as a result of his adulterous conduct. Had Joginder been the son of the appellant, the accused would have had a natural affection for the child and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child.

The plaintiff 's father obtained a preliminary decree for sale of a part of the mortgaged property, 20 Round Tank Lane and 20 Rung tank Lane. The mortgage was exe cuted on the 12th June 1936 in favour of one Mst. Gyarsi for a consideration of Rs. 80,000. For convenience I will call this the suit mortgage though this is not a suit on the mortgage. The mortgagee sued in the year 1938 and obtained a final decree for the sale on the 17th February 1939 for a sum of Rs 89,485 12 plus costs. The plaintiff claimed that he was entitled to receive the balance of Rs 79,744 4 from the two defendants and that each of them was liable for a half of that sum namely Rs. 39,872 3 8. The total claim against each defendant accord ingly came to Rs. 40,253 11 10 plus costs and that the plaintiff had incurred costs amounting to Rs 1,144 8 in resisting Mst. Rungarsi 's claim and in connection with the reconveyance. He also claimed one third share of this sum, namely Rs., Rs. 36,250 12 from each of the defendants. The balance of the amount due at the date of the mortgage from the three of them. There was no contract between them either in the mortgage deed or otherwise regarding their respective shares of responsibility in the Rs. 10,000 and C jointly mortgage their three estates for Rs. 20,000, the total aggregate sum due at that date were Rs. 30,000 to that extent. The defendants did not deny their liability to contribute. They only challenged the basis on which it was to be comput ed. They also set up a case which had failed on the facts. Held, further, that section 43 of the Contract Act applied and the suit was maintainable. Rani Chhatra Kumari vs Mohan Bikram (1917) I.L.R. , approved.

The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks from Karnataka Univer sity. The Govt. of Karnataka by notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil). The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the qualifying examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment) Rules, 1973. According to these rules total marks for qualifying examination were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. The applications were invited for 300 posts of Civil Engineers and 100 Mechanical Engineers initially and subsequently added additional posts of 150 Civil Engineers. Both the appellants applied for the posts of their choice in Public Works Department, Government of Karnataka. Appellant No.1 secured 29.50 marks out of 50 marks in the written examination thus in all 99.23 marks out to 150. The 2nd appellant obtained 24.83 marks in interview and 66.40 marks in his qualifying examination thus, in all 91.23 candidates out of 150.23 mark out of 151.24 marks out were 150. Both appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33. 3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court, the selection was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, therefore, they are bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellant. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. It is not necessary to examine 'the matter in detail inasmuch as the question involved in the instant case is whether the percentage awarded for viva l voce as33.3 were excessive or in violation thereof, and in any event, the selections on the above ground are liable to be quashed on the aforesaid ground. [495B C] Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on 11th April, 1983 when the deceased came on the landing, Yadav who was following them suddenly took out a bomb from the bag which he held and threw it at the Collector. The bombs exploded with a loud noise and as a result of the burst Mahesh Prasad fell rolling on the ground and part of his body was blown off. Yadav jumped off from the stairs through the side railing but was chased by P.W.62 and others and was apprended near a fruit stall. He made an order under the Crime Control Act, detain ing Sadanand in jail. Eviction proceedings from the en croached land had already been undertaken. On 14th July, 1982 the Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed on behalf of the Ashram and on 15th July 1982 the entire structure of the Trust was demolished under the direct supervision of the Collector and it was not disputed that from July,1982 Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder on 11.4.1983. In view of this fact, the prosecution has relied upon the allegation of conspiracy, confession and other features to establish the complicity of Sadanand. In these circumstances, the judicial confession has to be kept out of considerations. [408D E] The extra judicial confession is not substantive evidence against the other co accused persons at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. In Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State of Bihar, ; this Court observed that in dealing with a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have oc curred. P.S. Appeals dis posed of.

The appellants were the workmen of a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson (Works) India Limited and its main business was to manufacture oil engines and pumps. The last three companies were controlled by the first company, namely Greaves Cotton and Co., in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were nine awards though the main award dealing with the main controversy relating to wage and dearness allowances was common. It appears that wages and Dearness Allowance prevalent in the four companies had been continuing since 1950 when the last award was made between the parties. The main dispute which gave rise to the references was with respect to wages, dearness allowance and gratuity. The Tribunal dealt with clerical and subordinate staff separately from the factory workmen. So far as the clerical and subordi nate staff are concerned, the Tribunal after a comparison of wages and wage scales prevalent in comparable concerns revised them, held that it was not feasible to do so, though looking at the financial stability of the appellants, emoluments needed upgrading. It further ordered that the award would have effect from April 1, 1959 which was a week before the first reference was made with respect ' to the first Company. The High Court also rejected the contention of the appellant that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and the dearness allowance had not been properly applied by the tribunal and it had been carried away by the recommendations of the tripartite conference which suggested need based minimum wages. It was urged on behalf of the appel lants that the tribunal had gone wrongly in applying that formula which is the basis of fixation of wages, and that the High Court erred in not following the industry Cum region principle and in leaning on the recommendations made by the Tripartite Conference which suggested that the workmen based their claim on them and wanted that the matter should be remanded to the Tribunal for fixing the same rates of dearness allowance for factory workmen dividing them into six categories as at present and then fixing wage after taking into account wages prevalent in similar concerns. Held, further, that the principles laid down in the French Motor Car Co. 's case were more applicable to the present case than the principles enunciated in the English French Motor car Co. The French Motor Company vs Their Workman, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 379, relied on.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, executed a usufructuary mortgage (Ex. D 51) in favour of one M and his son Mallappa Tukaram Borgavi for Rs. 1,300 made up of Rs.1,100 due under a previous mortgage and Rs. 200 presently advanced in cash. That deed provided that the mortgage money would be repaid within a period of three years and that the mortgagors would pay the judi and incur the expenses of the Nand Deep and that on failure of the mortgagors to meet the said out goings, the mortgagees would incur the said expenses and add the same to their claim on the mortgage. On March 10, 1900, Shiddha alone executed a simple mortgage (exhibit D 52) for Rs., 600 in favour Of M and another part of the consideration for this simple mortgage consisted of moneys borrowed by both the brothers on bonds executed by both of them. This simple mortgage deed provided : " The mortgagees would bear the expenses incurred by the Nand Kishore and that upon failure of you to meet this out goats, the defendants would incur their said expenses, add the amount also under the simple mortgage and that, on failure, the mortgagors will incur the aforesaid expenses and added the same in their possession. On April 10, 1924, Shidappa and Annappa died without any issue. The mortgagee Lalchand died issueless and the mortgagee died leaving a son named Lilachand Tuljaram who became entitled to the entire mortgage securities. On November 1, 1937, the appellants applied to the Mamlatdar alleging that the mortgaged property was Devasthan Inam and praying for the cancellation of the transfer in favour favour of the mortgagees and for placing the mortgaged properties in his name. The trial court held that by the Rajinama dated May 5,1900, the Raj inama had not extinguished the title of the appellants in the mortgaged land and that as the mortgages were subsisting, the respondents could not acquire title by adverse possession. In appeal to the District Court, Belgaum, the High Court dismissed both the appeals. The present appeal was filed on special leave granted by this Court. Held: (i) On a correct interpretation of section 74(1), where there are more occupants than one in respect of the same occupancy each occupant has his own rights and the fact of registration of one of them as the registered occupant attracts the operation of the Code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupants as laid down in the Code but does not take away the rights of other occupants. It is true that if any of the occupants other than the registered owner desires to relinquish his occupancy, he cannot himself give a notice of relinquishment but must give it by and through the registered tenant occupant. But where there were more occupants between one, the notice of relinquished on behalf of any occupant must be given by the registered occupation also supports the contention that the Rajnama passed by the Registered occupant binds all the occupants.

The respondent company which was a company incor pated under the Indian Companies Act dealing in carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, stepler machines and steplers, despatches the said goods from its head office at Bombay to its branch office at Kanpur wherefrom sales there of are effected in the State of Uttar Pradesh. During the course of the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the aforesaid Notification but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6% prescribed in the aforesaid notification. The Sales Tax Officer taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 6%. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the same and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In popular parlance, the word 'paper ' is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing or printing, or for packing, orfor drawing on, or on for decorating, or cover ing the walls. Now carbon paper which is manu (1 ) [1831] 2 Dow & Clark=k 302; , referred to. (2) In the popular parlance the word "paper" in the common parlance means paper which was used for printing, writing and packing pur poses. [838E F] (3) The word ' Paper ' in the Common parlance or in the com criminatory sense means paper, which is use ed for printing. writing or packing pur posees. It is, therefore, necessary to know what is paper as commonly or generally understood. [889B C] (4) In our opinion, carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by Entry 2 of Notification No. ST 3124/X 1012(4) dated 1st July 1966 issued under section 3 A of the U.P.

The respondents purchased a building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at the Sugar Mills at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the owners of the appellant Mills at the sugar mills at Bulandshahr. In 1951, the partners of the appellants Mills purchased the building machinery, and other assets of another Sugar Mill at Kiccha in the district of Nainital. They closed the said mill at Kikcha and started it at Bulandshahr in Bulandshahr. The new factory was named Pannijee Sugar & General Mills, Bulandshahr. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager served a notice on the respondents 1, to 4 stating that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under the Standing Order. The Labour Union by its letter dated January 31, 1955 denied the charges. On February 2, 1955 the General manager served a show cause notice on respondents 1 and 4 stating: (i) that they have disobeyed the orders of transfer; (ii) that the interim bonus for last year at Amroha would be probably equal to II months wages and at Bulandshahr equal to about 4 or 5 days ' wages. The respondent No. 5, perferred an appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India and the said Appellate Tribunal held that the management had no right to transfer the respondents I to 4 to the new factory and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. The management appealed against the said order of the Labour Court. The Industrial Tribunal held (i ) that both the concerns, i.e., the mills at Amroha and the mills formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1950; (2) that both tile concerns, namely, the Mills ateted and the Mills formed one single unit, and the Appellate Tribu nal had no juris diction to set it aside that findings under section L(A); (3) that in view of proper organisation of their staff it was difficult to assume that the Bank would willingly agree that their employees should not he bound to serve outside the place where the contract was made except with their consent, and in their Lordships ' opinion such a condition of the contract would require to be clearly established. Held: (1) The workmen at Amroha are entitled to benefits under the Kaul Award while those at Bulandshahr are not so entitled. The question whether the appellant had the right to the transfer of the respondents from one concern to another was really to make a new contract between them. The decision assumed that the business was one unit and that the only question raised was that he should not have been transferred to a place different from the place when he was actually discharging his duties. (2)(a) A substantial question of law involved in the case and that it was well within the powers of the Tribunal to entertain the appeal.

The appellant company was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The contribution payable under Chapter VA of the Act was to be such percentage, not exceeding five per cent of the total wage bill of the employer, as the Central Government may specify. It was provided that the employer 's special contribution in the case of factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions Of both Chapters IV and V are in force shall be fixed at a rate higher than that in the ease of factories and establishments situate in areas where the provisions o the said Chapters are not in force. The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in the cases of sickness, maternity and employment injury and to make provision for certain other matters in relation thereto. It also provided that (1) establishment and maintenance of hospitals, dispensaries and other institutions and the provisions thereof of medical and other ancillary services for the benefit of insured per sons and where the medical benefit is extended to their families; (2) establishment & maintenance of hospital, dispensaries, and other institution and the provision of such medical benefit to their family in accordance with the provisions. of this Act and defraying the charges and costs in connection therewith; and (3) . . . (4) establishment, and maintenance Of hospitals, dispensary, dispensaries or other institutions, and the provi sions of medical treatment and attendance to insured persons and where medical benefit was extended to them. The appellant company challenged the vires of Chapter VI A of , on the ground that it was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contribution payable by the appellant under Chapter VIA was a tax, fee or neither it had sufficient constitutional protection; and that the provisions were ultra vires. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1 ) The scheme of Chapter IV A of 'the Act is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. Merely because the benefits to be received are postponed, it cannot be said that there was no quid pro li quo. [1093 B C] (2 ) The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It is not fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contribution and thereby help to set up a corporation.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they were discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such, there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a continuous long time. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the ordinary workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked from him. [620G] 1.2 The principle in regularisation of the daily wage rated workmen and payment "to him" of the wages equal to the that of regular workman arise only when a dailyrated workman is doing, the same Work as the normal workman and therefore there being no vacancy available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners, and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid in spite of there being any work available for them.

The appellants were the purchasers of a tea estate. They claimed title to and recovery of possession of a property known as the Azambad Tea Estate which comprised about 378 acres of land in Touzi No. 911 of the Darjeeling Collectors. The contesting defendants were the Azamabad Tea Co. Ltd., who was also a full owner of the 16 as. share of the property mortgaged. The claim to have obtained the full title to the Tea Estate was resisted by the appellants on various grounds, namely, (i) that by reason of the renewal of the lease in 1928 in the name of Ismail and the entry of his name as sole lessee in the revenue records, the leasehold became his sole property; (ii) that the plaintiffs ' suit was liable to be dismissed for default. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court as regards the rest. In appeal by certificate: Held:(i) The contention that section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act afforded no defence to the defendants, and that the bar imposed by it would be rendered meaningless if the plaintiff whose suit was dismissed for non default had only to transfer the property to another and the latter was able to agitate rights which his vendor was precluded by law from putting forward. (ii). The rule would obviously have no value and the bar placed by it will be rendered nugatory if the plaintiffs whose suit is dismissed for ' default had merely to transfer, the property in execution of a decree is only the right title and interest of the judgment debtor and nothing more. (iii) Even assuming that the sale deeds exhibit 12(i), and 12(c) on which the claim was based were filed in the trial Court, and Pir Baksh who was examined as a witness admitted this fact. The plaintiffs did not raise any specific ground touching their right to this share nor did they raise any objection before the courts below that the suit property was sold under exhibit 12 (i). (iv) Even if the sale deed were proved to have been executed it was a sham and nominal transaction and therefore inoperative to pass title.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad. The trial court convicted and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court dismissed all the appeals and confirmed the convictions and sentences passed against all the four accused persons. Held, that the omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions of section 162 or section 360 of the Code. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (1947) L.R. 55 I.A. 96 and Pulukuri Kotayya & Ors. vs King Emperor ([1929] L. R. 55 1. A. 96), referred to. In cases exclusively triable by a court of Session, it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself that the documents referred in section 173 had been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. After considering the relevant provisions of the code, their Lordships came to the conclusion that it was a mere irregularity which could be cured by the provisions Of section 537 of the Criminal Procedure Code and that the irregularity was curable by reference to section 537(a) of the Cr. P.C., as no case of prejudice had been made out. Abdul Rahim vs The State of Punjab ([1952] S.C.R, referred to and distinguished. In the instant ease the facts as stated above were extremely simple. It was a case of either believing or disbelieving those two eye witnesses. As already indicated, all the accused persons including the appellant were named at the earliest opportunity in the first information report which was lodged without any avoidable delay within a few hours after the occurrence. The courts below have preferred to rely upon the testimony of the two eye witness, corroborated by the circumstantial evidence referred to above.

The respondent Municipality, after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955. The appellant replied that the effluent was being discharged until 1943 through a Katcha Channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad. In 1944 it was felt that as the water of some of the wells in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent, which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas. still further away from the city which lies on the western side of the railway lines whereas the factory is at a great distance away on the eastern side of railway lines. It was pointed out that during the last 3 or 4 years periodical surveys of the water, of various wells in a city had been taken by the appellant and these tests had shown that the water was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluent being discharged through the existing channels, that all the papers and reports relating to the tests carried out periodically by the respondent Municipality were available for inspection by the Municipality and that they could be inspected by appointment. The Special Officer held that the question whether the discharge of the effluents from the factory of the respondent company was polluting water and adversely affected the fertility of the soil was one for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality, and was beyond the scope of the enquiry before him. He accordingly dismissed the petition. On appeal by special leave: Held: (i) The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned.

The appellant was charged with the offence of committing an offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case was that the appellant failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. On the strength of some information received on 28th July 1964 that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police searched the premises of the motor transport company at Lucknow and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a railway engine. The usual formality of preparing a recovery memo and the sealing of goods in bags in the presence of witnesses was gone through. One Jaswant Singh, described as an expert of Railway machinery parts and Foreman and Chief Inspector of N.E.E., Kotwali Chowk, Lucknow examined the goods said to be railway stores and kept in 11 bags and made reports to the Government effect that these were all Railway stores being part of a Railway engine. It was the case for the prosecution that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 2 did not arise. The trial court found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) In order to prove that the goods belong to any particular Railway administration it has to establish that the article were the property of a ' railway administration. Evidence to the extent that the 'goods conformed to the specifications of the Indian Railway Standards they held that they belonged to any of the railways in India. [188 C] (ii) The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Again the mere description of the ' goods as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 1(b).

The appellants had leave under 9 Article 136 of the Constitution to appeal against the judgment and decree of the High Court of Rajasthan at Jaipur Bench in Second Appeal No 240 of 1978 dated July 5, 1985 reversing the decrees of the Courts below and decreeing the suit for ejectment of the appellants from the demised shop in Jaipur. The appellants during her life time had not carried on the business with her till date of her death. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Anandi was the tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control of Rent and Eviction) Ordinance 26 of 1975 which was replaced by Act 14 of 1976 introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "tenant" means the person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and 10 (b) In the event of death of the person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the ease of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally carried on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. " The appellants amended the written state ment adding therein paragraphs Nos. 16 and 17 contending that they have been jointly carrying on the businesses alongwith Smt. A.N. Sen, J. speaking for the Court held that Smt Anandi, the appellants did not carry on business in the demised premises alongwith Smt A. N. Anand i Bai, therefore, they are entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. The amendment was allowed by the Appellate Court and it called for a finding from the Trial Court in that regard. After giving an opportunity to both the parties to adduce evidence afresh the Court recorded the finding in negative. On its receipt and consideration thereof the appellate court confirmed the finding but confirmed the decree of Trial Court on other grounds. The High Court held, that as the appellants had not com pany carried on their business with the tenant during her lifetime time as family business they were not entitled to continue in occupation of the demised Premises premises. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment of the Appellate court, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Amending Act does not apply to the facts of this case. But the appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the tenanted premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to t he rights in favour of the respond ent created under Section 13(1)(a) to (k) and other provisions of the Act.

The appellant Board maintained a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contributing equally. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Industrial Tribunal held that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the State Government is the financier of the Electricity Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4% per annum and that the services of the workers of the company are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies would be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. HELD: 1. The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should have looked into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities, the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. [44C D] 2. The decision might very often depend on a close analysis of the financial condition of the Company. It has made no effort to work out the financial implications of its order. It had not made it clear what exactly are the total wages.

The respondent, who is the wife of the appellant filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate held that the appellant was physically incapable of having sexual relations with the respondent, and dismissed the application filed by the respondent for maintenance. Thereafter, the matter was taken up in revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that having regard to the means of the husband he was in a position to pay Rs. 150/ per month by way of maintenance to the respondent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contention of the counsel for the appellant is sound and must prevail. It is true that there are several decisions of the High Courts taking a contrary view but they seem to have proceeded on a totally wrong assumption and we are constrained to observe that in taking such a narrow view they have followed a most outmoded and antiquated approach. The learned Magistrate mainly relied on a decision of the Allahabad High Court in Smt. Mahrul, found that the mere ground that the husband was impotent was not a just cause for the refusal of the wife to live with her husband and hence the wife is not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live alongwith the husband merely because her husband had been impotant and unable to perform his marital obligation. [707C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the High court has taken a contrary decision but they have proceeded to follow the same view. The decisions of this Court in Dr. Srikant Rangacharya vs Smt. Anuradha Sijhawan, ; , relied on by the counsel are purely obiter and self explanatory and takes within its fold not only the two instances mentioned therein but other circumstances also of a like or similar nature which may be regarded by the Magis trate as a just ground by the wife for refusing to livewith her husband. [700G H] 1:3 The contention that the various authorities of the Bombay High Courts seem to had overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 Cr. P.C., is sound, and must be prevail. [608A B] 2.1 In the context of the changing status of woman in society such a proposition would seem outdated and obsolete. The concept of mental cruelty cannot be different in a civil case and in a criminal case when the attributes of such a cruelty are the same. In the matter of the Petition of Din Mohammed, Mahmood, J.

The plaintiff respondent Municipality filed a suit for declaration of its title and possession of the suit property described in the schedule to the plaint. The defendants pleaded that by virtue of these orders, the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint had been vested in the Municipality, that the structures in the land covered by the Survey numbers referred to in part 2 of the Schedule to the Plaint did not belong to the plain tiff, that barracks and other military build ings used for accommodation of the Ex Bhavnagar state forces known as Lancer 's Lines were in existence for a long time prior to 1948 in the suit land property known as Rasala Lines and that consequent upon the Bhavnagar State acceding to the Indian Union and consequent on the Federal Financial Integration of States, accommodation lands and buildings in the use or occupation of the ex state forces were transferred to the Government o[ india and became its property. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit lands and that they were in possession in the said suit property till 7th July 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Gov ernment of India to the State Public Works Department of the State of Saurashtra, and since the suit was filed on 3rd March 1964, the suit had been not barred under section 65 of the Limita tions Act, 1963. However, on the ground that in respect of Rasala Line the plaintiff has admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they were not entitled to recover possession of lands covered by Survey numbers de scribed in the second part of the schedule of the plaint to the plaintiff. Accordingly, the Trial Court decreed in respect o fendants 'Parade and Rasala lines.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshop Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code for having induced the said Nanak Singh to deliver to him currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 by dishonest representation that he could secure a job for the said Kallu. The Special judge, State of Ajmer convicted him of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same. Both the sentences were to run concurrently. In appeal by certificate the appellant contended that he was an "officer" within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal code, and therefore a public servant be fell within the definition of a public 'public servant contained in section 2 of the Act II of 1947. Held, that the appellant was an officer within the terms of section 1(9) and therefore he was not an "Officer". The word "officium" in the service or pay of Government" within section 21 of the Indian Penal Act is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some pulice duty. In this sense, the peon would come within section 2 Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act II Of 1947 and therefore the appellant could not be convicted of the offense under section 165(1) (d) Of the Act 11 of 1947 as he was employed as an "workman" in service or paid by Government to do public work.

The Respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The licences paid a sum of Rs. 86,450 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated reminders. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. Excise and Taxation Department, Patiala issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the Respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share of the respondent in the said property was notified for June 14, 1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the auction sale the Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C, being Suit No. 472/13 77 against the State of Punjab and the collector cum Deputy Excise and the Taxation Commissioner, Patiala Division, for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collec tor from auctioning his said half share. The contention of the Respondent was that a part of the building standing on the said plot of Land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and therefore his half portion was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The Respondent then filed an appeal before the District Judge, Patiala, being Civil Appeal No. 554 of 5.9.79. The Additional District Judge dismissed it with costs but the respondent approached the Punjab and Haryana High Court in second appeal, being Regular Second Appeal No 294 1 of 1980. The learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the property used for residence was exempt under clause(ccc)(c)of the proviso of sub section to Section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent order restraining the state and the Commissioner cum Deputy Collector from auction ing his said one half share and dismissed it so far as it related to the portion in Which the liquor shops was situated. The parties were further directed to bear their own costs. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 60 has no application to an attachment and sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said section is concerned it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provision of the aforesaid Act. [848E F] 1.2 The opening words of sub Section (I) of section 60 are "The following property is liable to attachment and sales in execution of a decree".

The respondent, a Hindu widow and the 'accountable person ' filed before the respondent on December 26, 1963 on account of the properties passing on the death of her husband under section 53(3) of the Land Acquisition Act. The estate duty assessment was completed by the respondent in March 1966. With regard to the lands acquired both during the lifetime of Rashid as well as after their values 320 were taken at the respective figures of compensation (Rs. 20,000 and Rs. 4,29,360) awarded for them by the Special Deputy Collector. On receipt of information that enhanced compensation was awarded by the Civil Court in respect of the above lands the respondent issued two notices both dated November 14, 1969 one addressed to Mrs. Khorshed Shapoor Chenai and the other to Mrs Freny Rashid Chenai. The notice under section 59(a) of Act calling upon Mrs. FrenY Chenai to show cause why the estate duty assessed on December 30, 1966 should not be reopened and revised in view of the extra compensations awarded by Land Acquisition officer in respect thereof by Rs. 1,90,000 for the lands acquisition acquired by the Government while the latter notice was issued under section 61 of the Act requiring Mrs. G. Khonshed Chenai (the appellant in C.A. No. 2205/1972) as his widow and son filed before tho respondent on November 6, 1965 on account Of the properties passed on the died of her deceased husband under Section 53(1) of that Act. Since the former notification was issued during his lifetime and the latter after death possession of both the lands was taken after his death by the government on December 4, 1963 and March 15, 1964 and by two separate awards both made on January 31, 1963 the Special Dy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20 lakhs. This compensation was received in April 965 by the heirs of Rashid, namely, his widow Mrs. Hreny Chenai, and son Shapakoor Rashid Chekata. The respondent as well the High Court upheld the impugned notice. Hence these two appeals by certificate granted by the High court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 Under section 11 of the Collector after holding the necessary inquiry determines the quantum of compensation by fixing the market value of the land and in doing so is guided by the provisions contained in sections 23 and 24 of Act the very provisions by reference to which the Civil Courts fixes the valuation. It is also true that under section 26 of the , the Collector 's award is, under section 12, declared to be, except as otherwise provided, final and conclusive evidence as between him and the persons interested. Even so, it is well settled that in law the Collector"s award under section 11 is nothing more than an offer of compensation made by the Govern ment to the claimants whose property is acquired (vide Privy Council decisions in Ezra vs Secretary of State for India and this Court 's decision in Raja Harish Chandra vs Dy. Land Requisition Officer and Dr. G H. Grant vs State of Bihar, [1971] 2 S.C.R. 891; Commissioner of Wealth Tax West Bengal vs Hindustan Housing and Land Development Trust Ltd., , referred to.

The appellant, a Director of the Bank, was elected as Director of a Cooperative Society. The notice stated that he had borrowed a loan from the Bank and he kept the loan constant in arrears till 21.10.1986 and being elected as Directors of the bank on 18.8.86. He was removed from the Committee of Directors of respondent Bank on 18 8.1.1987, and he was elected on 18th August 1986. The appellant 's election was not called in question under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, as it had been accepted that he paid the dues on 21. 10.1986, on 188.1986. The Assistant Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 79(1), of the Act to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from its Board of Directors as per the provisions of Section 73FF and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 1167 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The said notice stated: "That you have remained in arrars of the loan instalments as referred above to the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank, under section 73FF(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960 and order No. CSL/1481/24982/15 C(87) dated 1.7.1981 of Agriculture and Cooperation Department of Maharashtra Government. I, K.M., Deshpande District Dy Registrar, Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur, hereby ask you to show Cause in writing as to what he should be removedfrom the Board of directors of the said Bank. Your explanation in writing should be submitted to this office within 15 day from the receipt of this notice. " The appellant showed cause and also filed an additional reply on 10.11.87 stating that he "had not committed any default after the amended section 73F came into existence". The Assistant Regisrar, Cooperative Society, Chandrapur by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the committee of Directors holding that appellant was defaulter on 31.1 .1986, and rejected the appellant ' s contention that section 73 FF became applicable from 6.8 1986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.86 and that as he had accepted that the appellant paid the amount on 21 10.10., 1986 on 18, 8.86 when he was declared elected as director, he was defaulter under Section 73 FFF(I) of The Maharashtra State cooperative Societies Act. 1960 and rejected his contention that Section 73F became attracted from 6 8.81986 as per G.O. issued on 19.4.86, and that since the appellant had repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 80 FF(1). The order of the Assistant Registrar dated 7 12 1987 was served on the appellant on 8.12 .87. The appeal against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of the Cooperative Societies Nagpur on 15.2 1988 holding, inter alia, that Section 78FF became applicable and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The Appellant 's writ petition in the High Court challenging the above order was also dismissed by a Single Judge of the High court on 30.8 .89 holding that the dues calculated on 31st January 1986 became recurring dues every following day, and on 12.5.86 he could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and the mere making of payment on 21st October, 1986 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's representation to the State Government was rejected by the State government. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Bombay. A Division Bench allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State Govern ment had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from the service. Placing reliance on a decision of this Court in B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., [1987] 2 SCC 179 and State of Uttar Pradesh vs Brahm Datt Sharma & Anr., [ 1987] 2 SCR 981, it was held that merely because a Government servant retired from serv ice on attaining his age he could not escape the liability for misconduct and fault and negligence or financial irregularities which he may have committed during the period of his service and the Government was entitled to withhold or reduce the pension granted to a Government Servant. The State Government 'S power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government employee even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. 35 Allowing the appeal partly, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner be convicted of serious crime or be found to have been guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or after the completion of his Service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a government servant depend upon the good conduct of the Govern ment servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold, or withdraw any part thereof if the pensioners be convicted off wholly during or after completion of the service provided that before any order to this effect is issued, the procedure referred to in Note I to Rule 33 of the Bombay Civil Services Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules shall be followed. [189F G] 1.2 The State Govern 's power to reducing or withhold the pension by treating proceedings against Government servant even after retirement is specifically preserved by Rule 189. The validity of these Rules was not challenged either before the high Court or before this Court. In this view, the reduction of pension by 50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [190G] 1:3 The State government had power to reduced the amount of pension payable to the respondent. [191F] 2.1 The reduction of 50 per percent was too severe harsh and disproportionately disproportionate to his misconduct proved. The reduction was disproportionate to that the respondent had retired from Service and the reduction was in pension to the extent of Re. 1 per month be made. The Government accepted the findings and passed the impugned order reducing the pension.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents from the premises in dispute on the ground that they had applied for permission to the District Magistrate under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, and that the said permission was refused by him whereupon they moved the Commissioner in his revisions jurisdiction under section 33(2) of that Act. The respondents resisted the claim on several grounds. They urged that the suit was bad for non joinder of necessary parties; that the permission to sue granted to the appellants by the Commissioner was not valid in law and that, therefore, the permission granted by the commissioner under section was invalid in law. The trial Judge decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that it was valid. In appeal to this Court on the question: whether the permission given by the Commis sioner under section3(3) of U. P. ( Temporary Control of rent and Eviction) Act, 1950, was invalid, HELD : The words used in section 3 (4) and section 16 are clear. Section 16 in terms provides that the order made under this Act to which the said section applies shall not be called in question in any court. This is an express provision excluding the civil courts ' jurisdiction. [558 C] Lala Shri Bhagwan & A nr. vs Shri Ram Chand & Anr., ; , referred to. The words "any order passed under this section" are clear and unambiguous and they indicate that intention was to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner. The amendment in question has been introduced by Act 17 of 1954. [559 D] Lala Sri Bhagwan & Ors. vs Sh Ram Chand, A.I.R. 1924 P.C.

The first reference of its kind and nature enough to justify the President 's opinion that a prima facie case exists for an inquiry and report by this Court. In pursuance of the notices issued by this court, the Attorney General of India appeared in these proceedings. Certain other persons who claim to have knowledge of the incident or of its alleged background had also filed their affidavits. Amongst them were: Dr. Vinod Gupta, Ujagar Singh, Avtar Singh, Hakam Singh and Smt. Santosh Chowdhary and Shri Gopal Krishan Saini who was alleged to have assaulted her. All of them had filed their affidavit in this Court denying the allegations made against him. In response to the notices, issued by the court, Attorney General appeared in those proceedings. The Attorney General also appeared in the proceedings. He contended that before making this reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of the alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. According to counsel, this Court cannot, through the medium of a Reference, be called upon to discharge functions which ordinarily fall within the jurisdiction of a trial court, civil or criminal. The danger of such a procedure is said to be that if we hold that the incident is proved, Shri Saini will automatically be held guilty by a criminal court of the charge of assault and he will have to suffer a decree for damages in a Civil Court. Counsel says that under Article 317(1), the limited function of this Court is or ought to be to be determined whether the facts found upon by an independent fact finding Body show that the person concerned is guilty of misconduct and, secondly, whether the misconduct is of such nature as to require his removal is in direct opposition to the plain words of article 317( 1).

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (the Act) on 4 8 1950 for the management of the deity by which the temple of the appellants was declared to be a public temple and a trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and therefore governed by the Act. The Subordinate Judge decreed the plaintiffs suit holding that the deity installed in the temple was a family deity of the Hindu family and the dedication being of a private nature, the Act had no application and the order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. The respondent defendant preferred an appeal before the High Court against the decision of the Subordinate Judge which was heard by the Division Bench referred to above. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. It is well settled that under the Hindu law, however, it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the founder is to instal a family idol in the Temple and worship the same in order to effectuate the spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and his descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the Chairman. [835E F] 1.2. The concept of a Private endowment or a private trust is unknown to English law where all trusts are public trusts of purely charitable and religious nature. Thus, under the English law what is a public trust is only a form of Charitable Trust. [ 834G H] 2.1 In the instant case, however as there are two documents which clearly show the nature of the endowment, its task is rendered easier. It cannot be said that the endowment had been created near about the date when this document was executed. Some of the extracts of this document which are undisputed, in our opinion, clearly and conclusively show that the dedication was of a purely private nature and the intention of founder was merely to instal the idol in temple. [829A B] 2:2.1 The High Court has not properly construed some of the important features contained in the documents and the evidence and has in fact overlooked certain important aspects which completely negative the fact that the Endowment was of such a public character.

The appellant Bank originally known as the Bharat Bank Ltd., agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement, Malhotra executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys had agreed to Finance contracts and advances moneys to Malhotra. The appellant Bank formerly known as Bharat Bank Limited, agreed to advance sums of money against supply bills for payments to be received by it under the contract. For this purpose of carry out this agreement, Malhotra made out a bill on the military authorities for Rs. 49,633/8 then due to him in respect of his supplies under contracts during 1945 46 and handed over the bill to the appeLlant for collection. On the bill, Malhotra, made out the following endorsement: "Please pay to Bharat Bank L.Jabalpur." The appellant was also authorised to sue for recovery and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaLhotra, to conduct and defend proceedings in consultation with him and to take steps in his name and on his behalf. Malhotra promised and declared that "all powers hereby granted are and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorney 's against us whether for principle, interest, costs, charges or otherwise remain outstanding and unpaid." Intimation of the power of the Attorney was given by the appellant to the military authorifles. On July 19, 1948, Malhotra filed objections in the execution proceedings. On September 11, 1952, the objections were dismissed. On December 12, 1952 the appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhat Mal had no right to attach it. The trial Court held that the appel lant was the assignee of tho bill and decreed the suit. TakhatMal filed an appeal against the decree. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that the power Of attorney dated July 13 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill in favour. It also held that there was no transfer of the decree, or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the borrower continued to be the owner and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. The question whether a document amounts to an equitable assignment or not is primarily one of construction but it may mention a few decisions which throw light on the matter. Held, that there can be no valid equitable assignment of future debts, see tailby vs Official Receiver (3) and Loonkaran Sethiya vs State Bank of Jaipur ([1953] S.C.R. 969), referred to. Palmer vs Carey ; , relied on.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and the said company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. But on further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee with which he was not a recognised provident fund, was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3)(ii). HELD: The receipt of the said amount by the asses see was undoubtedly an income as defined by section 2(24) of the Income tax Act, 1961. [438E] In defining the expression "profits in lieu of salary", the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assesses from a provident fund. The receipt was therefore not income. [441F G] The meaning of section 16(3) (ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High court. [442G H] In view of the provisions of section 56(1), all receipts of profits in lieu thereof have to be considered as salary.

The Bihar Legislature passed the Bihar and Madhya Pradesh Acts which were in force on the face of it violated articles 19(1)(g) and 31 (2) of the Constitution. The Act was challenged by the petitioners on the ground that the impugned Acts infringed their fundamental rights under article 19(i)(g). Held, that the ban on slaughter of she buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which were useful as milch or breeding animals and which were not useful is reasonable but of those which are not useful was not valid. The restrictions imposed by the impugned sections were reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public and did not offend article 19 (1)(f). The impugned Acts were made by the States in discharge of the obligations imposed on them by article 48 to endeavour to organise agriculture and animal husbandry and in particular to take steps for preserving and improving the breeds and prohibiting the slaughter of certain specified animals. The impugned Act was constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibited the slaughter Of cows of all ages and calves of buffaloes, male and female, but that it was still possible for the Legislature to enact a law imposing a total ban on the slaughter. The State of West Bengal vs Subodh Gopal Bose ([1954] S.C.R. 710), relied on. Per Subba Rao, J. (dissenting) The impugned sections did not contravene article 19 as they imposed and do not prevent the State from making any law imposing, in the interest of the public reasonable restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19. The provisions of the impugned Act were not enforceable by any court of law but nevertheless they were fundamental in the governance of the country and it was the duty of the State to give effect to them. (6) It was not for the Court to say that such a policy should not have been adopted. Both on the question of policy at the extent of the restrictions imposed, considered them to be reasonable. The validity of the Act was not challenged for breach of the fundamental rights of the petitioners under article 31(2). The provisions in the impugned legislation were not saved by any Court of law and it could not be challenged for violation of the said fundamental rights. The Bihar Act made no distinction between she buffaloes and bullocks which were used as milches or breeding or draught animals and those which were useless as milching cattle and sheep, butchers who killed cattle and the Madhya Pradesh Act also made a like discrimination in that slaughter of buffaloes was permitted, although under certificate, while slaughter of cows, bulls, bullocks and calve. The ban on her slaughter of all animals belonging to the species of bovine cattle which included buffaloes (male or female adults or calves) ceased to be useful and became useless and unserviceable was a matter for legislative determination. There was no provision in the Bihar Act in that behalf. It was, therefore, not possible to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban under article 14(1). The restrictions were reasonable but they did not infringe article 19 because they imposed unreasonable restrictions on them in the public interest. The petitioners ' case was that the provisions of section 9 of the Bihar & Madhya Pradesh Prevention of Cow Slaughter Act, 1949, infringed their right to carry on their trade and that the Act violated articles 14(2) (g), 31(1) and (2).

The respondent submitted his explanation on December 3, 1955, in which he said that the charge was vague and that after 1949, he was not in any way concerned with the preparation of summaries and annual statements of accounts of the consumers department. On December 19, 1955 a memorandum was served on the respondent terminating his services with effect from January 31, 1956. The company 's Managing Director was satisfied that it was not possible to enter into a discussion with the respondent as to the propriety of the orders passed against him or for reinstatement etc. The Company 's managing director was satisfied and he was asked to explain why certain double adjustments had been made in the accounts of 1954 relating to the consumers ' department of the Company, the allegation being that a sum of Rs. 1,05894 7 which represented the amount of bills of the Railway had been deducted twice in the account. The respondents filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court at Nagpur praying for the issue of appropriate writs or directions quashing the orders of suspension and termination dated December 5, 1955 and December 7, 1955 respectively and asking for certain other reliefs. The Division Bench allowed the appeal, quashed the orders Of suspension and terminated the service of the respondents and declared that the respondent continued to be an 'employee of the company on terms which were applicable to him on the date of his suspension, namely, December 5. 1955. On appeal by special leave: Held (1)(a) The Standing Orders do make a distinction between `employees ' and `work men ' and there may also be employees who have no tickets.
