The expression "employee" denotes a larger group namely, all persons, male or females who are employed in the Office, Mains Department, Stores, Power House or Receiving Station of the Co. either at Nagpur or Wardha, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the Company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order NO. 4. (b) is not exhaustive in the matter of issue of tickets; it talks of an issue of a ticket to every permanent workman, a card to every badli workman, temporary ticket to Every apprentice and an apprentice card to any other train. It does not prescribe the issue or of a pass or token, though the definition of a "ticket" includes a passor token. The suggestion further is that Standing Order no.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act No. 21 of 1965 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into production. The dispute between the work men and the Company could not be resolved amicably and consequently a reference was made under the which came up before the Ninth Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Projects were covered by the definition in clause (16) of section 2 of the Act and that the word establishment ' has been used in this Act to indicate a "Company" as called in common parlance. It was further held that the Tribunal committed an obvious error, as it ignored the indications which are manifest from the language used in the Act. In appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) The Tribunal committed a manifest error, because it ignored certain indications which were manifest from its language used In the Act, and in section 2, sub section (15), establishments have been divided into two classes and their meaning has been defined. [631 A] (ii) The expression "establishment" is intended to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . This is further clarified by the provisions of sub section(3) of Section 1 which lays down the applicability of the , Act. The proviso to sub section 2(2) of s 16 also does not stand in the way of this claim, because there is no evidence at all that in any year, after Alloy steel Project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. [643 B C] (iii) The proviso under section 3 will apply to establishments consisting of different departments, undertakings or branches which are owned controlled or managed by persons other than companies. This is clear from the provisions Of sub section 1(3).

The appellant State Government and the State Governments were concerned for the prevention and control of water pollution. The Cess Act 36 of 1977 provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industries and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the state Boards constituted for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution. Section 3 of the Cess Act which may be termed as the charging section states that "there shall be levied and collected a cess for the purposes of the and utilisation thereunder". The cess is payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed in such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column II thereof as the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. "Specified industry" is defined in the Act as meaning any industry specified in Schedule I. There are 15 entries in Schedule 1 and they read as follows: SCHEDULE I (See Section 2(c)) 1. Ferrous metallurgical industry. Oil Mill. Ore processing industry. Petroleum industry. Petro chemical industry. Chemical industry. Certificate industry. Fertilizer industry. Refining Industry. Petro Chemical industry, Petroleum industry, Petro Chemical Industry. Chemical Industry, Oil Industry. Oil Industry (including coke) industry. Powerthermal and diesel generating industry. "Processing" 15. Processing of animal or vegetable products industry. The concerned assessing authorities have in all the cases under consideration issued notices demanding water cess from the sugar manufacturers on the ground that this industry falls within Entry 15 as "processing of animal Or vege table products industry". The Punjab and Haryana High Court have taken the view that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry No. 15 of Schedule I to the Cess act as " Processing vegetable products" and that it could not be given the meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. It was further of the view of the High Court that in interpreting the word "vegetable" one has to keep in mind the object for which the CessAct was made.

The respondent an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The appellant contended that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of section 10(3)(a) (iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the appellant required the building for the purposes of carrying out his profession. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction against the appellant. Before the High Court, in revision, it was contended by the Appellant that there was a clear distinction between 'business ' and 'profession ' and that the use of expression 'business in section 10 (3)(b) (ii) used the expression ' business ' only and not the expression "profession". The appellant also urged that the Court should favour a construction which would be beneficient to the tenant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression business occurring in section 2(a)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice ' of the professions of an advocate.[14C] 1.2 In a broad sense it is taken to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of livlihood or profit '. [15D E] M.P. Sethurama Menon vs Thaiparambath Kunhukutty Amma 's daughter, Meenakshi Amma & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.3 The expression "business" in section 12(1) (a)(ii) is not used in the sense of business within that phrase in the Landlord and Tenant Act, 1927. [16E] 2. The word "business " occurring in the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 is used to include activities of a commercial nature. It is a word of large and wide import capable of a variety of meanings. It was not a sound principle of construction tn interpret expressions used in one Act with reference to their use in another Act; more so, if the two Acts in which the same word is used are not cognate Acts. [17F] M/s. Seth Thai Parambathun Kunhikutty Amma vs Thailparambatukutty Pillai & Ors.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 with the appellant and the appellant was the partner of the firm. The loan was made on 30th December 1942 by the appellant from the respondent as a banker and along with interest from time to time the amount of Rs 4 lakhs was paid in the name of the appellant. The respondent accepted the proposal and thereafter a letter dated 29th September, 1942 written by the respondent to the appellant recording the agreement that "a sum of RS. 4 lacs (Rupees four lacs only) should be debited to India Supplies as deposit at the usual rate of interest as agreed upon". The respondent was to place to the credit of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills a sum which was withdrawn on 30 September 1942 by it from the appellant in the deposit account with the respondent thus reducing the indebtedness of Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills from Rs. 9,00 to Rs. 5 lakhs. Disputes and differences arose between the two groups thereafter. In 1944 there was an arbitration award. The Singhanias went out of both India Supplies and Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills and the Gupta group carried on both the businesses. One of the books of account of the respondent was that Lakshmi Rattan cotton Mills a limited company acted as financiers and bankers of India Supplies. In 1942, Lakshmi Ratan Jute Mills was the creditor of M/s. India Supplies for the approximate sum of money Rs. 3 lacs (Rs. 4 lakhs) was deposited in the names of India Supply on 30 9 1942 by Lakshmi Ratan Lal Gupta and Lakshmi Rattan Jute Cotton Mills. The appellant 's case was that it was money lent under an agreement that it had been made on demand and therefore the suit not having been filed within three years from the date of the loan under Article 59 was barred by limitation. In the year 1942 Kailashpat Singhania and Pushpa Devi wife of Lakshmipat Singhania were partners of India supplies along with the defendants. The father of Lakshmi Narain Cotton Mills, a limited Company acting as financier and bankers. In 1943, Lakshmi Rattan Mill was the debtor of M. L. Supplies for Rs. 2 lacs (the amount of money) was debited to Indian Supplies as deposits at the ordinary rate of Interest as agreed on by the partners of the said firm. In 1945, there was a dispute between the partners and Lakshmi Narain Jute Mills which was later transferred to the High Court in its original civil jurisdiction. The High Court heard the suit and decreed the suit in favour of the respondents. At the trial the issues were first whether the respondent deposited the sum of the money with the appellants under an Agreement that it would be paid on demand, and secondly whether the suit was barred under Article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The entire controversy in the suit is whether it was a case where money was deposited under an agree ment and that it Was payable on demand or whether it Was a case of an ordinary loan of Rs, 4,000. The appellants contended that Article 60 Of the Indian limitation Act, as amended by the Indian Law Amendment Act, 1963, was the relevant Article because if was a ease of money deposited under agreement that the same would be payable on demands and therefore limitation would commence from the time of demand and the suit should be filed within 3 years from that date. The respondents contended that it could not repay Lakshmi Ratan Sugar Mills. It was further urged that there was no payment of money in cash and adjustment entries were made in the books. Thirdly, monies were required by the appellants for their own business because Lakshmi Rattan Spinning Mills. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the background of the transaction was mercantile loan, would be more a conjecture than a conclusion to be arrived at. The financial transactions between the respondent and Lakshmi Rantan Cotton Mills were running accounts. It would be most consistent to hold that by allowing India Supplies a deposit of Rs., 4 lakhs (Rs 4 lakhs only) for a long time.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue dated February 28, 1986 made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The petitioner made an application to this Court under Article 32 in Writ Petition (Crl.) No 292 of 1986 challenging that order of detention. In the earlier writ application on 15th May, 1986, the Vacation Judge of this Court made an order for the release of the detenu on parole on the following terms: "The detenu is released on parole until further orders on the condition that he will report to the Directorate of Revenue New Delhi every day and the Directorate will be at liberty to direct him to explain his con duct during this time. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is al ready in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining authori ty was aware of the fact that he was already in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of deten tion became necessary. [848C D] 2. The facts of the instant case indicate that the detain ing authority was aware that the petitioner was in custody when the order was made, yet he Was satisfied that the preventive detention was necessary. This Court therein pointed out that it was not a matter of jurisdition but had to be decided on the facts of each case. [850E F] 3. The averments in paragraph 2 of the writ petition are without foundation against the Bench hearing the matter, and have been raised only one contention which was dealt with by the judgment in the Writ Petition. [851C D; 849A B] 4. In order to be passed for preventive detention of a person already in jail, it is necessary that he should disclose awareness of the facts that the person against whom an order is being made is to the knowledge of the authority already in Jail and yet for compelling reasons a preventive deten tion order needs to be made. [852C] 5.

The petitioners were working as 'Daily Rated Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The 'D Daily Rated casual labour ' includes three broad categories of workers, namely, unskilled, semiskilled, skilled, unskilled semis skilled and skilled. The unskilled labour consists of skilled labourers, wiremen, draftsman, A.C. mechanics etc., who have technical experience but do not hold any degree or diploma. The skilled labour consisted of labour doing technical work, who hold requisite degrees/diplomas. The principal complaint of the petitioners is that even though some of them had been working for the last ten years as casual labourers, the wages paid to them were very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to the regular employees of the Posts & Telegraphs department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc. which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. They also alleged that they were being exploited by the union of India. They have produced the order of the Director General, Posts and telegraphs Department bearing No. 28 II/77 SR/STN dated 15 5 1980 which prescribes the rate or rates of wages payable to casual labour in the Telecommunication Wing of the Department. It further provides that no scheme had been prepared for absorption of casual semi skilled/skilled workers against regular vacancies as and when they occur. The petitioners contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers and are not being regularly employed, they were not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employee are enjoying. They relied on the order dated 26 7 1984 passed by the DirectorGeneral, Posts & telegraphs, New Delhi, dated 15 4 1980 which prescribed the rate of daily wages for the semi skilled or unskilled labour in similar grade.

The assessee, a public notice under section 22(1) of the Income tax Act, was issued requiring every person whose total income during the previous year exceeded the maximum amount which was not chargeable to income tax to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days. The Income tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59,026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. The assessee appealed, in turn, to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal. The High Court upheld the contentions of the assesses and gave its opinion that the Department ought to have issued a notice under s.22(2) within the assessment years, and if no return was made within the time fixed by the notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 23(4) to a 'best judgment ' assessment ' Held, that the notice under S.22 (1) requiring in a general way what a notice tinder s. 22(2), requires of an individual, is not a decisive argument and fell within the mischief of cl. (c) of sub s.(1) Of section 28 of the Act. The short answer to that notice could be raised now. In the present case, the return was filed on January 5, 1950, but disclosed an income which was below the maximum not chargeable. The notice under sec. 22 (1), requiring in general way, what a " notice under Sec. 22, requires of the individual. If a return of income below the taxable limit is a good return in answer to a notice unders.22, there is no reason to think that a return Of a similar kind in answer was no return at all. The conclusion does not follow from the words of section 22 (I). No doubt, under that sub s only those persons are required to make a return, whose income is above taxable limits, but a person may legitimately consider himself entitled to certain deductions and allowances, yet file a return to be on the safe side. He may show his income and the deductions and allowance he claims. But it may be that on a correct processing his income may be found to be above the exempted limit. No doubt it is futile for a person not liable to tax to rush in with a return but the return in law is not merely a scrap of paper. It is a return which, such as the assessee considers, represents his true income.

The petitioners, who are principal office bearers of the first petitioner and are officers of different nationalised banks. They are aggrieved by Circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi. The said circular was purported to have been issued in terms of Clause 3 of the Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme, 1980. They further contend that Clause 3(a) of the Scheme in terms whereof the circular was purporting to have be issued is ultra vires Section 9 of the Act unless the said clause is so read as to be in harmony with the Section, and when so read, the said Clause does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. The petitioners contend that the circular is contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and the Natio nalised Banks ( Management and Miscellaneous provisions) Scheme 1980 (hereinafter referred to as 'the 'Scheme '). They further contended that Clause 2(a), which provides for non workmen employees to warrant the same type of representation as in the case of workmen mentioned under sub clause (b) of Clause (3) regarding non workmen to warrant their same type, is violative of Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43A of the Consti tution of India. The Additional Solicitor General representing the Central Government and Mr. Harish N. Salve, contended that there is no justification whatsoever to issue any such circular for the very object of the act is to encourage democratic selec tion of the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various categories of persons mentioned in the Act. To discourage trade unionism is contrary ly to the very spirit of the statute and repugnant to constitutional principles enshrined in Article 19 (1)(C) and article 43A, of the Constitution of India and Article 44A of Consti tion of India respectively. The Addl. Solicitor General also submits that appointment by election is not the only mode of representative appointment but nomination is perfectly valid and more effective from the point of view of the true institutional interest, par ticularly with reference to management efficiency. In the light of these rival contentions, it was open to the Central Govern ment to amend the Scheme suitably for the purpose of improving on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it is incumbent upon it, until any such amendment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives.

The respondent was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 18,000/ , 1,700/ , and 14,000 respectively in respect of the assessment years 1954 55, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The penalties were imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalties imposed. The Tribunal declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. The High Court in appeal held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) By the provisions of the Act or the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 powers have not been expressly conferred upon the Appellate tribunal to stay proceedings relating to the recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. At the same time it is significant that under section 220(6) the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income ' Tax Officer only when an appeal had been presented under section 246 which will be to the appellate Assistant Commissioner and not to the Tribunal. There is no provision in section 220 under which the IncomeTax Officer or any of his superior departmental officers can be moved for granting stay in the recovery proceedings of penalty/ tax.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Police Force on December 1, 1945, he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and posted as Station Officer at Sidholi. On February 27, 1953, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement in his character roll that a strong officer with plenty of push in him and met with a strong opposition in this new charge. The respondent submitted his explanation on November 29, 1952. On December 17, 1952, the respondent was forced to go on leave for two months. Before the expiry of his leave he was reverted to his substantive post of Head constable and transferred to Sitapur. On January 17, 1953 he was placed under suspension and on August 18, 1953. He was charged under section 7 Of the Police Act with mismissness in the discharge of his duties and unfitness for the same inasmuch as while posted as a Station Officer, Police Station, Intiathok, he had been guilty of dishonesty, corruption and misbehaviour in that he had on nine occasions, particulars of which were given in the charge accepted bribes. It was contended by the respondent that para 486 of the Police Regulations was only directory in nature and inasmuch as no prejudice was caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said regulations would not affect the validity of the order of dismissal. Held, that the departmental enquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial inquiry and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 489(2). The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect its validity.

The appellant was a doctor in the Medical College, Simla. He was promoted to supertime grade II post and was appointed at Simla. The promotion of respondents 4 to 24 was challenged by the appellant on diverse grounds but the principal contention is that their promotions were in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules. Rule 8 provides for future maintenance of the Service. Relevant for the present appeal is rule 8(3) which provides for recruitment to super time grade II both by promotion and nomination by direct recruitment. As the appellant claims promotion to super Time grade II from February 18, 1971 and simultaneously questions promotion of Respondents 4 to24 were promoted on different dates to super lime grade II, the respondents 4, to 24 were promoted in violation of rule8 of 1966 rules. Rule 9 provides for 50% of the vacancies in supertime Grade I to be filled by promotion of General Duty Officers Grade I and Specialists ' Grade Officers in the ratio of 2:3 and the remaining 50% vacancies to be filed in the following manner, namely: (i) Supertime grade I (a) 50 per cent of the posts in Supertime Grade II shall be filled in by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists ' grade, i.e. category 'C ' under 1963 Rules; (ii) Super time grade I(b) 50% (iii) 20% of vacancies in Super Time Grade II will be filled with promotion of: (a)(i) General Duty officers, Grade I, with not less than eight years of service in that category; or (ii). Specialists (b) Grade Officers (c) Grade I (d) 25% of posts in super time Grade II (a), (b), (iii), (iv) Specialists and (v) (vi) Super Time Scale Officers, Grade II. The appellant contended that the promotion to Supertime scale on February 8, 1971 was in contravention with rule 8 (3) of 1966 Act. Rule 2 provides for direct recruitment to Super time Grade I both by direct appointment and nomination. As these 28 posts were in Specialists Grade and the strength of Specialists was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to superfi grade II is required to be filling in, it can only be filled from promotion from among those originally belonged to specialist ' grade i. e. category `C ') under 1963 rules. The contention was that the 19 unspecified Specialists posts were meant only for promoting category 'D ' and were given promotions against 19 uns specified posts in contravention thereof. The vertical promotional channel is from specialists " grade and General Duty Officer Officers Grade II to superje grade I. On the date of initial constitution of Service there were 275 permanent and 102 temporary, in all 377 posts in Specialist ' Grade II were upgraded to superTime grade II. On account of various imponderables the service could not be constituted and 1963 Rules were amended by Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules 1966, which came into force on May 15, 1963. The Rules envisaged categorisation of personnel manning the Service into five different categories, namely, category I comprising supertime scale Rs. 1600 2000, category II consists of Specialist " grade Rs. 1300". On account Of various imember factors the service was not to be constituted, and 1963 rules were amended in 1966 by Central Government Health Service Rules, 1966.

Section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 provides that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of law, will go to feed the surplus pool. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, although its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before this Court arose from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: The Act came into force on April 15, 1953 but even before that date the Act came in force, he was the owner of about 178 bighas which admittedly fell short of the permissible permissible area of 30 standard acres. The Act was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country is one of the States where land reform laws are likely to to be implemented by banishing big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a few feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. The State enacted the Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others, peasant proprietorship created. The Scheme of the act with which the Haryana Security of Lands Tenures Act came to be amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High court has upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. A study of the history of the Acts and the provocation for and frequency of amendments thereto, suggests an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which we will refer to later. Suffice it to say that the law is construing a radical agrarian measure; its basic goals are to cut down large holdings and distribute lands to various landless people according to a design and to foster, according to legislative policy, an agrarian community of peasants proprietors. De hoarding and defeating hide outs are essential to make the twin objects successful and so sections 10A and 19B among others, have been written into the Act. To explore the import and ambit of these two provisions, particularly the former with a view to see whether it strikes at a gift made by, the respondent in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of their excess lands and look slim on as a small holder before the law Language permiting, the Court as interpretedor must fulfil, not frustrate the legislative mission. Factual Silhouette At this stage it is appropriate to set out the facts in the two appeals which are not in dispute and speak for themselves. C.A. No. 2023 of 1972: Respondent No. 1 owned 450 bighas and 9 biswas of land acting with foresight, gifted half of it to his mother in 1951, perhaps with a premonition of coming restrictions by way of ceiling on owner ship. The unhappy consequence was that his holding expanded to odd bighas far in excess of the permitted permissible area as set out in section 2(3) of the Land Reforms Act.

The appellants filed a suit for possession of the property in dispute on the ground that the property was granted to them as an impartible estate, devolving by the rule of primogeniture. The trial court held that the decree of the trial court was genuine and that the plaintiffs were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands and the decision of the Compensation Officer did not operate to deprive the plaintiff of the right to those lands or compensation payable in respect thereof; that the will set up by the appellants represented the true relationship between the descendants of the Gangashah, and that on December 8, 1950, the Zamindari was conferred upon the 1st defendant Dayaram as he was found suitable to hold the Zamindari and the said decision of compensation Officer did no operate to depriving the plaintiff 's right to these lands or compensa tion payable in favour thereof; and that, the will dated December 8. 1950 set up for by the defendants was not genuine and the will was executed without any right of appeal and to make his adjudication conclusive unless a suit be filed within two months from the date of the order. The High Court confirmed the decree passed by the trial Court in respect Of the Zamindari land. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Under the Chanda Patent the lands of the Zamindari held by the family were confirmed in 1867 in favour of Sitaram. On his death there was no evidence that any formal grant was issued in favour by the 1nd defendant. [334 C] (ii) The right of the Governor to remove a holder who is not loyal or does not manage the property or does affect the cultivation or who is guilty of bad behaviour or bad administration, it must be assumed that the holder of the zamindari has merely a life interest and on the death of the holder, the Governor re grants the land consistently with the rules of succession according to the law and custom amongst the members of the family but subject to the dominant purpose of good administration and loyalty to the Government. [333 B] (iii) The rights of the parties must be adjudged in the light of these findings.

The appellants paid rent to the respondent up to 31 August 1964. The respondent landlord terminated the tenancy of the appellants inter alia on the ground that the appellants were in arrears of rent for more than six months. The appellants received the notice on 6 December 1966. The appellant landlords alleged that the tenants were in arrear from 15 March 1960 to 15 March 1963, viz., for over six months and that they were not ready and willing to pay the rent. The trial court held that the contractual rent in respect of the premises was not unreasonable and excessive. The High Court also took the view that the provisions contained in section 12 (3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947 would apply. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the decision in Vora Abbasbhai 's case was not overruled by the Gujarat High Court in Ambalal 's Case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay High Court has not agreed with the view of the GujaratHigh Court in Dattu Subhana Panhalkar vs Gajananan Vithoba Bobhate & Anr., [1966] 2 S.C.R. 634. [637B] 2.1 In Ambalai 's ' case, the decision of this Court in Vamanora Abbasabhai 's ease was overruled by this Court. The view of Bombay High court nullifies the provisions of section 12 and Explanation thereto and confers a right on the tenant where the legislation does not contemplate such a right.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Limited, a company registered under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, held majority of shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1939 and December 31,, 1940, and January 31, 1943, and December31, 1942, and March 31, 1941, and August 31, 1942 and December 30, 1943 respectively. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Company. Two of these directors eventually retired and only one, namely Mr. L. G. Bash and continued to be a director of the company nominated by the Aluminium Ltd., Mr. K. L . G. Sag. Bash who continued to hold the majority of the shares in question. The respondent company thereupon appealed to the Incometax Appellate Tribunal which reversed the decision of the Excess Profits Tax Officer. The Commissioner of Excess Profits tax, West Bengal, has now come up on appeal by certificate under section 66 A(2) of the Income tax Act. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the directors of a company may well be regarded as having "a controlling interest" in the respondent Company. In order to have "a Controlling interest" the person or persons who hold the minority of the majority must have a beneficial interest in the shares held by them. The controlling interest which the holder of the minority share has never passed to the agent.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyd erabad. On 1st October, 1957, he opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promo tions Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Electricity Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30th December, 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their being promoted on the ground that he had not passed the examination. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. On 21st November 1972, the respondent 's representations were rejected. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition before the High Court on 13th February 1973. The learned Single Judge who heard the petition dismissed it and the respondent preferred an appeal to a Bench of the Karnataka High Court which held that the Writ Petition could not be thrown out on the grounds of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the view that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no longer open to the respond ent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. The Division Bench held that in the circumstances of the case the relief to the re spondent should not be denied on the reason of delay and limitation. In appeal by special leave, it is contended for the appellant that the Court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the respondent was exempted from passing the S .A. S. examination before qualifying for the promotion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Resolution dated 5.1.1970 as exempting the allottees from passing I.A.,S. test is not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the resolution the inference that the allottees are exempt ed from the passing of the examination is not justified. [502C] 2. The resolution was ' passed by the Board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Govern ment referred to in the Resolution itself. Paragraph 2 of the Resolution clearly states that the relaxation of the rule relating to passing of tho Departmental Examinations and Kannada language test is only as regards services where the rules do not specifically require the passing or the language test.

The petitioner 's son was taken in police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, alleging that it was a case of custodial death since he died as a result of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police detention. The allegation made is that it is a case where custodial death was caused by the multiple injuries sustained by him while his dead body was thrown on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraikela Railway Station. It is alleged that it has been a case that the deceased died on account of multiple grievous injuries inflicted while he had been in police possession and thereafter his dead bodies were thrown on railway track. The respondents, who are the mother of the deceased, contended that the evidence adduced during the inquiry did not support the defence of the respondents and there was no reason to reject the finding of the District Judge that the death of the petitioner was unnatural. It was further urged that it would be appropriate to spell out clearly the principle on which the liability of the State arises in such cases for payment of compensation and the distinction between this liability and the liability in private law for payment Of compensation in an action on tort. It may be mentioned straightaway that award of compensation in a proceeding under Article 32 by this Court or by the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution is a remedy available in public law, based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in private Law in an actions based on tort, through a suit instituted in a court of competent jurisdiction or/and persecute the offender under the penal law. This is a distinction between the two remedies to be borne in mind which also indicates the basis on which compensation is awarded in such proceedings. In a petition for writ of habeas corpus, the burden was obviously on the respondents to explain how Suman Behera sustained those injuries which caused his death. Unless a plausible explanation is given by the respondents which is consistent with their innocence, the obvious inference is that the fatal injuries were inflicted to the deceased voluntarily while he is in police ' custody. The burden is, therefore, clearly on the respondent to explain why Suman Behrahera sustained these injuries which resulted in his death, for which the respondents are responsible and liable. To avoid this obvious and logical inference of custodial deaths, the Additional Solicitor General relied on the decision of this Court in State of Maharashtra vs Ravikant S.Patil, ; , Sebastian M.S. Ganesh, A Women 's Resources Centre and Others vs Commissioner of Police Delhi Police Headquarters and Others, ; and State of Gujarat and others vs Ravindikant S Patil,. [1990] 2 SCC 1. The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of monetary compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only mode of redress available. The power available to this court under Article 142 is also an enabling provision in this behalf. The contrary view would not merely render the Court powerless and the constitutional guarantee a mirage but may, in certain situations, be an incentive to extinguish life, if for the extreme contravention the court is powerless to grant any relief against the State, except by punishment of the wrongdoer for the resulting offence, and recovery of damages under private law, by the ordinary process. It the guarantee that deprivation of life and personal liberty cannot be made except in accordance with law, is to be real, the enforcement of the right in case of every contravention must also be possible in the constitutional scheme, the mode of redressal being that which is appropriate in the facts of each case.

The petitioner, a prisoner under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President had rejected the petitions on the ground that the prisoners were willing to be interviewed. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 Rule 549(4) of the Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. [1187C] 1.2 The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for this Court to say that the two prisoners are ready and willing to interview them. [1108D] 1:3 Rule 549A also provides that all reasonable indulgence should be allowed to a condemned prisoner in the matter of interviews with relatives, relatives friends, legal adviser and approved religious ministers. Surprisingly, but we do not propose to dwell on that issue, this rule provides for a search of the person who wants to interview a prisoner. If it is thought necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview an prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. There is a provision in the Rules that if a person whom desires to interviews a prisoner is a female she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. Taking an overall view of the matter, this Court does not think it necessary to dwell upon that issue. [1087E F] 1 :4 The petitioner had been asking to interview two prisoners jointly and for not more than one hour on the whole. There will be no order as to costs.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden to M/s. Das Bank Ltd. On January 19, 1950 the Bank instituted mortgage suit against the respondent on the original side of the Tripura High Court for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit but allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. He directed that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. The appellant filed an appeal against that order but it was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner on June 29, 1970. On October 4, 1961 respondent filed in the Court of the Subordinate Judge Execution Petition No 39 of 1961 against the Receiver and the appellant praying that execution do issue against the appellant as directed by the Court. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the appeal and enhanced damages to RS. 4.525. In the meantime the respondent moved an application asking for damages from the Receiver on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence. The trial court decreed the Suit but he allowed the defendant 's application for damages to the extent of Rs 32,525 which it rendered itself liable under the terms of the bond. On appeal by special leave was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) The Subordinate judge who tried the suit was incompetent to enforce the surety bond executed by the appellant and as he was neither the successor nor the assign of the District Judge; and (ii) Under the terms Of the bond, the appellant is not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. Both these contentions turn on the terms and it was therefore necessary to have a look at that bond. HELD: The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court under the Tripura (Courts) order 1950.

The appellants who are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U .P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller and that the supplies were made pursuant to the directions issued under cl. 5 of the Order and not pursuant to any contract of sale. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax. The Additional Judge held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the Act, 1948. The High Court answered the two questions in the affirmative and the appellants appealed to this Court with special leave. HELD: 1. Under cl. 3 of the order every licensed dealer is directed to deliver to the State Government 50% of the wheat held in stock by him on the date of the commencement of the levy Order, and thereafter fifty per cent of the sugarcane daily procured or purchased by him every day beginning with the date on which such time as the State Govt otherwise directs. The price at which the wheat is sold is the maxi mum price fixed in the Wheat (Uttar Pradesh) Price Control Order 1959 as notified by the Government of India. Delivery of the goods has to be given by the dealer to the regional Food Controller or a person authorised by him in that behalf. The dealer has no option but to sell the specified percentage of wheat to the state Government.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. Though acquitted, he was not straightaway released from prison. The reasons are not clear to us from the record that Presumably he was required in connection with some other case. He had been due for release from prison on June 23, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory Board within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. On August 7, 1986, an order for his detention was passed under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The mandate of article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory board has reported within the time period of 3 months that the detenu had there been in its con struction to which a reference could be made under section 11 of the Act and whose report of its opinion regarding suffi cient cause for the detention was required to be obtained within three months of the detention under article 22 (4) thereof. The period of two weeks stipulated by section 11 expired on July 14, 1986 and the petitioner was entitled to be released on July 19, 1986 on July 21, 1986 in view of the revocation of that order. The appellant contended that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by Article 22(1) and therefore, the appellant is entitled to he set at liberty. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A law may be made providing for successive orders for detention in a manner as to render the protection of article 19(4). If there is to be a collision between article 22 and section 15 of the act, sec. 15 has to yield. But by reading down the provision, the colli sion may be avoided and section.15 may be sustained. So avoid ing the collision course, it held that if the report of the Advisory Boards is obtained within 3 months of its order, where the earlier order is revoked and a subsequent order is made. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. [207C D] 2. If a reference to an Advisory Board is to he made within three weeks, it is no answer to say that the report though not obtained within two months, was obtained before the hearing of the case.

The petitioner, father of the respondent, was a firm. Both of them were established Vaidyas in Rajkot. They came from a well to do family. The petitioner is advanced in age and both the father and the son have been fighting between themselves since more than a decade. The High Court found that the petitioner and the respondent had referred their disputes to one Kantibhai Vaidya (Shri Kantilal Dayaram Jani) who had intervened between them with the good intention to bring their dispute to an end. He made an award on 18th January, 1977. Belowow the award, both the parties and the arbitrator had signed. The endorsement reads, when translated in English, as found by the High Court that the award is agreed to and binding upon both the sides and that the entire responsibility of the arbitrator will lie on Shri Kantibhai Desai Vaidya and that he has taken the responsibility. Thereafter followed a spell of litigation. The respondent applied on 20th June, 1977 for filing the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). A notice consequent upon the filing of the Award was issued to the petitioner. The application was converted into Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977. It was stated in the application that the respondent has torn off the award. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made (3) the award was not set aside under section 30 and (4) that the Award is not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The learned trial Judge held that the First Appeal and Civil Revision Application were withdrawn in pursuance of an agreement reached between the parties on or about 14th August, 1978. A copy of the said agreement was also produced before the Court as Exhibit 40. It appears that the arbitration application was decided against him, against which he preferred an appeal/revision but later on, he withdrew the same. During the course of the execution proceedings, the petitioner preferred a civil revision application against the judgment and order passed by the Civil Judge raising practically all the disputes which had been raised by the petitioner in this civil revision petition. The same was rejected summarily. The main objection to the award being that there was no written agreement signed by both the party to refer the dispute to arbitration, was rejected outright. The Court dismissed the application in terms thereof. Allowing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer their dispute in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award; secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th 8 1978 (Exhibit 40). In that view of this matter, both of them had re affirmed the acceptance of the awards.

The appellants were the legal representatives of the respondent. The suit was filed by the appel lant against the respondent under section 36 of the , praying for reopening the trans actions and taking accounts from all liabilities in excess of the limits specified by law. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the decree holder had agreed to the same. On appeal, the High Court held that the decrees in suit No. 78 of 1922 were not liable to be reopened under the second proviso to section 36(1) of the Act and accordingly dis missed the appeal. Held: (i) The order of January 30, 1937 was a final order which brought the Execution Case No. 118 of 1936 to an end and could not be taken to have any wider operation. Promode Kumar Roy vs Nikhil Bhusan Mukhopadhya, (1901) L.R. 61 I.A. 593, referred to. (ii) The words "instituted or filed on or after the 1st day of January 1939" in section 2(22) of 'a suit to which this Act applies must be read as qualifying the words "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed or pending on or before that date and includes a proceeding in execution for the recovery of a loan advanced before or after that date. The words 'instituted ' or ' in the beginning of the definition as well as the words 'proceeding in execution ' occurring further down: see, per Spens C.J., in Bank of Commerce Ltd. vs Amulya Krishna, (1878) I.L.R, Cal. 958, referred only to an assignee (1) L .R. , and not to use the expression "for the present" occurring in the body of that petition.

One Venkatacharyulu was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. The appellant was the Chief Justice and himself, who had heard the matter in appeal under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the period of limitation prescribed by the special or local law is different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule. Held: (i) that the expression "different from those prescribed therefor in first schedule" occurring in section 29(2) cannot be construed as meaning that Schedule only to a case where the Act prescribes no time limit for a particular appeal, but the special law prescrib a period of Limitation different from that prescribed therefor under the first proviso. (ii)that the expression 'appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure" in article 156 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act means an appeal governed by the Code and not appeals arising out of proceedings to which the Code applies. The word "dispute" in section 2(2)(a) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, is not defined in the Code but includes a suit, appeal or application for which no period of time limit is prescribed in the first Schedule. (iii)that where a different period of period of 30 days prescribed by a special or general law prescribes a period Of limitation different from a period prescribed by that Act it is specially prescribed for the institution of a particular suit, such shorter period of limitations shall be applied notwithstanding this Act. The expression "appeal" in the second limb of section 29 (2) of 'the Limitation Act does not mean an appeal under the Indian Code but only so much of it as is expressly made applicable by the provisions of the Act. (iv)that a right of appeal is conferred under the Letters Patent, it is deemed to be an appeal from an original decree passed by a civil court situated within the local limits of its Civil appellate jurisdiction.

That petition was dis missed by the High court on September 8, 1986. This appeal by special leave is against the said decision of the High COurt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The District Magis trate had passed the impugned order in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area in ques tion. That appears to be so from the order passed by tho District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of Baldev Town Area Committee, Baldev to the President of the Union requiring the bus operators to stop their buses at the bus stand fixed by the district Magistrate. The letter dated October 10, 1986 written by Executive Officer, of Baldev town Area Committee to the president of the Mathura Dulaji Ghadigaonker Manikpur Eta Motor Operators Union, Mathura Road Transport Co. Ltd. & Anr., ; and T.P. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority, Tanjore, ; , relied on. 1.2 The District Magistrate fixed the area as a Bus stand. Regarding the authority which had the power to notify an area as bus stand, there are at least three decisions of this Court. In T. P. Ibrahim 's case (supra), this Court took the view that the fixing and alteration of bus stands was not a purpose for eign to the control of transport vehicles ' which was gov erned by Chapter IV of the Act and, therefore, rules could be framed by the State Government regarding the said subject under section 68(2)(r) of the . [717G H; 718A] T.B. Ibrahim Ibrahim vs District Magistrate, T.Tanjore & Ors., ; , referred to. 1:3 The Town Area Com mittee had passed an order in quia tion with the objects of establishing bus stand in the areas in question. That appeared to be a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specific provision in section 68 (2)(s) (r) for that pur pose. [718A] 1:4 The Town Areas Committee can derive any assistance from this rule.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the , and sentenced to imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and also be liable to fine. The High Court dismissed their revision petition on the ground that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) There is no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence punishable. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under sections 7 and 8 of the . [666 D] (ii) The appellants should have been warned that they had no licence to carry the paddy and they may have changed their mind at any place between Samalkha Barrier and the Delhi Punjab boundary and not have proceeded further in their journey. Section 8 of ' the states that "any person who attempts to contravene, or abets a contravention of any order made under section 3 shall be deemed to have contravened that order". [666 E] (iii) The fact that the appellant may have been warning that they did not carry the rice and they might have changed his mind at some place between the Samalka Barrier. Nor can he be convicted of an attempt to commit it is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted under the section, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit that offence and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt.

The Sassoons were the Managing Agents of a company under agreements dated the 24th February, 1920 and the 2nd October, 1934. The Sassoon agreed to transfer their Managing Agency Agencies of the said companies to Messrs Agarwal and Company, Chidambaram Mulraj and Company Ltd., and Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd., by letters dated the 3rd September, 1943, 16th April, 1943 and 27th April 1943 respectively. The agreement provided that the company was during the continuance thereof to pay to the Sassoffers their successors and assigns by way of remuneration a commission of 10 per cent on the net profits of the Company and a further sum of Rs. 1,91,304 in respect of the Managing Agency of the Apollo Mills Ltd., for the period of six months commencing from the 3th July, 1919, and it was provided that if the said commission was to become due to them yearly on the 31st March in each and every year during the continuation of the Agreement and was to be payable immediately after the annual accounts of the company had been passed by the shareholders. The Income tax Officer and the Excess Profits Tax Officer were of the opinion that the Sassoonons had not earned any part of the managing Agency commission which had been paid by the companies to the transferees and were not liable to tax but the Sasiffons were entitled to such remuneration from the managed Companies in the form of commission for services rendered up to the dates of the transfers. The Tribunal accepted the contention of the transferees that the Managing agency commission received by them should be apportioned on a proportionate basis and the transferees should be made liable to pay tax only on the commission earned by them during the period that they had worked as the Managing Agent of the respective companies. On appeal, the High Court held that the remuneration for the year accrued only on 31st December, 1943 when the Income tax Appellate Tribunal also took care to say in making their reference to the High court, as follows: " The question is not when the managing agency commission accrued but the real question was to whom it accrued. " Held, that the agreement of service between the Sas Soons and the assignee under the Managing Agencies Agreement was the effective source of the year 's income and was the joint income of both the assignor and the assignees. The mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source of income, as explained above, any term in the Managing Agreement between the principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year "s remuneration and negativing to the assignors any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of the income, could not have the effect of denying to the assigningor a substantial right to a share in the remuneration, if otherwise he has a vested right thereto. A term in a Managing Agency Agreement between two companies was an indivisible contract for a whole year ' and its work was that the managing agent was the sole owner of the business carried on by both the assignedor and assignee taken together and were hence taxable as income accruing to both and apportionable as such between them. The real legal position, therefore, is that what was assigned was an income bearing asset, viz., the Managing agent which was the source Of income and which entitled the respective assignees to receive all the remuneration from their companies under the terms of the agreement was that it was the income of the assignee and that it is the profits and gains of the Business carried on in both by them as their joint property and that such property had to be apportioned between them on some equitable basis. It could not be disputed that in the absence of any specific contract to the contrary between the persons who contribute to the work or business, the fruit of such work or of such business was the Joint property of both, when the same had in fact been realised.

The appellant was a resident of the District of Gonda. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. He lost his wife years ago. His eldest son, Badri, married one Sunderpatti. Badri was employed in Lucknow, and his wife was residing with his father. It is said that Sunderpatti developed illicit intimacy with Sahoo; but there were incessant quarrels between them. On August 12, 1963, the appellant brought her buck, and after some wordy altercation between them they slept in the only room of their house. The only other inmate of the house was the appellant 's second son, Kirpa Shankar, a lad of about 8 years. On the morning of August 13, 1963 Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the room of the said house where she was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. Sunderpatti died on August 26, 1963 at 3 p.m. Sahoooo was sent up for trial before the Court of Sessions, Gonda, on a charge under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The learned Sessions Judge on a consideration of the entire evidence came to the conclusion that Sahoo killed Sunderpatti and thereby finished the daily quarrels. On appeal, a Division Bench confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Hence the appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A statement whether communicated or not admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional soliloquy is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. Generally they are mutterings of a confused mind. [90 C D] Bhogilal Chunilal Pandya vs The State of Bombay, ; , referred to. (2) A confession whether communicated, or not, admitting guilt guilt is one of guilt; but, there is no clear distinction in principle in the case of an oral statement. Both must stand on the same footing. [91 C D E] Bhogu Narayana vs R. ; and Bhogilal Chhaganlal Pandya v The State Of Bombay, [1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi.
