Under Section 16(1), in Chapter V provides that if the Central Govt. is of the opinion that for the more efficient carrying on of General Insurance business, it is necessary to do so, it may by notification frame one or more schemes providing for all or any of the following matters; (e) the rationalisation or revision of pay scales and other terms and conditions of service of officers and other employees wherever necessary. Pursuant thereto, the central Govt. framed the New India Assurance Co operative Insurance Scheme 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. The appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The appel lant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a learned Single Judge on November 11, 1983 and was confirmed by the Division Bench in Letter Patent Appeal No.351/1984 dated April 23, 1984. Section 7 of the Act provides that every whole time officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance Business, immediately before the appointed day, shall become an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co. in which the undertaking of the insurer to which the service of the officer relates has vested and would hold his office on the same terms and condi tions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such transfer, as referred to in paragraph 3. He shall continue to remain an officer unless and until his employment, in the transferee company is terminated or the terms and condition are duly altered by any other scheme framed under the Act. By notification dated April 29, 1976 the Central government also framed the scheme called the General Insurance(Rationalisation of pay scale and other conditions of Service of Development Step) Scheme, 1976 which came into force on May 1, 1976. The central Govt., framed the new scheme called "General Insurance (Rationalization of Pay scales and Other Conditions of Service" Scheme,1976 with effectfrom December 31 1973. Thereunder by Rule 3, the undertaking was transferred to the respondent; under Rule 5 the existing whole time officers etc. became the officer of the transferee Company (New Indian Assurance Co.

The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice on February 3, 1970 by which he invited tenders for the grant of li cences for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops, in one lot, for Rs. 34,000/ per month. His bid was accepted and his name was entered in the prescribed register, and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. AjInterest Prasad, who was unsuccessful bidder, felt aggrieved and filed an appeal, but it was dismissed by the Excise Commissioner on March 16, 1970. The Board of Revenue also refused to interfere. Aj Ayodhya Prasad Shah filed a writ petition (O.J.C. No. 357 of 1970) in the High Court with the allegation that the Collector was not acting according to law as the State Government had issued instructions to him not to. issue the licenses. Ajripendra Prasad Shah amended his petition for quashing the notice also. The High Court held that the State Govern ment had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collector after it had "become final in appeal and revision" and could not direct a reauction. The appellant State Government issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 under the provisions of the amended section 29(2) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915 for fresh settlement of the shops, and wrote to the Collector of the Mayurbhuj to call for tenders in accordance with that order. The Collector called for fresh tenders within a week. 816 A hearing was held on March 28, 1974 and the Board of Excise refused to intervene. Ajendra Prasad Shah then filed another writ petition in the Orissa High Court challenging the validity of sections 22 and 29 of the Act. The writ petition was dismissed. In appeal by certificate, it was contended that: (1) the High court erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collec tor was not for the granting of an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor; (2) the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section 6 was therefore ultra vires the Act; (3) the Collector had no authority to issue such a notice under that sub section, as the power of the State ' Government in that respect had been delegated to the Board. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29 (2)(a) does not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and naked powers" in determining the sum of money 'as was sought to be done by the order dated 8th August, 1970; (4) the power to grant the exclusive privilege within any specified area, sub section (2), provides that no grantee of such a privilege shall exercise the same "unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or Excise Commissioner. [819 C E] 2. The expression 'fee ' in the rule is therefore inaccurate but that cannot detract from the real nature of the recov ery. [820 D] 3. Section 6 of the Amending Act of 1970 was not made retrospective in operation, the effect of section 6 is that thereby the Legis lature had directed the State to disregard the decision given by this Court in Ajodhya Pra sad 's case that the amount realized by auction is illegal. This virtually amounts to judicial exercise of power by the legislature a power which the Legislature does not possess. [821 E] 4. The powers of the Government to reject a bid were thus reserved both under the provi sions of law and by the express declarations made before the auction.

The appellant was charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with an approver. The prosecution case was that the deceased was a domestic servant of Dr. Nanavati, and that he had entered into criminal conspiracy with him for the purpose of committing the murder of Narendrakumar and com mitted house breaking and thefts in the house of his grand father Dr. P. Nanoli. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 302 read with section 120B as well as section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) It was necessary to find out whether the approver or accomplice was a reliable witness. [621 E] (ii) The rule as to corroboration is based on the reasoning that there must be sufficient corroborative evidence in material particulars to connect the accused with the crime. In the present case, the evidence of the deceased and his wife showed the place of occurrence. The house of the appellant was identified both by Dr. D. Nanuavati and his daughter to belong to Narendra. A girl of 14 named Garadin Bride who was a classmate of Narendra said that Narendra wore a chain similar to the one that was shown. The medical evidence did not assist the prosecution. [625 E G] (iii) It is obvious that silver lump could not be identified. At this stage it is to be noticed as to whether there was evidence to connect accused No. 3 with murder.

On June 26, 1965 the Surat Municipal Corporation, then called Surat Borough Municipality declared its intention to make a town planning scheme under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act 1954. The draft scheme was published which included among other lands an area admeasuring 1,37,961 sq. meters of which appellant as Karta of a Hindu undivided family was the lessee. On May 10, 1968 Government granted sanction to the draft scheme. Before the Town Planning Officer the appellant claimed compensation for deprivation of his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. by his order made on November 4, 1971. The Town Planning officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq.; but not satisfied with the decision of the Town planning Officer the Appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal which reduced his claim to Rs. 950 p. by its order dated November 4 1971. In the writ petition filed by the appellant it was contended that in case the Town Plan Planning Officer 's decision in the appellant 's case was appealable either under clause (viii) or clause (xiii) of section 32(1). The Town planning officer had a duty under clause(viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect of each plot included in the final scheme estimated on the assumption that the scheme has been completed would exceed at the same date the market value of the land. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 65 increment means the amount by which at the date of the declaration of the intention to making a scheme, the market Value of the plot rises and a part of the benefit which arises out of the unearned rise in prices is directed to be contributed towards financing of the scheme which enables the residents in that area to more amenities, better facilities and healthier living conditions. Under the Act the compensation payable to an owner for loss of land has to be determined on the basis of the market price of the Land at the time on which the declaration was made.

One of the properties was given to the daughters and after deducting the kist each year. The two daughters claimed possession of their lands and their claim was that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one veli of anja land and one vela which of them had been adopted by them. The trial court upheld the contention of the daughters, but decreed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) on a fair and reasonable construction of the Will it was for Seetharama to give such land as he chose to the daughter and not for the daughters to make the selection; (ii) the testator had indicated with sufficient clarity what he wanted his daughters to get. HELD: (i). The words " he shall deliver possession" in the case of the property which he was bequeathing to his daughters must be read together, and the will would have the right to select. [140 D] (ii). It is not correct that if the intention of the testator was not to give the selection to his brother, the case would clearly be of the third kind indicated by him above and the daughters would have their rights to select.[140 E F] In the present case the testator 's intention was clear. The words in the will mean the same. Therefore the direction of the deceased testator was that as soon as the children obtain majority the will deliver possession to them of the respective lands bequeathed to them.

The appellant, a co bhumidar, was the widow of one of his brothers. The respondents were in joint possession of the plots in dispute being co bhumidars, because after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950, the plaintiff appellant lost her title by operation of law. The allegation of the plaintiff that the defendants had committed fraud was stoutly denied. The trial court decreed the suit for joint possession in respect of Chakbandi plot Nos. 201 and 274 only. As regards plot No. 93, the dismissal of the appellant 's suit by the trial court was upheld. In second appeal, the District Judge held that on the admitted facts even after the Abolition of Zamindari, the position was that in 1357 Fasli the plaintiff 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The High Court also found that there was no evidence on record to prove that the plaintiff was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the respondents assured the plaintiff of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The possession of defendants, apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District Court has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the consolidation operation either by the defendants or by somebody else as a result of which the rights of the plaintiffs were sought to be extinguished. [867D E] 1.2 In the instant case, it is manifest that the possession was of the defendants, along with being in possession of land in the hands of the respondents. Apart, from this the fact remained that the district Judge has come into a clear findings of fact and even if it was wrong (though in our opinion it is absolutely correct) it was not open to the High Court to interfere with this finding of facts in second appeal.

The petitioner, who was a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was appointed as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him. The essential requirement of article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India.[1112C] 1.3. In view of the clear statement made by the Attorney General that Respondent No . 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Prime Ministers but the description of him as Deputy Chief Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers, along with his other submis sions, there is clear statement. made by Respondent No 2 that Respondent 1 is not just a member of the Com missioner of Ministers although he has be described as the Deputy Prime Minis ter but the particulars of Respondent Nos.

The appellant, a carding department of the Carnatic Mills stopped work on the night of 1st November, 1948. The stoppage ended at 8 p.m. and the stoppage ended in both the departments. By 10 p. m., the strike ended completely. The apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st Nov., 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on 1st ' November amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the Factories Act (XXV of 1934) and that the Management had decided that the workers who participated in such strike would not be entitled to holidays with pay under section 49 B(1). The appellant contended that the closure of work for a period of two to four hours was not to be regarded as interruption of service of a workman for the purpose of the said section. Held, that the action of the 859 workers on the day of 1th November, i.e., 10 p m.m., amounted to a strike and the workers thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal was clearly right and the conclusion could not be avoided that the workmen were acting in concert. That being so, the action on the morning of 1 st November, 952 fell within the definition of the expression "strike" in section 2(q) of the .

The respondent complainant, despite notice having been served on him, did not enter appearance. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the (for short, the Act), there is a justification for its display thereafter and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 of the Penal Code, the public exhibition circulation or distribution or the production of the film even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence. The appellant filed this appeal after obtaining special leave from the Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 79 makes an offence a non offence. When only when the offending act is actually justified by law or is bona fide believed by mistake of fact to be so justified. If, as here, the Board of Censors acting within their jurisdiction and on an application made and pursued in good faith, sanctions the public exhibitor connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 79 exonerates them at least in view of their bona fide belief that the certificate is justificatory. [516C D] 1.2 The prosecution has failed to establish that he was actually justified in committing the act or, alternatively, that he entertained a mistake of facts and in good honestly believed that he had been justified by Law in committing it. [ 516D E] K. A. Abbas. Maybe, art cannot be imprisoned by the bureaucrat and aesthetics can be robbed of the glory and grace and free expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any department, more so in cinema pictures. So it is that a special legislation viz. the Act of 1952 sets up a Board of Film Censorors of high calibre and expertise, provides hearings, appeals and ultimate judicial review, pre censorship and conditional exhibitions and wealth of other policing strategies. [616C E] 1:3 The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. If the offender can irrefutably establish that the he is actually satisfied justified bylaw or is bonafide believed by mis faith to be, then, the weapon of section 79 demolishes the prosecution. [ 515F G] 2.1 A special legislation namely the Act, of 1952 set up a board of Carsors of High calibre and experts, provides hearing appeals and final judicial review. Pre censorship or conditional exhibitions, wealth of others policing films under article 19(2) from the angle of public order, decency or morality. These concepts are themselves dynamic and cannot be whittled down to stifle expression nor licentiously enlarged to promote a riot of sensual display. The petitioner, a Government Pleader for the Patna District, was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case. I shall myself conduct this case and I have enough time for it." The petitioner was admittedly the Government Pleader and one other of them put in his charge of bunch of Land acquisition cases, as part of the professionalestate ' of a Government pleader. The Petitioner challenged the powers of Government under Article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the official income expected from this heavy harvest of cases, of Rs. 1 lakh was being taken away by a brother practitioner. In support of his alleged injustice, he has pressed into service Section 2(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs thus: "2.(7). 'Government Pleader includes any officer appointed by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code on the Government pleader and also any pleader acting under the directions of the Government Advocate. " The petitioner contended that his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in ordering about a Government Advocate is obnoxious but nothing savouring of such conduct is made out although we must enter a caveat that Governments under our Constitution shall not play with law offices on political or other impertinent considerations as it may affect the legality of the action and subvert the rule of law itself. [766C D] 2. The three criteria are, source of the office, the tenure and the duties. I have applied that test and I am of opinion that the conclusion that the office is a public office is irresistible. In this view, ordering about the Government Counsel is obnoxious, but nothing leg savouring or of such act is made Out though we must entering a caveat. [764C] 3. The State must evolve a policy in regard to its Law Officers which concedes to counsel freedom to recommend settlement of cases if they feel it just to do so and further practiced distributial justice which preempts the need for adjournment because of absence of counsel and, lastly, sets a limit on the total fee payable for government work executed. [774D] 4. The Court must evolve the policy in respect of its law Officers which conceded to counsel free to recommend settle of cases. When there were several thousand cases in the Patna courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality of tribunals, it was but right that Government did not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf, for the sake of the lucrative practice of a single government Pleader. It is inconceivable how he would have discharged his duties to the Court and to his client if this crowd of land Acquisition cases were posted in several courts more or less at the same time. adjournment to suit advocates ' convenience becomes a bane when it is used only for augmentation of counsel 's income, resisting democratisation and distributive justice within the profession. These principles make poor appeals to those who count, is a pity. [754D E] 5. The Government Pleader is not bound to encourage monopoly within the professions.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50 and the shareholders had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The Mills as the holder of 5,000 shares became entitled to receive 1,6662 shares of that Bank at the rate of Rs 100 per share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of the Mills passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5.,000 ordinary shares in the capital of the Bank of India Ltd. having now received an intimation from the said Bank that this company is entitled to get 1,6766,62 shares more ordinary shares on payment of Rs 50 as capital and Rs.50 as premium per each share and it is considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said bank the funds of this company to the extent of 66 shares only and to distribute the right of this Company to the remaining 1,600 shares of which the appellants had agreed to the allotment of these shares. The seven appellants as holders of shares of a Mills became entitled under section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, to receive Rs. 1,65,62,60 shares of one of the shareholders of the mills. The appellants agreed to this allotment of shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., which was the holder. The assessment of the seven appellants and other shareholders of that Mills was reopened under section 34(1)(a) of the Act by the Income Tax Officer on the footing that the release by the Mills amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A), it was still dividend within the ordinary meaning of that expression and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. The order of the Income tax Officer reassessing the income of the 7 appellants was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and by the Tribunal.

% The appellant was elected to Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency. He filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act, 1951 for short). To this petition, the returned candidate as well as all other candidates who lost the election were impleaded as parties. In the election petition charges of corrupt practice and irregularities in the conduct of election were made. The returned candidate submitted a list of witnesses intimating to the Court that he desires to examine them. This was objected to by the returned candidates. After hearing the parties, the Court framed appropriate issues. The appellant 's objection raised by the respondent was rejected by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 Rule 22 of the Rules framed by the Court clearly envisaged filing of a list only in respect of witnesses whom the parties desire to t examine and procure presence with the assistance of the court. [532C] 1.2 The obligation to supply the list of witness within the time prescribed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of order XVI is in respect thereof of witnesses to procure whose attendance the party needs the assistance. When a summons is issued by the court for procuring the presence of a witness, it has certain consequences in law. If the summons is served and the person served fails to comply with the same, certain consequences are in law ensue as provided in Rule 10 of order XVIII. The consequence is that where the witness summoned either to give evidence or to produce documents fails to attend or to production the documents in compliance with such summons, the court on being satisfied of the service as provided therein and is further satisfied that the person has without lawful excuse failed to honour the summons,the Court may issue is a proclamation requiring him to attend to give his evidence or produce the document at a time and place to be named therein; and a copy of such proclamation shall be affixed in the manner therein provided.

% The appellant, a double M.A., and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of principal of Shrinath Intermediate College, Garhmalpur Sahulie, Distt. Balia (College ' for short) issued by the Committee of Management of the College. The Selection Committee constituted by sec. 16F of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 held the interview on April 12, 1981 and the appellant was required to present himself before the Manager of the college and take over the charge within 10 days of the receipt of the order failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter of appointment the appellant presented himself at the College on May 1, 1981 addressed a notice to the staff intimating that he has assumed charge of the post as Principal and he had convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on the same day after college hours in the teachers ' room. The appellant sent a copy of it to the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia, requesting him to hand over charge to him. There was an endorsement below this communication by the Manager that the appellant had assumed charge and convened an extraordinary meeting of staff to he held on April 7, 1981. The Committee of management considered the matter and passed an order dated April 7 1981 communicated by a radiogram to the various authorities. The order was challenged in a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 While enacting the regulations prior sanction of the State Government is necessary and under sub section 4 of sec. 9 the State Govern ment enjoys the power to make appointments on the recommendation of the Selection Committee. The power to appoint is conferred by the regulations.

The appellants, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner. The appellants state that the manufacturers of goods to whom they manufactured, use it for the purpose of impregnating it with rubber, fall under entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954 (the Act). The appellants contended that the goods now sought to be taxed were not the "end product" and that the sales of these goods had wrongly escaped assessment. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the appellants ' objections to Sales tax on "rayon cord fabric". The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the order and provisional assessment dated 21st November, 1972. The High Court did not find any error apparent on the face of the record and that there was no error apparent upon the face or the record. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that (1) the goods were not "end products" and (2) the fact that the tyre cord fabric serves as raw material for another fabric which ultimately emerges by subjecting the goods manufactured by Delhi Cloth Mills to a process of impabricating with rubber fell under entry 19. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The term "textile fabrics" has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in the Oxford English Dictionary is: "A product of skilled workmanship". [501C] (b) The word "fabric" has been given in Webster 's English Dictionary, that is "a product ofkilled workmanship." The term fabric has a wider meaning. its first meaning has given in a Oxford English dictionary is: 'A product 'of skilled work experience". The first example of such a product is "an edifice, a building". [500D] (c) The question whether the tyre fabric is the end product or not in the final manufacture of an other fabric was quite irrelevant. It was, therefore, difficult to find fault with the view of the High court that there is no error on the part of the Tribunal. [500E F] (d) The essential question to determine is the stage at which the goods under consideration become a "textiles fabric". [ 500G] (e) The meaning of the term "Textile" given in section 2(C) of the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act, 1957, is: that woven fabric any kind of cloth. It must acquire a body and a texture. Presumably it is not just the skeleton of a textile textile. Apparently, it is more than that. But, against pushing this point of view too far it may be urged that in the technical and commercial parlance we are dealing with a "feel fabric".

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under Section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour court Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Appellate Court Patna. The High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the writ petition with an observation: "Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, we are not inclined to interfere with the order under challenge". This application is dismissed" The management in the appeal challenges the Government notification withdrawing and transferring the pending case from the Labour court Dhanbad to Labour Courts, Patna. Since the impugned notification has been issued under Section 33 B of the , it is obligatory to record reasons in support of its decision. Reasons would be necessary for immediate reference set out that Section 33B of the . The expression 'may ' in sub section (1) of Section 33 A only makes it discretionary in so far as the appropriate Government taking a decision as to whether the power conferred thereunder has to be exercised or not. But when once a decision is taken to transfer a pending case then the requirement of giving reasons becomes mandatory. [294D E] In the instant case, the key question for consideration is whether the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring it from the labour court, Dhanbad should have given an opportunity to t he management? The validity of the reasons given by the Government for transferring the case was another question to be considered. [292G H] In Pioneer Ltd. vs Labour Court, Hyderabad, ; , referred to.

The appellant was the manager of a hotel. The main contesting respondent was that the reference was incompetent inasmuch as the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and (2) the reference in this form was incompetent. Held, that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer, namely, the management of the hotel and its employees, which were mentioned as its workmen. The addition of the words "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " was merely for the sake of convenience so that the tribunal may know to whom it should give notice when proceeding to deal with the reference. That however did not preclude the workmen, if they wanted to be represented by any other union, to apply to the Tribunal for such representation or even to apply for being made parties individually. Held further, that in view of the fact that more than three years had passed since the reference, it was necessary to refer the said industrial dispute for adjudication; and that the present reference as compared to the references in that case could not therefore be called vague at all. The fact that in the order of reference the quoted words were added for the purpose of convenience as to where the notice to the workmen should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C.R. 334, followed. State Of Madras vs M. C.P. Sarathiyathy, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a bushings and bearings imported by the appellant were assessed to duty under the Customs Tariff Act. The appellant claimed that the goods imported by him were parts of the engines referred to in Heading No. 84.06 and not under Heading No 84.07. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of exemption under the Notification No. 281 Cus/76, granting part exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by them. The Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appel lant and affirmed the orders of the Customs authorities. According to the Appellate Tribunal, the bushits and bear ings were the same and as the bearings come under Heading 84.63 and not Heading No . 84.09. The Notification grants exemption in part from payment Of the Customs duty in favour of the appellants. Hence this appeal by the Revenue under Section 130 E of the . Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Notification No 281 C.us/ 76 granting exemption in parts from payment to the parts of engines mentioned under Heading Nos. 8406 and 84. [226F] 1.2 In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect Of parts of tile engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, it is not possible to uphold the contention that they are parts of internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading no. 84,06. [227G] 1:3 The Notification does not only intends to grant exemption to internal combustion Piston engine engines, but also to 'parts thereof '. When, therefore, the intention is clear and manifest, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notification and not to extend its benefit to the part of the engine referred to In Heading No, 84.05. [228H] 1 :4 The Notification exempts also parts of tractors mentioned under heading No.8406. The notification does not mention 'part 's of such engines.

The plaintiffs alleged that after the death of his mother, nobody was employed as an agent. The defendants served a notice on 23.3.1972 calling upon the defendants to recognize the right of management of the plaintiffs in the Dargah. The respondents sent a reply stating that the plaintiffs claiming through female were not entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Wakf and even if they were entitled to claim any right or claim the same was barred by limi tation. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the plaintiff were entitled t he reliefs of declaration that they are entitled to be in management of Dargah and to bein enjoyment of the Hundial income during the said period. The High Court allowed the second appeals and while setting aside the judgments and decrees of the Courts below dismissed the suit filed by the plaintiffs. Hence this appeal by the defendants contending that the courts below proceeded upon an erro neous assumption as if it was the duty of the defendants, to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster has been established. It is further contended that even the answering defendants were paying such share to their sisterunnissa (lOth de fendant) in the Hudial collection of the Dargah and even though she was not a party in the aforesaid litigation and any judgment given in that suit cannot be held as res judi cata or binding on Fathima Bee or the present plaintiffs. It was further alleged that even if she had got any right, the same could be lost as she did not claim any rights till her death. The appellants and their counsel submitted that they were paying the share of 27 days may be fixed jointly and so far as their own proportion of 18 and 9 days is concerned they will make their arrangement inter se. After hearing the parties and considering the entire facts and circumstances of the case, this Court uphold ing the decree passed by the First Appellate Court with the following modification in the arrangement of days in the Management of the Wakf in question. The plaintiffs would be entitled to such management from 17th to 30th June and 1st July in the next year from 18th to30th June, 1990 and they shall continue to follow such cycle by rotation every year. For the reasons stated above, this court set aside the judgment and decree of the High Court dated 17th Nov., 1987 and re store that of the Trial Court as affirmed by the first Appellate Court and restored that of First Appellate Bench with modifications as stated earlier.

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. At that time his wages were Rs. 18 per month plus dearness allowance. With effect from 1st November 1947, the Railway Board under the Ministry of Railways introduced a scheme of grant of compensatory (city) allowance and house rent allowance at rates specified in their memorandum No. E47 CPC/14 dated 1st December 1947. The first respondent put in his claim before the Authority for Rs. 290 on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to any house rent allowances. The Authority condoned the delay and allowed the claim for Rs, 290. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled. Whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him, will depend upon the construction to be placed on the following material portion of the definition of "wages" in section 2(vi) of the Act: Held further that the rule which must include the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee, is inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 1 of the , and therefore the grant of house rent cannot create an indefeasible right in the employee at all places wherever he may be posted and in all circumstances irrespective of whether or not he has been offered Government quarter.

The detenu was one of the detenus. The two detenus were carrying on business in diamonds and precious stones in partnership under the style of "M/s Gems Impex Corporation". 35, New Marine Lines Bombay, since 1971. On November 16, 1979, the Customs Officers at Bombay raided the residential premises of the son Indru 's, and seized two cameras and three wrist watches worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. On the following day, the customs officers raided the premises of that firm and seized the diamonds, pearls worth about rupees 55 lakhs. The detenus were arrested on November 23, 1979 and interrogated. During interrogation, the detenus claimed that the gems and other articles seized were not smuggled goods but were local materials, locally acquired. They also gave the names of four persons from whom these gems had been acquired. Both the father and the son were arrested and were produced before a Magistrate. They were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs officers and cooperate in the investigation. This condition was later on related. On February 16, 1980, an order of detention was passed purporting to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short called COFEPOSA) by the State Government was served on the detenus alongwith the order of Detention on February 15, 1980. The detenu had also sent a petition through the Central Government complaining of the non supply of copies of the necessary documents. They further made representations to the detaining authority that their request for revocation had been rejected. The Central Government advised the State Govt. to furnish the detenus with the copies of required documents. As a result, on April 3, 1980 copies were received by the detenus from the State Governments under their covering letter dated March 31, 1980 and were actually received by them on April March 25, 1980 respectively. On March 24, 1980 the detenu also made a representation to the State government which, according to the information furnished at the Bar by the detenu, was declined. The order of the Central Govt. was authenticated by the Under Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra, Home Department, was served upon the detenus along with the order dated February 18, 1980 on the direction of the Chief Minister that the copies were supplied. On April 3. 1980, the wife of the detenu addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to The State Government) requesting him to furnish them with the material relied upon by the detaining Authority in the grounds of detention. On May 4, 1980 a representation was made to the Central government for revocation of the order.

The Gujarat High Court in its order referred to section 258 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960 was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI Of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Full Bench of the High Court on an exhaustive discussion held that a joint appeal to be maintainable in law was not binding on it. On the view that the decision of this Court in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's case was wrong, instead of following the usual procedure in case of difference of opinion with an earlier decision of referring the question to a lar ger Bench. Judicial decorum no less than legal propriety forms the basis of judicial procedure. If one thing is more necessary in law than any other thing, it is the quality of certainty. That quality would totally disappear if judges of co ordinate jurisdiction in a High Court start overruling one another 's decision. If two Division Bench of a High 'Court is unable to distinguish a previous decision of another Division bench and holding the view of that the earlier decision was wrong itself gives effect to that view, the result would be utter confusion. The other decisions containing similar observations are: jai Kaur and others vs Sher Singh etc. [1960]3 S.C.R. 78 (2) (4) I.L.R., 37 All. 604 (P.C.) A.I.R 1962 Guj. 125, followed. Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , referred to.

The appellant was a firm carrying on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family but rejected the contention that the family was not liable to pay tax on the profits for the said period. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such is not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 Act but only receipt of the income in British India is assessed and it cannot therefore be held that the foreign business of the appellant was charged to tax under the 1918 Income tax Acts. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee in part. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (i) The assessee received the entire profits of the foreign company in British Indian India and the entire income of the Foreign business was remitted to the assessee and tax imposed on that income under the 1920 Act. [908 H] (ii) The High court was in error in holding that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act with regard to the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. [09 C D] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others ; , followed.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of the Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. The Deputy Commissioner held the supplied of bricks by the assessee as sales. The assessee then appealed to the Tribunal against that order. The Tribunal following the ratio of Chandra Bhan Gosain vs The State of orissa and others, came to the conclusion that the supplies of bricks were sales. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department for the construction of Capital Project; pervershinagar." The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a works contract. In coming to that conclusion, the High court held as follows: (1) The decision of the Supreme Court in Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain 's case is clearly distinguishable on facts and the decision of this Court in Chander Bhan Gosai 's Case will govern the facts of this case. (2) The question will depend upon the intention of the parties executing the contract. As we have observed ill our judgment in State of Gujarat vs Variety Body Builders, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 879, the property in the bricks was entirely of the asses see. He had not only to manufacture that but also to stack them for facilitating delivery. The essence of the contract was, therefore, the delivery of the bricks after manufacture.

The petitioner, an assessee under the Income tax Act and Wealth Tax Act during the assessment year 1976 77 was liable to pay income tax and Wealth tax in accordance with the rates prescribed by the Finance Act, 1976 which was passed by the Lok Sabha during its extended period which was extended under the provisions of the House of People (Extension of Duration) Act,1976 after the expiry of five years from the date appointed for its first meeting. The petitioner contended that the duration of the Assembly could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 83 of the Constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House was passed. The contentions raised on behalf of the petitioner were that the two Proclamation of emergency dated 3nd December,1971 and 25st June,1975 were either intra vires the constitution or had lapsed to be operated on 4th February, 1972; (2)(a) the proclamation of Emergency issued under clause (1) of article 352 of the Constitu tion was ultra vires, and (b) the two proclamation of Emergency had been duly issued by the President acting as President by the Proclamation dated 27th March, 1977. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Pro Clamations issued in India right from the days of Queen Victoria on many important occasions which had been widely published in the official Gazette and by other means. The newspapers, Radio and television are also the modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament and the Legislatures of the States. [439C D] 2. If the Constitution requires that a particular mode of publica tion is necessary then such mode must be followed but if there is no mode of publication prescribed by it then it must be considered that the Constitution has left the method of publication to the authority issuing the proclamation in order to make it known to the members of the public. [442D] 3. If there is some delay in the publication of the Central Act in the Official Gazette, its operation does not get suspended until such publication unless the contrary is expressed in the statute itself. While on the face of it, as observed, by Sir C.K. Allen in his Law and orders (2nd Edn.) at page 132, it would seem reasonable that legislation of any kind should not be binding until it has some how been 'made known ' to the public, "that is not the rule of law and if it were, the automatic cogency of a statute which has received the royal assent would be seriously and most inconveniently impaired. [443E F] 4. The present case must fall within either the one category or the other. [444F G] 5.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The application was subsequently converted into a suit. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the premises constituted a temple and set aside the decision of the said authorities. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by it did not involve directly or indirectly a claim or question res pecting property of the value of Rs. 20,000/ . The High Court was therefore wrong in proceeding on the aforesaid assumption. [157 B] In the present case, the appellant 's case was that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of his family and that it was alienable property and therefore capable of a valid transfer. That being the dispute between the parties, the question whether the property was theprivate property of that family or was a public temple as held by the High court. [158 C] The appellant ' case was accepted by the trial court but was rejected by theHigh Court and the High Courts held that the property in question constituted a Temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. [159 D] In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High court was wrong in proceed on the assumption that whether the properties were private or a public religious temple was incapable of valuation as it could have in either case no market value. It may be observed that the appellant claimed that the properties belonged to the Thoguluva family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf of the family. The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 37 of 1950 under section 84(2) of Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 11 of 1927. Under that Act only a fixed court fee was payable.

The appellant company, which had given rise to the present appeal centered round two items of claim made by the respondents. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangements at present made by them and they urged that the practice started by the appellant of employing retired persons should be discontinued. The Tribunal found that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiff in lieu thereof, because he argued that it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffs employees by way of giving them a cash allowance. Held, that the question posed by the respondent ' demand must be considered. The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the said re employed person are bound to support the appellant. The result is the appeal fails and is dismissed with costs. Appeal dismissed. There was a dispute between the parties, one of the items in dispute being the claim made in respect of tafiffin allowance and dearness allowance. The question posed for by the respond ent 's demand must he considered. Held further that the Tribunal had overlooked the fact that it appeared to the appellant that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant sympathetically and generously considered their request for re employment and that was, the basis on which some of the re employments have been made.

The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Financial Adviser and Chief Accounts Officer, East India Railways requesting that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident fund Account be remitted to the Westminster Bank, Birmingham. The respondent then drew two cheques one for Rs. 14,428 8 9 and another for Rs 23,018 11 10 in favour of the Reserve Bank of India with instructions to convert amounts covered by the cheques into sterling and to transmit the fund in sterling to the bankers of Browne in England. The Union of India also applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The executing court overruled the objection observing that the respondent 's property had ceased to be provident fund, but it was not immune from the attachment. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The money in the hands of the respondent Bank had ceased lo be provident Fund money and were liable to be attached. [31 F] (ii) The Union Government was a trustee for the subscriber of the money. When the amount lying with the Reserve bank as the agent of the Railway Administration was attached, the Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal. The order of attachment of the amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . [31 G] (iii) The High court was in error in holding that the sum in the hand of the Union Bank had become ceased to he provident fund and was liable to pay attached. It was somewhat faintly suggested that the Union of india had no interest in maintaining an application for removing attachment. But the Union Government of India was a Trustee for the subscribers of the moneys. When, the amount remained under the control of the railway Administration as provident fund property, it was exempt from attachment.

The appellant, a former Regional Manager of the respondent company, was dismissed from service by an order dated September 2, 1970. The appellant challenged the said order before the Labour Court under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the action being a simple termination without a sting process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. The Labour Court held that the punishment for misconduct was a colourable exercise of the power to terminate the services of a workman under the provisions of the Standing Orders. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Labour court. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The social justice ice perspective and particular facts are important though. The plethora if precedents need not be covered in extenso as the law laid down is the same except that judicial response to each case leads to emphasis on different facets of the principle. Even so some milestone decisions, if we say so, may be considered. In Murugan Mills Case (supra) Wanchoo J. (as he then was), speaking for the Court made the following observations: "The right of the employer to terminate his services simpliciter under a standing order like cl.17(a) in the present case, which amounts to a claim 'to hire and fire ' an employee as the employer pleases and thus completely negatives security of service which has been secured to industrial employees through industrial adjudication came up for consideration before the labour Appellate Tribunal in Buckingham & Carnatic Co. Ltd vs Workers of the Company. The matter then came up before this Court also in Chartered Bank vs Chartered Bank Employees Union ; and the Management of U. B. Dutt & Co. vs Workmen of U . B. Datt & Co., [1971] II L. J. 620. 423 1.2 In the instant case, the catalogue of circumstances set out in the earlier part of the judgment strikes a contrary note.

The Lions Club, Pottery Town at Khurja in Uttar Pradesh arranged and conducted as part of its social service programme, an "Eye Camp" intended to extend facilities of expert Ophphthal mic surgical services to the residents of the town. The club invited Dr. R.M. Sahay of the Sahay Hospital, Jaipur and his team of doctors to offer the surgical services. The Camp was arranged in 'Aggarwal Dharamshala ' at Novelty Road, Khurja. Dr.R.M., Sahay returned on the 24th April and undertook himself some ameliorative treatment. But the operated eyes had been damaged completely. Similar mishap, but on lesser scale affecting some patients, repeated itself at Moradabad. Some of the victims were later sent to and treated at Dr. Sahay 's Hospital at Jaipur. But their condition did not improve. It was now undisputed that this terrible medical misha p was due to common contaminating source. The suggestion in the Report of the 245 enquiries that ensued is that, in all probability, the source of the infection, referred to as E coli cation of the intra ocular cavity, was the "normal saline" used on the eyes at the time of surgery. Dr., R. M. Sahay and his staff members and para medical staff, who arrived in Khurja on 21st April, 1986 examined about 122 patients. One hundred and eight patients were operated upon, 88 of them for Cataract which, with the modern advances in Ophthalmic Surgery, is considered a relatively minor and low risk surgery. The doctors present at the Camp got in touch with Dr. Suresh Kumar Balakrishna Joshi, Sub Divisional Magistrate, Khurja as to the incident, are also before the Court. The petitioners have made serious allegations about the very bona fides of, and the intention behind, the sponsoring of the iII fated "eye camp" and have alleged that motives of monetary gains by way of State and International subsidies. But no material is placed before the court to substantiate this allegation.

The petitioner, a registered society under the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984 was renamed as Assam Rashtraba Prachar Samchar Samiti with its head office at Gauhati. It was contended that the procedure stated in Section 16 of the Bidhan Act was followed and as only one person opposed the Constitution amendment was passed. The petitioner also prayed for perma nent injunction restraining the respondent No. 4 and other members of the Ad hoc Committee, their agents and servants from giving effect to the order. The petitioners also filed an application under Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the issuance of a temporary injunction. It is alleged that in early part of 1983 President 's rule was lifted from Assam and a Ministry headed by Shri Hiteswar Saikia was installed in power in Assam. But in the meantime the Samiti in its meeting of the Byabastha Sabha held on 17.7.83 passed a resolution for 167 amendment of the provisions of the bidhan Act in the following manner: "That the words contained in Section 1(ii) of Article 230 of the Constitution of India may be amended as follows: (Ka) The proposal for amendment must reach the head office within the month of January every year. (Kha) The amendment proposals will be sent for information to all the members of Byabas thapika Sabha from the Office. (Ga) The amendments will be carried out by the 2/3rd members present." According to the petitioner, the procedure that stated in this Section of the constitution was followed, and as a result of that management only under this Act was taken over, but neither in the counter nor during the course of arguments anything could be said on behalf of the State for a perma tion reason of taking over of the management of the Samiti depriving its members the right under Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitu tion. In the counter it was contended by the petitioner that as this amendment was made in accordance with Section 30 of the Consti tution, which provided that the Board may constitute a Board for the purposes of takingover of the Management temporarily it could have provided for the restoration of the elected body in due course. It would have been different situation if the state felt that it wanted to do the same thing what this Samiti was doing and further the acts of education and for that purpose if it had taken steps to start similar functions at the state level probably the things would have gone different. But here we are simply concerned with the taking over over of management of a registered Society having large membership and assets and properties following programme and policies living to the ideals which could not be in any way chal lenged or adversely commented. It has been contended that even the assets and the properties of the Rashtra bhasha Samchar samiti Samiti are being mismanaged by nominated board as it has no moral attachment to the image nor aptitude with the work of the Society and the assets are being neutralized.

The appellants were the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal Sao, a resident of Asansol in Bengal. They were married in 1938 and the respondents executed a deed of gift in favour of Kamala Devi on March 10, 1940, which was later confirmed by the occasion of Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938, and possession of the houses was also given to her. After the death of Kamla Devi, the appellants filed a suit for declaration that a deed dated March 10. 1940, executed by Sumitra Devi in favour Of Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on them. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed it. In appeal to this Court by special leave: Held: (i) The gift made by Smt. Sumitra Devi on April 25, 1940 was valid and binding on the reversioners. (ii) The evidence of the witnesses did not make out any promise of a gift of four houses as marriage dowry. Nor did it affect the power of a Hindu widow to make an alienation of a reasonable portion of her husband 's estate in favour thereof. (iii) The finding of the courts below that there was an overuptial agreement by Sumitra, that she would give four houses at Asansi ceremony and that such a gift was made subsequent to the marriage and not on the occasion when any particular ceremony. There were many other criticisms of the evidence regarding the verbal gift at the time of the marriage but for the unfortunate confusion between Parasuram Sharma and Pashupati Sarkar, the High Courts did examine with care the oral evidence with regard to the alleged verbal gift made at the date of the marriages and its acceptance by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala 's party and that the acceptance of such a gifts was subsequent to her marriage. The finding that there were no " sankalpa" or promise of any gift of the four houses was not correct. (iv) It is open to a Hindu father to make a gift in respect of his daughter 's property at the, time of her marriage and it is only necessary for him to hold that the gift is not in excess of the powers of the brother and cannot therefore be recalled by him or avoided by his son.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the State Legislative Assembly, was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The polling took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. Tej Singh secured 25694 votes whereas Avtar Singh (appellant) secured 25571 votes. There were three other candidates also in the field, viz., (1) Sathi Ruplal (2) Bhagat Puran Singh and Jagdish Chander; (3) Jagdish Chander and Ruplar secured 140 votes while Bhagat Puran Chand and Jagdish Chandra secured 14056 votes respectively. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh (respondent) and Avtar Singh was only 123. Avtar Singh filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices, detailed in the petition in a statement of facts. Ruplod supported the appellant but Bhagat Puran Sing and Jagdish Chand were not put in appearance despite service and, therefore, the proceedings were taken ex parte against them. The appellant denied having indulged in any corrupt practice as alleged by Avtar Singh. It was also contended that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency wherein he had mentioned that Ruplad had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him (Tej Singh) would be deemed to be a vote for Ruplul, and the said posters were printed not by Ruplary but at the instance of Tej Singh on a perusal of the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by Tej singh have been clearly proved. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to the appellant cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was elected to the State Legislative Assembly. The said election was challenged by twelve Indian Forest Officers including the appellant by filing a writ petition in the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appellant. The learned Single Judge of the High court, after considering the application, affidavits and the submissions made on behalf of the parties, took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view of the matter, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule niisi. It is apparent from the facts stated above that the allegations against the appellant, if proved would consitute a criminal contempt. It was also not disputed by the parties that it had been a case of criminal contempt as defined in section 2(c) of the Act, and the appeal was incompetent. Section 19(1) provides as follows: "19(1). An appeal shall lie as of right from any order or decision of a High Court passed in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt (a) where the order or judgment is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court; 892 (b) where an order or decisions is that by a Bench, to the Supreme Court. Provided that where the Order or decision is that the Judgment is that or decision be that of the court of the Judicial Commissioner in any Union territory, such appeal shall be lie to the High COurt. " The right of appeal will be available under sub section (1) of section 19 only against any decision or order of a high Court passed by in the exercising of its jurisdic tion to punishfor contempt of itself. In this connection it is pertinent to refer to the provision of Article 215 of the Constitution which provides that every High Court shall be a court of record and shall have all the powers of such a court including the power to punish, for contempt of themselves. The right to appeal will also be available in accordance with sub section 1 of section 20 only against an order of the Supreme court passed in exercise of their jurisdiction to punishing for contempt.

The appellant was a minor at that time and became major in or about 1925. In the year 1928, rent for six years was in arrears. Vinayakbhat filed a suit against the present respondents for possession on the ground of forfeiture. The trial court decreed the plaintiff 's suit and negatived the contentions raised by the defendants. On appeal the District Judge confirmed the decree of the trial court with two modifications. One of the questions that fell for determination was whether the High Court should have interfered with the discretion of the lower courts in refusing relief against forfeiture in the circumstances of this case. The appellant contended that as no notice had been given to them, the forfeiture was not enforceable. Held, that the provisions of section 111(g) of the , which are but a statutory recognition of the rules of justice, equity and good conscience, govern those transfers. If, therefore, the Court is satisfied that the discretion was not judicially exercised or was exercised without proper materials they would not ordinarily interfere with it in second appeal. The rule laid down by the legislature in section 111 (g) did not represent a principle of justice and good justice to transactions which come up before them for determination even though the statutory provisions of the Transfer of Property Act are not made applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the . In the present case, the tenant was a recalcitrant tenant and was a habitual defaulter. The High Court was right in holding that section 114 of the confers a discretion on the court, that discretion except in cases where statutory provisions were made to the contrary.

The Appellant, a retired Judge of M.P. High Court, was dismissed from service by the Respondent on 30th January 1969. The Award was served on the Respondents on 30.1.1969. 365 A dispute having been raised with regard to their dismissal, by common consent, the same was referred to arbitration of Shri T.C. Shrivastava, a former Judge of the M. P. High court under section 10 A of the on 14th April 1969. During the course of which at one stage the Respondents withdrew from the enquiry on 24th October 1968 on the plea that the Quarry Agent should be examined first which was not being done, whereafter the enquiry proceeded ex parte and on a consideration of the entire evidence led before him the Enquiry Officer came to the conclusion that the first three charges were fully proved and the fourth charge was partly proved against all the Respondents while the additional charges against Emmanual and Mohd. Rauf were also proved. The Arbitrator gave his Award on 9th February 1970 whereby he came to be the conclusion, that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to the Respondents of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. 17; he further held that though before him, the Management had by leading evidence proved their mis conduct by establishing the first 3 charges against all, the fifth charge against Em manual and Md. Ruf was more grave than that of Rama Shankar and Barmapradhan while fomenting the strike; counsel urged that since the Arbitrator had power to interfere with the punishment in the instant case having to the facts and circumstances of the case he was not justified in setting aside the dismissal of Rama Shanker and Barmas and had directed their reinstatement. On behalf of the Respondents it was contended that the learned Arbitrator as well as the High Court have erroneously construed the certified Standing Order 17 as requiring a second opportunity being given to a workman at the conclusion of the enquiry into his mis conduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment of dismissal; he urged that the concept of second opportunity having been given to an delinquent which obtained under section 240(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 or article 311 of the Constitution prior to the insertion of the Proviso to Article 311 (2) could not be invoked or applied to the instant cases nor was such second opportunity any requirement of the ordinary law of the land or of Industrial Law and in this behalf reliance was placed on two decisions of this Court in Hamdard Dawakhana case and in Saharanpur Light Rly, case. The Respondents contended that Standing Order NO. 17 had been properly construed by the Arbitrator and the High court and that construction should be upheld and in any case if two constructions were reasonably possible no interference by this Court was called for and counsel in that behalf relied upon the decision Agnani (W.M.) vs Badri Das & Ors., [1969] 2 S.C R. 940, and in particular relied on the decision of this court in Ham dard Dawkhana case, and the decision in Agnini (WM.) v Badri Das and ors. [1970] 2 SCR 940. On a plain reading of the relevant words no second notice of showing any cause against tho proposed punishment is contemplated either expressly or by necessary implication. In other words, it is clear to us that the opportunity spoken of by para 3 OE S.O. 17 is the opportunity to be given to him to meet the charge framed against him. In this connection it will be pertinent to mention that the concerned S.0.O., was framed and came into force on March 1, 1946 and was duly certified on October 16, 1954 under the Industrial Employment (Standing orders) Act, 1946 i.e.

Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969 provided that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , or any law, or in any judgment, decree or order of court, any person in occupation of the land of another at the commencement of the Act, shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation thereof for not more than two years within a period of twelve years immediately preceding the 11th day of April, 1967. Explanation I to Section 7D provides that certain person occupying land under leases granted by incompetent persons to be considered deemed tenants and notwithstanding anything contained in any law or in the decree or court, no person who was in possession of the lands of another on the 11 th day of 4th April 1957, was in occupa tion of the said land for a period exceeding ten years immediately following the 11st day of March, 1967, and was cultivating the nilam at the commence ment of this Act, he shall be liable to pay an amount equal to the value of the rubber trees standing in plots. Explanation II to Section 8D provides for the purpose of this section a person shall be considered to be in continuous occupation notwithstanding any order of Court for delivery of possession to another person or any court record of dispos session. The appellant 's contention before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. In such circumstances, the High Court held that the benefit of the section would apply only to persons whose occupa tions had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. It was not within the contemplation of the legisla ture to confer the benefit Of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The expression "in occupation" occurring in Section 7 D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". In the present case, the finding of fact entered by the High court is that the appellant had come in possession o f the lands by trespass. His plea before the courts below was not accepted.
