The appellants were the President of a registered Association formed for carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The Association functioned through a President and a pioneer worker. They kept accounts and distributed the profits. Respondent No. 1, Nagar Mal, was the President, of the said Association from January 1946 to June 26, 1946. Before that, Seth Badri Prasad, one of the plaintiffs appellants before us, was President of the Association from December 1946 to May 1948. The association functioned by a President, and a Pioneer workers worker; they kept accounts, distributed the profit. Respondent 1, who was President, continued till Febr uary 1948. On June 25, 1949, thirteen members of the association out of the twenty five brought a suit, and in the plaint they alleged that respondent No. I, who had been President of an Association from Jan 1946 to July 26,1946, had given an account of income and expenditure for the months of January, February and March 1946 but had given no accounts for the month of April May and June 1946. They therefore prayed (a) that defendant No.1 be ordered to pay the amount whatever is found due to the plaintiffs on account being done, along with interest at the rate of annas 12 per cent; and (b) that interest for the period of the suit till realisation of the dues be allowed. The District Judge who dealt with the suit in the first instance passed a preliminary decree in favour of the plaintiff appellants. The decree directed Nagar Mal to render accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1946 to March 26, and it further directed that leaving out 106 bales of Gwalior cloth which Nagar Mal gave to the Association an option of taking over the consignment; if the Association did not exercise the option, the consignment would be taken over by Nagar Mal. The preliminary objection was not taken in any of the two courts below. Held, that the preliminary objection must succeed and must be upheld. It is enough if it is shown that ultimately there was an order to the effect that only 390 bales should be allotted to the association Out of which Nagarmal had given the Association benefit of the sales of 106 bales, and the dispute related to the share of profits made on the remaining 284 bales. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Company Ltd., [1924] L.R. 52 I.A. 126, referred to.

The respondents, who were accused in two Special Leave Petitions, moved the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the order taking cognizance against them. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the respondents. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the specific allegation in the present case concerns the specific act of killing of an elephant, al1d that such an offence at all events, falls within the overlapping areas between section 42 IPC on the one hand and 9(1) read with 50(l) of the Act on the other and therefore constitutes the same offence apart from the fact that this argument does not serve to support the order of the High court in the instant case. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The policy and object of the Wild life laws have a long history and are the result of an increasing awareness of the compelling need to restore the serious ecological imbalances introduced by the depradations inflicted on nature by man. [465G] 2. In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence under more than one Act. If there two distinct and separate offences with different ingredients under two different enactments, a double punishment is not barred. In the instant cases, even if the jurisdictional police purported to register a case for an alleged offence against the Act, section 210(1), would not be attracted having regard to the position that cognizance of such an off offence can only be taken on the complaint of the officer mentioned in that section. Even where a Magistrate takes cognisance of an offence instituted otherwise than on a police report and an investigation by the police is in progress in relation to same offence, the two cases do not lose their separate indentity. The section seeks to obviate the anomalies that might arise from taking cognisance more than once and, accordingly, section210 has no role to play. [467C D] 3. In view of the fact, that cognizance can be taken only in one way and that on the complaints of a particular statutory functionary there is no scope or occasion for taking cogn Cognizance more than Once and, therefore, section 209 has no application. [468D E] 4. The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act" in section 56 of the Indian Penal Code merely imports the idea tat the same acts or omission might constitute an offences under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. [473E F] 5. In a case where cognizance can have been taken only on the report of the police officer mentioned therein, there is nothing further. [472G] 6.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, on the ground that he had committed a serious breach of bail conditions imposed in his favour by the Chief Judicial Magistrate. The High Court rejected the application of the petitioner for bail. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the accused that the power of the Supreme Court to enlarge a person during the pendency of a Special Leave Petition or of an appeal is very wide, as order 21 Rule 27 of the Central Civil Procedure Code disclosed. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The legal literature, Indian and Anglo American, on bail jurisprudence lends countenance to the contention that bait loosely used, is comprehensive enough to cover release on ones own bond with or without sureties. [455C] 2.1 In a liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on one 's own recognizance with punishment provided for violation will go a long way to reform the bail system and help the weaker and poorer sections of the community to get equal justice under law. Conditional release may take the form of entrusting the accused to the care his relatives or releasing him on supervision. The court or the authority granting bail may have to use the discretion judiciously. When the accused is too poor to find sureties, there will be no point in insisting on his furnishing bail with sureties, as it will only compel him to be in custody with the consequent handicaps in making his defence. [441D E] 2:2 The legal legislation which prescribes the various forms of bail in the Code and prisoners ' rights, when cast in ambiguous language become precarious. Where doubts arise the Gandhian talisman becomes a tool of interpretation: "Whenever you are in doubt apply the following test. recalled the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen, and ask yourself, if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use of him. " Law, at the service of life must respond interpretatively to raw realities and make for liberties. Primarily Chapter XXXIII is the nidus of the law of bail. [442E F] 2 :3 The legal jurisprudence, Indian & Anglo American on bail legislation lends countenance the contention of counsel that baits loosely use, is a comprehensive enough enough to covers release on cycles with orwithout sureties. Even so, poor men Indians in monetary terms indigents young persons infirm individual and women are weak categories and courts should be liberal in releasing them on their own recognisances put whatever reasonable condition you may. It Shocks one conscience to ask a mason like the petitioner to Furnish sureties for Rs. 100,000/ The magistrate must be given the benefit of doubt for not fully appreciating that our Constitution. enacted by 'We the People of India ' is meant for the butcher , the baker and the candle stick maker shall we add the bonded labour and pavement dweller. To add insult to injury, the Magistrate has demanded sureties from his own district. (We assume the allegation in the petition). What is a Malayalee, Kannadiga, Tamilian or Andhra to do if arrested for alleged misappropriation or them or criminal trespass in Bastar Port Blair , Port Bolair ,Port Blaiir , Port Bamouleir Pahalgaam of Chandni Chowk? He cannot have sureties owning properties in these distant places. He may not know any one there and might have come in a batch or to seek a job or in a morcha . Judicial disruption of Indian unity is surest achieved buy such provincial allergies. What law prescribes the sureties from outside or non regional linguistic, some times legalistic. applications? What law prescribe the geographical discrimination implicit in asking for sureties from the court district?

The assessee company had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills and sought to include in the computation of its capital so employed Rs. 2,21460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that there were two undertakings, the same eight partners with a share of /2/(two annas) each, and that the constitution of both the undertakings being the same, 'Cartle ' could not be regarded as a separate entity. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order but the Income tax Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the assessee in the calculation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15C. An application under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act to the Tribunal to refer a question which it was contended by the Commissioner arose out of the order of the Tribunal was rejected and the petition of the Commissioner under section66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal not to state the case and refer it to the High Court was also dismissed. The Commissioner appealed to this Court. Held, that the finding of the Appellate Assistant Commission that in the previous year to the year of assessment 1951 52 the income from 'Ctastle" had not been computed and included in the assessment of the assessee, could not therefore be regarded a relevant factor. Section 66(2), invests the High court with jurisdiction to require the Appellate Tribunal to state a case and to refer it if the Appellate tribunal has refused to state its case on the view that no question of law arises, and the High Courts being approached by the aggrieved party within the period of limitation prescribed, is not satisfied about the correctness of the decision of the appellate Tribunal refusing to state it the case.

The Minister concerned, heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition was thereafter amended and 97 in the amended petition, Duggal respondent also challenged the validity of the later order of February 18.1975. At the hearing of the appeal before this Court, the learned Counsel for the appellant contended that looking to the facts of the case if the High Court came to the conclusion that the Minister was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matter. Dismissing the appeal partly, HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the ease, this court does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order of the High COurt adding the Minister to the writ petition. [97 F] The direction of the high Court in so far as it has directed that the Secretary should file his personal affidavit is set aside. [98 C D] In the instant case, the High Courts were in error in directing that the Chief Minister concerned should file an affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister concerned to decide in the light of the allegation made in petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavits. [99 G H; 99 A B] The other part of the order whereby the Minister con cerned was directed to file his Personal affidavit is struck aside.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, on January 7, 1960 for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 259 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge Ambala, contending that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of rent due under a lease under section259 of the Act and in any case that could not be done without taking into account the objections of the respondents. The Sessions Judge accepted the view of the Sessions judge and set aside the order of the Magistrate dated June 13 1961. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in setting aside the orders of the magistrate under article 227 of the Constitution. [350 B] (ii) Section 259 provides that in the event of non compliance with the terms of any notice, order or requisition issued to any person under this Act, or any rule or bye law made thereunder requiring such person to execute any work or to do any act, it shall be lawful for the Board, whether or not the person in default is liable to punishment for such default or has been prosecuted or sentenced to any punishment therefor after giving notice in writing to such person, to take such action or such steps as may be necessary for the completion of the act or work required to be done or executed by him. [351 B] In the instant case, the Magistrate was not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure and, therefore, neither could a reference be made by him to the High Court under section 438 of the Code. [352 C] (iii) The provisions of section 259 do not bar the right of the Board as an owner or holder of land and buildings to take action for recovery of rent thereof by suit under the general law of the land. Further, the section does not bar a right of a Board as owner orholder of land & buildings to taking action for recover rent thereof from a tenant who was liable under an express provision of the Rent Acts or the Rules to pay rent to the Board. [353 G] (iv) The words "rent on land and building" which appear between the words "any tax" and "any other money" must equally be governed by the words 'recoverable by a Board etc." Therefore, the provisions of sections 259 and 260 of the Cantonment Act can be utilised for realisation Of arrears of rents on land & building only if such rent is recoverable by a board or a Military Estate Officer under the Act or the rules made thereunder.

The appellant was employed to do canvassing and promote sales for the company. The appellant was appointed as a section Salesman for the districts of Bikaner, Ganganagar, Merta and Barmer in Rajasthan with his head quarters at Bikaner. There were seven other local salesmen and local travelling salesmen in his area. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was employ ed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company 's product in his areas. The Tribunal also found that the appel lant is required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. Some of the documents relate to matters of publicity in melas, some relate to the existing position of the stock of the goods of the Company in the area and the action taken to ameliorate stocks. It was not the duty of the appellant to procure orders for the Company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell the product of the companies in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company, but the Tribunal noted that the Appellant was required to supervise the work of the local sales men and local travel salesmen appointed in the areas of his operation as well but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting sale of the product. The section salesmen & the local Salesmen and Local Trav elling salesmen who were employed by the Company at Calcutta in order to canvass and promote the sales and promote them the sales. From 475 perusal of the records produced before this Court, it was apparent that the appellants was employed for canvassing, and ping ing and promoting sales for them the company and promoting their sales of products in his Area. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study and study of its market condition. He was also required to suggest about the advertise ments including the need for posters, holder and cinema slide. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could not be termed as either manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical in nature. The supervising work of other local Sales men was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental ties to his primary work of canvassing, promotion in the Area of his opera tion. Such a person cannot be termed a workman is also the ratio of the decision of this Court in Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah Corporation and Burmah Oil Storage & Distribution Co. vs Burmahs Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and others (1974 11 LLJ 9). The finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before it. It is seen from the facts found that in the instant case, the appellant has been employed to carry canvassing and promotion sales for its company. He is also required under the employment to do the work as well as to collect the amount of sale. The Section salesmen Act and the local salemen and the Local Salesmen are appointed. The appellants were ap pointed as a Section salesman for various districts of Jodhpur, Gangagar Merta, Merwara and Barland in Rajasthan. The other evidence on record showed that they were employed for the companies.

The appellant Company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Sampatram. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant, and that it had not become a `Pakka" tenant under section 54(vii) of Part II of the Act. The High Court also held that the Company could not be evicted by summary proceeding provided for under that section. In the appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant Company it was contended: (i) that the High Court had wrongly held that a `gair Mauriusi tenant ' and that the company could not, by virtue of the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, become a Pukka tenant thereof; (ii) that in terms, of Act No. 66 of 1950, the company was not an occupancy tenant under Section 185 of the Code as it had neither become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act No 66 of 1960; and (iii) that even assuming that the appellant company had brought to this court Civil Appeal No. 299 of 1967 and that appeal was, as unconditionally withdrawn by the company in 1971, the State entered into an agreement with the Company to grant a fresh lease for a periods of ten year from 9.2.1971 subject to the payment of enhanced rent as agreed upon between the parties. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the High court to the contrary was totally unjustified and opposed to law. [179E] 2. Section 182 of the M.P. Land Revenue Act, 1959 defines 'pakki tenant" as "a person holding land from the State Government under section 181", Section 181 of the code reads: "181.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions of section 39 of the said Act other than those contained in Chs. III and IV were brought into force. The Legislature of the State of Orissa amended the principal act by Act 13 of 1965. By that Act 13 Of 1965 amendments were made in the principal Acts : the expressions "ceiling area" and "privileged raiyat" were defined by clauses (5) & 24 of section 24 and the expression "classes, of land" was defined in section 2(5a). The original Chs III and 4 of the Principal Act were deleted and were substituted by fresh provisions. By the amendment made in 1956 the principal Ordinance was incorporated in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution with effect from July 1, 1964. The Act is not liable to be attacked on the plea that it is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. But the power to repeal or amend the Act incorporated in tho Ninth Schedule is not thereby taken away. the enactment of the of the competent Legislature to amending Act passed after the (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964 does not therefore qualify for the protection of article 31 B. The contention that the Travancore Act 14 Of 1124 (M.E.) was not law in force when the United State was formed, the notification bringing the Act into force is ineffective.

A deed of surrender was executed by a Hindu widow to recover possession of the properties belonging to the last male owner during the lifetime of the widow from persons who acquired title to the same by adverse possession against her. The suit was resisted by the defendants on the ground that there was disruption of the joint family in the year 1913 and that even if it was valid, the surrenderees could not claim possession so long as the widow was alive. The trial judge held that there were no partition between Mathurbhai and Kashibhai but he dismissed the suit on the grounds that a suit of this character was not maintainable in law. On appeal by the plaintiffs to the High Court, the Full Bench confirmed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the appeal. It was contended for the appellants that as the mother 's estate was in this case completely extinguished by adverse Possession exercised by the respondents she had, in fact, no interest left in her which she could make a surrender of in favour of reversions. Held: (i) The legal position has been correctly indicated by Kumaraswami Shastriyar J. in the Full Court Case (1) as well as the Privy Council that on a surrender by a widow of her husband 's property without any justifying necessity, or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse posses sion against her, the interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrenders must take it subject to such prior interest. The legal fiction involved in adoption also when a son is adopted by a subsequent widow subsequent to the death of her deceased husband. In the present case there was no material difference between an adoption and an act of surrender by the wife. (ii) The widow 's self effacement by the reversioner that forms the basis of surrender and not the ex facie transfer by which such effa tion is brought about(2). The widow at the time of surrendering her husband his estate can, if she likes, stipulate for a right to be maintained out of the property for her lifetime; but reservation of such small benefit absolutely necessary for her maintenance does not invalidate a surrender as has been held by the Privy council in more cases than one. (iii) The reversionary right to challenge it is no part of the estate which operates in the same manner as her physical death. It is open to the widow by a voluntary act of her own to remove this obstruction and efface herself from the husband ' s estate together. If she does that, the consequence is the same as she died a natural death and the next heirs of her late husband then living step in at once under the ordinary law of inheritance. In spite of some amount of complexity which is unavoidable in a law evolved by judicial decisions, this fund. mental basis of the doctrine of surrender can be said to be established beyond doubt. (iv) The law of limitation that has legalised what was originally a clear act of usurpation is based upon this analogy or legal fiction of the widows 's death. In order to decide whether a gift made by a wife prior to the date of surrender, acquired by adverse pos session, an inte rest in the widow ' s Estate can be excluded from the property so long that she remains alive and his expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the part of her widow which operates as a life estate. (v) The reversioners are not bound to surrender the estate, nor is the reversioner bound to accept it except on terms which would apply to any other transfer of immovable property so far as prior alienees are concerned.

The respondent company was the adopted son of Mangturam Jaipuria. After his adoption, he got a natural son, Rajaram Jaipuri and his family in 1946. Sitaram Jaipra became the Managing Director of the Cotton Mills Company and Sitaram Jaimuria family in which the Cotton Mill Company had acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each. From about 1975 76 on account of a very serious set back in its financial position the Cotton mills Company could not meet the wage bill, the dues of the U.P. Electricity Board and several other monetary claims against it. There were serious labour troubles in its factory and its work virtually became paralysed. The total liability of the cotton Mills Company was in the order of Rs 2 34 crores in the year 1977. On October 27, 1977, the Collector passed an order under section 128 A of the Act appointing a Receiver in respect of the shares in question attached them and ordering that the Receiver shall exercise the following powers: 1. The Receiver shall have supervision over the sales of products of the said mills and the disbursement of receipts from day to day. Ltd., involving the business and assets of the mills and which are not in the interest thereof or may be detrimental to the same in his opinion. In view of urgency, the order was being made expert with the direction, however, that a notice to show cause shall issue to M/s Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. and others be held at the Registered Office of the Company on 15th February, 1984 from Swadesi Cotton Mills co. Ltd.; (a) Shri L.N. Batra, A.D.M., Kanpur as Receiver of the aforesaid mills belonging to M.K. Cotton Mills; (b) Shri Ashok Jaipahuria be and is hereby appointed as a Director of Swadeshy Polytex Ltd. (c) Shri Sitaram Jaamuria and is accordingly appointed as the Chairman of the meeting by the Division Bench on March 23, 1984. The High Court of Allahabad dismissed the application for appointment of a Receiver under section 169 of the . In appeal to this Court it was contended that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collector in respect Of the shares held by the Cotton Textile Mills Company, they could not be taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice under section 170 of the , and that if those shares were omitted from consideration then the shares holding by the other requisitionists would not be sufficient to issue a notice under s. 169 of tho Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The order of the Collector appointing the Receiver in the suit of Sir Padampat could not acquire the newly issued shares in his name. That privilege was conferred by section 105 only on a person whose name was on the register of members. [882C D] (b). A receiver appointed by a court or authority in respect o property holds it for the benefit of the true owner subject to the orders that may be made by such Court or authority. The different kinds of rights of ownership flowing from the ownership of a right depend upon the nature of the right owned.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in possession of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the Suit was simply one of title to the suit property, and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit Land was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat mallat deh, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Aggrieved by the said finding recorded by the trial court, the Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Petition No. 571 of 1986. The learned Judge who heard the Revision Petition came to the conclusion that the issues involved in this Suit were not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Act and accordingly he held that the Suit filed was not barred by the provisions of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The High Court also found that the plaintiff in that case had only stated in the plaint that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat kukkas; that the Panchayat was entitled to the Suit land. Aggrieved against the said order of the High court, they preferred this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution of India before this Court. Dismissing the Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The decision is clearly distinguishable from the present case since in this case the Panchayat which had been impleaded as a defendant had raised the plea that the disputed land was a part of shamlatted deh and that it had been vested in it. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamil deh or was not deemed to have been vested In a civil suit even though the defendant had contended that the said land belonged to him or that it did not belong to the Gram Sabha. [835E F] Bhagu and Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors. , ; Bhagu & Ors., v Ram Sarup & Ors.

The Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board is constituted under Section 5 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948. The said board is engaged in generation, distribution and supply of electricity in the State of Andhra Pradesh. Electric energy is supplied for industrial, commercial, agricultural and domestic purposes. To such industries using about a particular level, it is supplied at a higher voltage. They are classified as high tension consumers (H.T consumers). All the appellants belong to that category. Section 49 empowers the Board to notify the terms and conditions upon which it will supply electricity to a person. It is also empowered to frame uniform tariffs in that behalf. Sub section 2 specifies in fixing the uniform tariff, the Board shall have regard to all or any of the following factors namely, a) the nature of the supply and the purposes for which it is required; b) the coordinated development of the electricity supply and distribution of electricity within the State in the most efficient and economical manner, with particular reference to such development in areas not for the time being served or adequately served by the licensee; c) the simplification and standardisation of methods and rates of charges for such supplies; d) the extension and cheapening of supplies of electricity to sparsely developed areas. Sub sections 3 empowers the board to enter into a special agreement with any consumer prescribing different tariffs for Wm. The terms and condition were notified by the Board and the B.P.M.S. No. 690 dated 17th September, 1975. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the various terms and condi tions. However, what requires to be noticed is the terms & conditions oblige every consumer executing an agreement in the prescribed form, undertaking to abide by the term and conditions prevailing on the date of agreement and also agreed to be bound by the terms, and conditions as may be notified from time to time. It further provides that the Board may, in the case of industrial consumers, accept by way of consumption deposit a sum equivalent to two months ' demand and energy charges, as consumption deposit. The security deposit is liable to be reviewed by the board periodically once in every year and/or at any time during the year if so warranted to upward revision of tariffs, enhancement of the con tracted demand by the consumer charges in the pattern of consumption by the consumers relaxation of power restrictions or such other factors which in the opinion of the Board warrant review of the adequacy of the existing consumption deposit, etc. The appellants are covered by the general terms and Conditions notified under Section 49 (1) of the Act. The term and condition notified under section 49(1) was notified by it and the Board. The B. P.M.,S.No. 690, dated 17.9.1975 issued notice requiring the consumers to deposit the enhanced amount of cash security as well as the bank guarantee on the basis of maximum power consumption of three months. The appellant No. 1 in W.P No. 11162/84 challenged the said notice by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that there is no statutory provision which casts an obligation on the Board either to pay interest on security deposit or to satisfaction of any money (For example, theft), which may become due and payable to the Board by the purchaser; and that the power based unit must be treated separately. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The true nature of transaction in these cases is one of advance payment of charges. [216G] 1.2 In the instant case, the Electricity Board has fixed the period of security equal to energy consumption of 3 months. Under Section 49 read with section 79(j) regulations are made, the validity of the regulations could be examined by the Court, whether they are reasonable or not. The scope of enquiry, therefore, would be to examine whether the power conferred upon the Board under section 50 is not exercised arbitrarily or unreasonably.

It is seen that the Indian Telephone Research Centre consists of the three posts: (i) Scientific and Engineering Officers Grade III; (ii) Assistant Directors and (iii) Deputy Directors. [1012C] (b).
