The appellant, a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor, was employed as a mamshi in a appellant ' s Bidi area at Bhandara. The appellant had framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty, insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry in respect thereof was held on May 15, after receipt of written statement from Nathu. Holding that the charges levelled against him were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965 and directed reinstatement of the third Respondent with all back wages. The said respondent filed an application under section 78(1)D of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946, for relief under section 7(1D). The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse, that the order of dismissal was passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Court directed reinstatement. The State Industrial Tribunal confirmed the order. The High Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour court for relief thereunder under section 8 (1D) of the Act. In appeal by certificate, HELD: 1. The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an industrial matter there must be compliance with the provisions of that chapter. [737 A] 2. The object of which was to make numerous changes in the Act shows in its Statement of Objects and Reasons that clause 31 of the Bill was meant to "enlarge the powers of the Labour ' Court under section78". According to this clause "the Labour Court is empowered (by paragraph D) to direct temporary withdrawal of any change the legality of which is a matter of issue in any proceeding before it, pending its final decision.

The contesting respondents, who were the successors in interest of the lessor company, filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellants ' application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif was not maintain able. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that in absence of a month 's notice under section 10(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsiff, and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. It was further held that the respondents were not liable to eviction. The High Court also directed the respondents to vacate the premises. On appeal by the respondents, the learned Judicial Commissioner agreed with the findings of the Trial Court on merits and concluded in paragraph 48 of thejudg ment thus: "In view of the findings on the disputed issues of fact between the parties, it is not necessary to deal with this aspect now. Apart from pleading that the application under Section 12 was not filed by the appellants as an applica tion under section 13 of the Act before the civil court was maintainable and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise. The respondents filed a regular appeal from the decision before the District Judge, Ranchi designated as Judicial Commissioner, and he also went into the entire controversy thoroughly. The learned Munsif accepted the appellants case that they were the successor in interest and the legal representatives of late S.N. Ganguli had formed a partnership, as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created, and that the respond ents were liable to vacate within the time allowed by court. The appellants ' revision application before the Patna High Court failed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that on the expiry of such a tenancy the only remedy is to file a suit and in any event section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the facts of the case as the responden ts, by their notice, did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the court is concerned. [975G] 2.1 In the instant case, both the parties dealt with every aspect of the matter from their respective angles elaborately and led their full evidence both oral and documentary and the case was tried by the learned Munsif in the same manner as the trial of an eviction suit. The decision of the learned Munsiff is also a detailed one considering every relevant question in the case. [76H; 977A] 2:2 In view of section 12, the civil Court is the proper forum.

The appellant a registered Society filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of the District Judge, Jaipur City. The counsel engaged by the appellant were Sri Satya Narain Sharma and Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal. The suit was later transferred to the Court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1 Jaipur City where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as Secretary of the society. In support of his claim, having been elected, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was nominated and when he 236 learnt about the fate of the Suit, an application was filed for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit to its file. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High Court by a petition under section 1 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. The High Court agreed with the trial Court that the application under section 15 1 of the code of Civil Proce dure, was not maintainable. While agreeing with the argument of the appellant that the trial Judge had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected Secretary of Society on the relevant date in favour of the respondent, the High court observed that the mistake could not be corrected in the present situation. It has been contended by the learned counsel for the appellant, that the High Courts in C.W.P. No. 1406 of 1975 did not decide the dispute finally and left it to be settled by the civil court. The case was accordingly remanded to the trial judge for reconsideration of the evidence on this point. The parties shall be allowed to lead further evi dence in support of their cases.

The appellant was charged along with the accused Nos. 2, 3, 5 and 6 with having on or about July 11, 1953 transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes of the Denomination of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs. I,800 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The trial ended in the conviction of the appellant along with co accused of the offence with which they had been charged. The High Court confirmed the conviction recorded against the appellant by the Additional Chief Presidency Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Ordinance promulgated under the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 Of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, and it was urged that Ordinances promulgated under that subsection during the period specified in section 3 of the Act were subject to no time limit as regards their existence and validity, unless imposed by the Ordinance themselves or other amending or repealing legislation, whether by Ordinance or other. Held: (i) The Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the currency of the emergency power vested in him under section 2(3) Of the India and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, was a temporary measure and continued in force until it was repealed; (ii) the Ordinance in which the GovernorGeneral was invested with the power to make and promulgate Ordinances for the peace and good Government of British India or any part thereof under section 74 was the condition of the exercise of such power, by the Governor. The words "except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" were omitted from section 1(3), sub section (2) and section 26A was added after section 26 of the , which provided that in respect of Ordinances made during the periods specified in s. 3 of that Act, section 72 should have effect as if the words "for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" were substituted; and (iii) the period of their duration had to be determined having regard to the provisions Of section 72 as they stood with the omission of the words ' for the space 'of not more then six months ' from its issue. The Ordinance having been passed during the year between June 27, 1940 and April 1, 1946, was perpetual in operation on July 11. 1953, the date on which the offence in question was committed by the appellant and the appellant was rightly convicted by both the courts below.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the sentence should be limited only to the extreme penalty; (2) the court 's attention was not drawn to Ediga Annamma 's case ; (3) the question whether the death sentence should he awarded or not must, in my view, be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case; (4) the Court 's power to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special reasons ' occurring in section 354(3) of the Code merely requires 'special reason ' to the indicated for imposing the death penalty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The court 'has to choose between a sentence of death and a sentence Of imprisonment for life; while under section 354 (3), Cr. P.C., 1973, the Court is enjoined with a duty to record 'special grounds ' in case the extreme punishment is awarded. But the question is essentially of political expediency and as such, it is the concern of the statesman and, therefore, the domain of the Legislature, and not the Judiciary. [1075G H; 1076A] 2. The Court 'has, in this instant case, examined the evidence liberally applied the rule of benefit of doubt and climaxed its judgments with sentences of death passed by the courts below. [1178C D] 3. In the instant case the earlier provocation came from the deceased 's side by beating up Appellant No. 3. The latter bent on reprisal for the flagellation and humiliation, waited till sundown 1068 and returned armed with friends and weapons from outside. Abuses were the provocative invitation for the fracas. The tipsy response brought the opposite party out. Jarnail Singh, the 3rd appellant who was the victim of the earlier beating, ignited the attack by instigation and his party went into violent action. Guns boomed, dangs, dived three men and later a fourth feel dead and the curtain was drawn after the catastrophe was complete. Probably, the accused party was also drunk. And alcohol makes men besides themselves and buries sanity. The role of intoxicating drinks and drugs in aggressive behaviour and explosive crime has not been the subject of sufficient criminological research in the country. [12E F] 4. Taking the cue from the English legislation on abolition, it would be impermissible for any Judge to advocate its abolition in judicial pronouncements. [13C D; 14A] 5. The question whether death sentence be awarded or no sentence must, therefore be left open to the Court of the judge trying the appellant and the questions of sentence should depend upon facts and circumstance obtaining in the case. When a sentence is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High Court under section 366(1) of Cr.P.C.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. The appellant also claimed arrears of salary but he reduced this claim to Rs. 16,561.29. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry held by him, imposed a charge on him. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, who was appointed by the Commissioner of Incometax as the Inquiring Officer, found that the appellant had made various investments in the name of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the application for a certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is only after the appellant 's activities had become more notorious that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. [583 C] (2) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is merely when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial. [585 C] State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N. Roy Biswas, and R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State, do not help the appellant. If an inquiry is held at a particular stage, possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started, it does not debar a departmental trial merely because they held preliminary inquiries before framing charges. [584 D E] (3) The High Court had given its judgment eight months after it had heerad argumenst. He urged that the result was that the High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently, been forgotten. The Civil Procedure Code does not provide a time limit for the period between the hearing of arguments and the delivery of a judgment.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales of manga nese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. were complete within the state of Andhra pradesh. The Sales Tax Authorities considered only one contract, and held that these contracts were intrinsically linked and connected with the contract entered into by the appellants with the M/s.M,.T. C. On appeal, the High Court held that there existed a bond between the contracts of sale entered into between the appellants and the M M. M.T.,C. and the actual exportation of the goods. The High Court also considered only two contract. In the special leave petition, the appellants assailed the assumption made by the High court to the effect that all contracts between the appel lants and the foreign buyers on the one hand and the contracts between them were two separate and independent con tract of sale. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The contracts between M/M.M.,T.c. and their foreign buyers are different contracts and it is the S.T .C. which entered into direct contract with their foreign buyer. Under the contracts both the M and M.Ms. They entered into independent contracts with their Foreign buyers on F.O.B. contract with a foreign buyer, this Court in Serajuddin 's case held that all the contracts were integrally connected with and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export of mana nese goods out of the territory of India. This Court found that the contracts entered into with the foreign buyer and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. [444C D] 2. The reason given by counsel for the State are these.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi. On a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973 he was terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court, Delhi for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" As the respondent management failed to participate in the proceedings, the reference was heard ex parte. The Labour Court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, the period of probation was extended upto 8th Sept., 1974 and on the expiration of this extended period of probationary period, his service was terminated. The appellant further contended that he was a Salesman appointed in probation for 6 months and thereafter on the extended period upto September 8, 1974. The contention was negatived by the Labour court which held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper nor unjustified and therefore the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The termination of service of the appel lant is ab initio void and inoperative and a declaration is made that he continues to be in service with all consequential benefits, namely back wages in full and other benefits, if any. However, as the Award is to be made by the Industrial Court, we remit the case to the Industrial Tribunal to make an appropriate award in the light of the findings of this Court. [522D] 1.2. The termina tion takes place where a term expires either by the active step of the master of the running out of the stipulated term. To pro tect the weak against the strong policy of comprehensive definition has been effectuated. Termination embraces not merely the act of termination by the employer, but the fact of termination howsoever produced. May be, the present may be a hard case, but we can visualise abuses by employers, by suitable verbal devices, circumventing the armour of section 25F and section 2(oo). Without speculating on possibilities, it is not necessary for the purposes of sub section (2) to determine first the relevant date, i.e., the date when termination of serv ice which is complained as retrenchment.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The Deputy Commissioner by order dt. March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of Madan Gopal Inspector be terminated forthwith and that in lieu of notice he should get one month pay as required by the Rules. The appellant challenged the authority of the Deputy Commis sioner or the Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. On the report of the enquiry officer that the work and conduct of the public servantas unsatisfactory, an order of termination of employment was passed without affording him an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to hold his post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant were not dismissed or removed from service but his employment being terminated in exercise of authority reserved under the terms of employment, and no penalty was imposed upon the appellant, Held, that the protection of article 311 (2) of the Constitution applies as much to a temporary public servant. The protection of Article 311 (1) of 'the Constitution applies only as much as to a permanent public servant but it will make no difference whether the appellant is a probationer or a temporary employee. State of Bihar vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 689 and State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das, ; , referred to.

The appellant State Government was aggrieved and had filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotions of respondents Nos. 1 to 46 and others as Professors in supersession of the claims of the writ petitioners who contended that they were senior and more qualified for promotion, and that the High court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's Order No. 643 HTETE dated July 25, 1969 in regard to the appointments of respondents nos. 3 to 46. The State Government filed a review petition against the judgment but was dismissed on September 14, 1972. In the appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Commission was not consulted either in regardto the principles to be followed in making the promotions in question or on the suitability of selected candidates for the promotions; and (ii) the State had placed on record the minutes of the Commission dated July 22, 1969 which make it quite clear that the State Govern ment referred the selections to the Commission, a Committee was appointed by the Commission for that purpose, the Committee was presided over by a member of the commission. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court erred in holding that the Commission 's recommendation for selection was invalid for that reason. [873H] (2) The State Govern ments at first framed rules on November 15, 1968 for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. By Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25,1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The Commission set out the reasons for its decision and finally made its recommendation on merits.

The petitioner was the Chairman of a Committee of Privileges. The Assembly of Bihar, which was run by Dr. section K. Sinha, the Chief Minister and cited certain instances of favouritism. At this stage the Speaker held that a portion of the speech was objectionable and ordered it to be struck off and expunged. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner (i) that the speech in question was not put to vote; (ii) that even if article 194(3) Of the Constitution excluded the operation of article 19(1), the petitioner would not be in a worse position; (iii) that, as an editor of a newspaper he was entitled to any privilege under article 19 (1) (a); and (iv) that it had the privilege to prevent the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect of the proceedings. HELD : (i). The provisions of clauses (1), (2) and (3) of article 194 of the Constitution indicate that the privileges intended to be attracted are not of the dark and difficult days, when the House of Commons passed through strife and struggle but only those obtaining in 1950 when it was functioning as a model Legislature in a highly democratized country. The provisions Of clauses (2), (3), (4) and section 194(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, show that the privilege intended to he attracted are neither of the black nor difficult days and, when they were reported mala fide, the publishers of newspapers were liable to punishment. [858 E F] (ii). The powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House Of Commons at the commencement of the constitution indicate that they shall be those of the House, of Commons of the Parliament of the United Kingdom and its members and committees, at the beginning of the period of their stay in the House. [888 A B] (iii). The right to freedom of speech conferred on a citizen under article19(1)(a) is subject to the provisions of the Constitu tion and the rules and standing orders regulating procedure of that Legislature. That clause provides for powers, privilege and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State and of the members and the committees thereof shall be such as may from time to time be defined by the legislature by law. The right conferred on the Legislature under article 194 (3). [859 C] Romesh Thappar vs The State of Madras, ; , referred to.

The Respondent was a private college known by the name of Khallikote College. This is an institution which grew out of a school established in 1856. The management had to meet with financial crisis in the past and obtained financial help in the shape of liberal endowment under a trust deed from the then zamindar of Khalikote. The institution, it was stated, became one of the premier colleges in the town of Behram pur, Ganjam District, Orissa. The College was taken over by the Government in pursuance of the unanimous resolution of the managing committee of February 18, 1970 and the transfer to the Government was of all the assets of the college but without any liability. The Managing Committee continued to be liable for the outstanding liabilities, if any, of the College for which Government was not liable. The college after taking over was administered as a Government College. The eight writ petitioners in the High Court (Respond ents) were working as Readers in different faculties in the said College on the date of the aforesaid transfer in the scale of pay Rs.510 860/ whereas the Govern ment scale for Readers was Rs.600 1000/ . On the date when the Government issued a circular dated March 23, 1971, it prescribed that the Government had been pleased to order that follow ing principles shall be forward followed in the ap point Readers, namely (a) no officer who has not at least 8 years of teaching experience as a Lecturer would be eligible for consideration; and (b) the post of Reader shall originally be filled up by promotion subject to the satisfactory performance and conduct of the officer as a lecturer. On March 23 1971, the Government prescribed qualifications for appointment as a Reader by a Circular of that date addressed to the Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education), Orissa which appears to supersede the earlier circulars on the subject. The grievance of the Respondents is that although they had all the requisite qualifica tions for the appointment as Readers under the Government, they were drawing a salary of less than Rs. 600/ per month on the dates of take over. their names were not referred to the Public Service Commission for consideration of their suitability for appointment. The High Court accepted the Writ Petitions and held that the Respondents were entitled to consid ered by the Public Services Commission for appointment to as Readers ' and hence these appeals by the State which are against the decision of the Government. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1. All the Respond ent Nos are eligible to be referred to.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority granted temporary permits to ply their vehicles on the route. The appellants made applications to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition to the High Court did not meet with success. It was a common ground that in respect of the route a scheme has been prepared and published under section68C of Chapter IV A of the . The route in question is an inter regional route and therefore an application for temporary permit for the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date on publication of approved or modified scheme has to be made to the state Transport Authority under sec. 68(1 C). The State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application to grant of three temporary permits for the same purpose and the application of the Corporation for three permits was granted while the application made by each of the appellants was rejected on the ground that once a scheme had been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A) the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others is entitled to apply for temporary stage permit and if such application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, to obtain a temporary permit. This decision of the State Road Trans port Authority has been upheld both by the State Appellate Tribunal as well as the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Regional Transport Authority or the Regional Transport Officer as the case may be will have to examine the application for number of temporary permits made by them. If the Corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permits and section 68 E(1C) would be squarely attracted. [986G] 2. The expression 'any person ' would comprehend any person even other than the Corporation. One has to read section 68 C (1 A), and section 69 F( 1 C). If the corporation applies for temporary licences undoubtedly the State transport Authority cannot grant permit to any one else if the Corporation had applied for all of the permits. But section 68 G(1 D) clearly envisaged a situation where application for a temporary lease is not made under section 66F(I A), by the corporation. And there is felt need for providing transport service on the routes in question. [876H; 888A] 3. The Corporation has published a scheme in respect thereof of the routes. Even when a scheme is published it is open to the Regional State Transport authority or the State Regional Transport Authorities as the ease may be to fix or increase the number of vehicles that may operate on the road. But the power to increase strength of fleet operating on the said route is conferred and has to he exercised in public interest meaning transport facility to travelling public. [884C] 4. The word 'any persons ' would not comprehend any persons even other except the Corporation, and one has to look read section68 F(I C) and section68F( 1 D). If it applies for all permits but also for some others, the inevitable conclusion isthat for the balance strength the corporation has made an applica tion for the permanent permit and section 64 F(lC) will be squarely applicable.

The appellant, the son of respondent 10, inherited the suit properties from his maternal grandfather Moti. On March 22, 1927 he executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the said properties in favour of Shibba, the ancestor of respondents I to 9 for Rs. 5,000. Subsequently on April 12, 1929, he sold the equity of redemption to the said mortgagee for Rs 11,000 and in suit No. 145 of 1946 filed by the appellant in the Court of the Sub Judge, Panipat, from which the present appeal arose, the appellant had claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned alienations were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property in dispute was ancestral qua the appellant 1101 and that the impugned alienation were not effected for consideration or for legal necessity, but he ordered that the memorandum of appeal should be returned to respondents 1 to 9 to enable them to file an appeal before the High Court. That is how respondents I and 2 filed a suit against the appellant on the ground that they were ancestral. The appellant contended that the high Court was in error in not following the earlier Full Bench decisions on this point and it was urged on his behalf that the decision of the last Full Bench in Narotam Chand 's case should be treated as good law, and that in the village community where a daughter succeeds, either in preference to or in default of heirs male to property which, if the descent had been through a son, would be ancestral property, she simply acts as a conduit to pass on the property as ancestral property to her sons and their descendants and does not alter the character of the property simply because she happens to be a female Chatterji. Held, that the doctrine of stare decisis is applicable because the decision in Naratam Chand vs Mst. Durga Devi (19O) L.R. 35 I.A. 206, and Narotham Chand ' case (1908) 30 P.R., are not correctly decided. The principle of stare overruling is thus stated in Corpus Juris Secundum(1) " Under the stare decisis rule a principle of law which has become settled by a series of decisions generally is binding on the courts and should be followed in similar cases. This rule is based on expediency and public policy, although generally it should be strictly adhered to by the courts, it is not universally applicable. The Corpus Juris secundum (2) however adds a rider that "previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that grievous wrong may result; and accordingly, the courts ordinarily will not adhere to a rule or principle established by previous decisions which they are convinced is erroneous.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, on charges under section 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The Sessions judge accepted that verdict and convicted them all under sections 449 and 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307/149 of the Code. He also sentenced the other three appellants to rigorous imprison ment for two years under s.425 of the Act. On appeal by the appellants, Held: (i) The fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449 of the I.P.C. [83 E] (ii) There can be no doubt that the words "in order to" have been used in section 882 mean "with the purpose of". If the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of an offence punishable with death, the house trespasser becomes punishable under section 448 of the IPC. [84 G H] (iii) The act did not result in death. So he became punishable under s 307 of the . [851 E F] (iv) Section 449 of I. P.C., does not apply to an act done "in Order to" the committing of an ' offence even though the offence may not be completed. Therefore, if a person commits a house trespass with the purpose Of committing theft but has failed to accomplish the purpose, it will be proper to say that he has committed the house in order to the committing 'of theft.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration of his title as collateral within four degrees of Gurdial, who was a Sarswat Brahmin Brahmin. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable; (ii) that in any case he had fully discharged the onus that was on him by producing in evidence the Riwaj i am recording the custom of the district of Gurdaspur which was compiled by Mr. Kennaway himself in 1913 and (iii) that there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. Held, that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus cast on him as a result of the production by the appellant of the Rwiwaji am of 1913 and consequently the appellant must succeed. The general custom of Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collateral 's from succession, to the ancestral property of their father, the initial onus, there fore, must be on the collateral for showing that the general custom in favour of the daughter 's succession to self acquired properties of their respective father are reliable and trustworthy documents. The appellant had not discharged the initial burden cast on her as a consequence of the absence of evidence of particular instances. Gopal Singh vs Ujagar Singh (I.L.R. , Mst. Subhani vs Nawab (2) and the matter is now well settled. The question whether there was a custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a collateral within the fourth degree excludes the daughter of the last female holder from succession even though they are within the four corners of the custom. Held further, that in order to enable the appellant to displace the general customs custom recorded in Rattigan 's work and to shift the onus to the respondent, the appellant should produce a Riwaz i am which is a reliable and credible trustworthy document. It has been held by the Privy Council in Mst.Subhani vs Balmath (19O8) P.R., 191, that if the Rawaj iam produced is a genuine and trustworthy document, had been carefully prepared and does not contain within its four corners contradictory statements of custom and in the opinion of the Settlement Officer is not a record of the wishes of the persons appearing before him as to what the custom should be, it would be a presumptive piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up.

The respondent was acting as Managing Agents of several companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. He was also a Director of a number of other companies and had on occasions acted as liquidator of some Commis sioner of some companies registered in Calcutta under the . The Collector referred the matter to the High Court which held that the stamp duty payable on the power "foras many respective capacities as the principal executes the power" was Rs. 10 under article 48(d) of Schedule 1 A of the Stamp Act as amended by section 13 of Bengal Act III of 1922 and that the proper duty payable thereon was Rs 10 under Article 48 (d) Schedule 1A of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 as amended in by section 7 of Bengal Amendment Act III Of 1922. The Board of Revenue appealed to this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that : (i) the instrument in question consisted distinct matters and must be stamped in accordance with section 5; (ii) the words "distinct matters" in section 5 meant the same thing as "descriptions" in Section 6, and that they both refer to the several categories of instruments which are set out in the Schedule. Held: (i)(a) The object and scope of sections 4 to 6 are the same, which in fact they are not. Section 4 deals with a single transaction completed in several instruments, and section 6 with a Single transaction which might be viewed as falling under more than one category, whereas section 5 applies only when the instrument comprises more than two transactions, and it is immaterial for this purpose whether those transactions are of the same category or of different categories. (b) The words "continct matters", in section S.5 meant thesame thing as 'description ' in section 6. (ii)(a). In construing a document one of the members of a mutual insurance club executed Single power, it related to one matter, and the decision was that they were distinct matters. (iii) The instrument in the present case did not comprise distinct matters but consisted one matter only with reference to the capacity of the executant as trustee, executor and so forth, but in respect of every transaction entered into by him in his personal capacity. (iv) The document in question did not contain any provision in the statute law of this country similar to the above, and was therefore not liable for the duty specified thereon.

The assessee was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948, the name Kathiawarawar was changed to Saurashtra. On March 16, 1949, the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. This Ordinance was in force for one year only the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of business by the two appellant companies for the year 194950 the Income Tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance. For the purpose of calculating the depreciation allowance to which the assessee was entitled in computing the profits or gains of the business, the written down value of the building, machinery and plants or furniture had first to be ascertained in accordance ' section 13(5) (b) applied. The Income tax Officer, in ascertaining the written up value deducted depreciation allowance which would have been allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, if it had been in force and a claim had been made supported by prescribed particulars. This amount was computed as Rs. 17,21,041 and in the case of the Master Silk Mills Ltd., the appellant in C.A. No. 601/62 was calculated as Rs 2,02,500. The obvious result of deducting 220 this amount was that the written off down value became considerably lower than what it would have had been otherwise and so the depreciation allowances become less. The assessee 's contention before the Income tax authorities was that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words which would be allowed to him if the Indian Incometax Act, 1961, was in fact in force in the past as in fact no claim was made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income. tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Incometax Tribunal took a different view and held that this expression "or which would had been allowed to the assessee if the income tax Act 1922, was In force in Saurashtra, the depreciation that would have be allowed if proper claim had not been made and therefore no depreciation had been actually allowed. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Ordinance had not used the words "would have been allowed" in the Ordinance as it would be meaningless to speak of a depreciation allowance being allowed without a claim. Held, further, that the expression "actually allowed" means "allowable" under the law in force. In the present case the assessee 'show was entitled to deduction under section 10(5)(b) of the Indian income tax Ordinance as amended by the Taxation Laws (Part B States) (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 1950, paragraph 2 and the Notification No. 19 (S.R.O. 477). The words "actly allowed" mean "allow ableable" in section 13 (5) of that Act. The words used are apt and sufficient to express the intention that if the Income Incometax Act 1922 had actually been in existence, depreciation that will have been allow ed as depreciation.

The petitioner, an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.) was an instrumentality o the State Government in favour o f the Mysore construction Company. His writ petition and a further writ appeal in the Karnataka High Court having been unsuccessful he has preferred this special leave Petition from the judgment of the High Court in the writ appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in declining to inter fere. Thirdly, the conditions and stipulations in a tender notice like this have two types of consequences. [234C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent issued the tender has the right to punc tiliously and rigidly enforce them. Thus, if a party does not strictly comply with the requirements of para III, V or VI of the N.I.T., it is open to the K.P.C. to decline to consider the party for the contract and if a Party comes to Court saying that the K .P. C. should be stopped from doing so, the court will decline relief. The second consequence, indicated by this Court in earlier decisions is not that the respondent was not entitled to act arbitrarily in accepting the tender of the 4th respondents but was bound to conform to the stand ard or norm laid down in paragraph I of the notice inviting tenders which required that only a person running a regis tered. [235D E] 1:3 The conditions and stipulation in a contract notice like the instant have two kinds of consequences; (a) that the applicant should supply information to show that he had experienced in insulation work and that he could carry out brick work in a month to the extent indicated; (b) that it "is constructing" a building in Hyderabad for the National Geophysical Research Institute "in which they have done wall insulation works and that they were really meant to supplement each other. It is clear from para I of this notice that apart from para 1, there are some other requirements in the N .I. T. which have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply of tender forms; (counselled by the T.C., E.) and (d) that all the documents referred to in the other paras can be supplied at any time before the final award of the contract.

The appellant was the owner of a house. The property in dispute was evacuee property and the Custodian General of Evacuee Property (Rural) Ordinance, 1949, which came into force on the 12th December, 1947, provided for an appeal to the High Court against an original order of a Custodian or Additional Custodian or authorised Custodian but there was no provision for revision of such an order. The appellant filed an application in 1948 for confirmation of the transaction of exchange and of the consequent transfer to her of the property in agricultural land. The Additional Custodian recommended that possession may be given to the appellant and that the Patwari may be informed accordingly to take necessary action in the matter. But it did not appear from the record whether this was done or whether possession was in fact delivered. At this stage a notice under section 27 of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947 ( East Punjab Act XIV of 1947), appeared to have been issued to the appel lant asking him to show cause why the order of the Additional Custodian dated the 20th March, 1952, confirming the exchange and further orders sanctioning mutation and other consequential orders made in connection therewith be not set aside. The Custodian General passed an order confirming the transfer and also the further orders dated the 21st May, 1953, sanctioning mutation, and other incidental orders made by him in connection with the aforesaid proceedings. The High Court held that the application for confirmation which was made by the appellant in 1948 and which remained pending until Act XXXI of 1950 came into operation and superseded the earlier legislation in this behalf had to be disposed of in accordance with sections 5 A and 5 B of the Act, and that there were no provisions for revision or review of such orders. Held: (i) The contention that the revisional power cannot be exercised when there was an appeal provided but no appeal was filed, that it was open to the Assistant Custodian who appeared before the Custodian in support of the notice for revision and to the allottees of the properties in whose interest the revisional order appears to havebeen passed, to file an appeal under the Act as persons aggrieved. (ii) The application for the confirmation pending on the date when the Central Act XXXI Of 1950 came to be applied was not open to appeal or revision but became final and conclusive. It is only the second portion of section 58(3) which continues them as though the appointments were made under the new Act a position which could scarcely be controverted. (iii) The revisional power can be exercised in cases where there is repeal of an enactment followed by fresh legislation. Section 6 would be applicable in such cases also unless the new legislation manifests an intention incompatible with or con trary to the provisions of the section. Such incom patibility would have to be ascertained from a consideration of all the relevant provisions of that new law. (iv) The principle of Colonial Sugar Refining Co. Ltd. vs Irving, [1924] 1 K.B. 284, State of Punjab vs Mohar Singh, ; , followed.

The appellant, a locality in the city of Bombay, was studded with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings, nuts and bolts, tools and other small products were made and sold. These establishments, well over a thousand, employ a considerable number of workmen in the neighbourhood of 5,000 although each unit had (barring four), less than the statutory minimum of 20 workmen. The appellant 's demand for bonus was resisted by the respondent on the ground that what was pleaded was profit based bonus only and therefore fell squarely within the Bonus Act. The Tribunal dismissed the reference but dismissed it in limine on the score that the demand for the bonus was barred by res judicata. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The claim put forward by the appellant before the Tribunal was on the face of it unsustainable on the short ground that whatever might have been the species of bonus demanded in 1965, the present dispute referred by the State Government related to a totally different type of bonus namely customary bonus and one which was a term of the employment itself. [596G] (2) The award has rejected the claim not substantively but on the grounds of two legal bars and care must be taken not to mix up maintainability with merits. A short cut is a wrong cut often times and the Tribunal 's easy recourse to dismissal on preliminary grounds may well lead and it has, as will be presently perceived to a re opening of the case many years later if the higher Court reverses the legal findings. Be that as it may, let us test the validity of the plea that only a profit based Bonus has been claimed by the workers. The claim for bonus is not inflexibly and solely pegged to profit as the one and only right. There is no law which lays down that the service conditions of the employees under all these employers should be uniform. It is true that if the Bonus Acts are a complete Code, on a true decoding of its scheme and spirit, the industrial court cannot take off the ground with any other forms of bonus yes, that is the implication of 'a complete code '. [606B C] (3) The Tribunal understood the former way and followed it up with a rejection, on the plea of constructive res judicata but is silent on, and cannot therefore annihilate by implication, other distinct and different kinds of bonus such as the One oriented on custom. Whatever be the position of subordinate courts ' casual observations, generalisations and sub silentio determinations must be judiciously read by Courts of coordinate jurisdiction and so viewed, we are able to discern no impediment in reading Ghewar Chand as confined to profit bonus, leaving room for non statutory play of customary bonus. [507C E] (4) The argument that the claim put up by the workmen before the tribunal was on their face unsustainable on a short ground because what was alleged was profit founded bonus only, and therefore falls squarely within section 1(3) of the Bonus act cannot be accepted. [599E F] (5) The contention that the Union figured as the appellant in the present case but being no party to the dispute (which was between the workers on the one hand and the establishments on the other), had no locus standi, is not correct.

% The Haryana Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 as amended from time to time, provided for the application of a rule of quota at the time of their appointment. Rule 12 provided that seniority inter se, of the substantive members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined with reference to the respective dates of their confirmation. The petitioners who were promotees, challenged the validity of the Punjab Superior Judicial Services (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976 by filing a Writ Petition in the High Court contending that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that is to say, not only at the point of appointment but at the date of confirmation also. The High Court set aside his reversion on certain other grounds but it held by a majority (N. section Rao vs State of Haryana), that the power to confirm a District and Sessions Judge resides in the high Court and not in the Governor; that even if a substantive vacancy is available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruits; for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive vacancies in which he can be confirmed, is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation, and that, the High court applied the principle of rotation as between promotees and the direct recruits at the times of their Confirmation when, in fact, that the relevant rules provide for is the application Of a rule by quota at tho time of his appointment. The State appealed to this Court contending: (1) that the seniority of the members of higher Judicial Service was not arbitrary; (2) that even assuming that a substantive post is available and the confirmation is not a part of the process of appointment, it is open to the High Courts to deny to a member of the subordinate judicial service of the State the right of appeal given to him by the law which regulates the conditions of his service. Dismissing the Writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1.

The respondents Nos. 4 and 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, in this appeal filed R.P. No. 1615 of 1984 before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal, Hyderabad, contending for promotion from Senior Assistant to Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal local area comprising of Warpur, Karimnagar and Adila bad is the criteria. The State Government in exercise of its power under cl. (5) of article 371 D annulled that order which had given rise to filing of W.P No. 998 of 1986 in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution, was issued. The G.O.Ms. No, 1648 and GO. Ms. No., 1900 dated December 22, 1981, were challenged by the respondents Nos 4 and 6 before the Tribunal contending for promo tion from Senior Assist ant to Assistant Tax Officer, zonal seniority of warangal local areas comprising of Adilabad and Karimnagar Districts of the Commercial Taxes Division cannot be treated to be a zone and the divisional seniority prepared by the department is bad in law. It was held by the Tribunal that in the im pugned order that G. O.Ms No. 1648 dated November 20, 1982 was issued under Para 5(2)(c) of the Andhra pra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 1975 for that "the order" no allotment of cadre in terms of para 4 of the order was issued, it was issued; that the G.Os. No,. 1648 & G. 0.Ms., No. 1900 do not mention the constitution of new local cadre for Adilabad Division and no order was issue constituting a separate cadre in term of Para 4 of order; and that the order dated April 29, 1988 was made pursuant to the power given to the President under Article 371 D, which is a special provision made under the Constitution (Thirty second Amendment) Act, 1973 peculiar to the State of Andhra Pradesh due to historical background. Hence omitted. The Tribunal allowed the Representation Petition and directed that "to examine the legal effect of the Government order in G.S.R. No . 524 E dated October 18, 1975 after again hearing the parties". Thereafter, the Tribunal held that in view of the fact that the State Government had not undertaken the class or classes of posts in the civil services of and class or class or Class of Civil posts under the State as local cadres, it ceased to have any power to bifurcate or reorganise a zone within a zone, cadre or cadres therein. Accordingly, it reiterated the original order dated 4th November, 1988. The Constitution (Shirthysecond Amendment) Amendment Act, 1974 through Section 3 thereof brought into the Constitution Article 371D with effect from July 1, 1974. This is a Special provision in respect of the State and the general rule of reservation made in Rule 22 in Andhra Pradesh State and Subrodinate Service Rules. It would appear from the record that pursuant to this power given under clause (5), it was for the President notwithstanding the expiry of the period of twelve months prescribed in sub para (1) of para graph 3, by an order require the State Govern ment whenever he considers it expedient so to do to have the power under paragraph 3(1) exercised. Thereby, it is clear that the state Government shall have to place necessary material before the President; the President shall consider that it is expedient to organise any class or category of posts within the zone already prescribed and to pass an order in that regard requiring the State Govt. to so organise it. It is made clear that for the purpose of effective administration or convenience, the State Gov ernment may create a local cadre instead of re quiring the State government to organize local cadre.

The appellant was the owner of a certain land in which he executed a simple mortgage of Gadi Sirampur in favour of the Chota Nagpur Banking Association Limited. In 1920 the Bank filed a suit against his son Wazir Narain Singh to enforce the mortgage security and obtained a mortgage decree. The suit was decreed by the trial court but on appeal, the High Court held that the lease was valid and was not affected by the appellant 's mortgage decree or by the execution sale under that decree and accordingly dismissed the plaintiff 's suit. Held, that the question whether the mortgagor in possession had power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. The true position has been stated in the following terms by Mukherjee, in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar (I.L.R. , and Madan Mohan Singha vs Raj Kishore Kumari (I L.R . , referred to. Held further that the appellant had no power to grant a permanent lease in question to the defendants so as to bind the plaintiff. The only relevant consideration is whether, the mortgagor was not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing took place,to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage, the appellant could not repudiate it specially as the mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of temporary leases to middlemen or cultivators.

% The petitioner, who was the arbitrator in a dispute between him and the respondent, sent bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5, 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal, the Division Bench set aside the award and directed the arbitrator to appoint an arbitrator and on its failure it was open to him to approach the court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Act for appointment of an arbitrator. The High Court allowed the appeals and held that though the petitioner was said to have made the claim for payment for the first period in July 12 1979, he had not taken any action from then. On further appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the Respondent, the Respondent is duty bound to appoint a arbitrator and that on its refusal it is open to the Court for appropriate relief under section 37 of the Arbitration Act. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that Clause 68 of Contract provides that where any disputes or differences had arisen between the parties at the instance of either party to the contract, the contract shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference referred. The question whether the High Court was justified in permitting the respondent to rescind the contract of Arbitration provided in clause 68 is a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or he should enter upon reference for adjudication. Dismissing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Clause 68 provides reference to an arbitration of all or any of the disputes or difference enumerated therein that have arisen between them at the instances of either Party to the Contract. It empowers either partyto issue notice calling upon the Engineer to refer the dispute or difference for arbitration. In this case, as found by the High court that though there is no proof in that behalf and the Respondent claimed that the petitioner had abandoned the contract even assuming that any claim was as a fact made in July 1979 and payment was made, the petitioner did not take any action thereafter for well over 10 years. It was open for him to avail of Clause 68 to the agreement seeking reference to the arbitration.

The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. That property included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. The Act came into force after the passing of the aforesaid preliminary decree. The decree holders filed petition for passing a final decree on September 19, 1955. The Estate mortgaged vested in the State on January 1, 1956 as a result of a notification issued under section 3(1) of the Act. A final decree was passed in the mortgage suit on October 1,1956. Thereafter the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the , and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act, but that objection was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds namely (i) that the objection in question was barred by the principles of res judicata; and (ii) that it was barred under section 4(d) of Bihar Land Reform Act, 1I955. The appellants contended that the execution application was barred because the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the . Held: (i)(a) The decision of the majority of the judges in the Full Bench decision in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh is not correct. (b) In construing section 4 (d), it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the section. (c) The true effect of the decisions of this Court in Sidheswar Prasad and Ors. vs Gauri Kumari Devi, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564 is as explained by Kamla Sahai J. In construing a provision contained in section 16 in regard to the scaling down of the debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under s.3.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, had been dismissed. The appellant challenged his order of detention on the ground that he was not very much acquainted with him and that he had sought the assistance of a friend at the hearing and for the reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit the request was turned down. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have been better placed before the Advisory Board, and that, therefore, he had prayed the assistance for by a friend. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority had the assistance and the Deputy Collector of Central Excise and a Superintendent of Central excise. In order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer, it does not disentitle him from making a request for the services of a lawyer. [792C D] 2. The rule in A. K. Roy 's case made it clear that the detenu was entitled to the assistance by a 'friend '. The word 'friends ' used there was obviously not intended to carry the meaning of the term in common parlance. One of the meanings of the word 'content, according to the Collins English Dictionary is "an ally in a fight or cause; supporter". The term 'friending ' used in the judgments of this Court was more in this sense than meaning 'a person known well to another and regarded with liking, affection and loyalty. A person not being a friend in the normal sense could be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. [789E F] 3. The refusal by the Advisory board to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend was bad and continued detention of the Appellant became vitiated. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed and the order of his detention is quashed. [788F G] 4. The failure by the Board to permit him to be represented by an array of lawyers is not justified. It is quite clear upon the terms of sub section (4) of Section 11 of the Act that the detenue had no right to legal assistance in the proceedings before the Board, but it did not preclude the Board from allow such assistance to detenu, when it allowed the State to be represent by an impleaded array of Lawyers. [781A B] 5. The Rule in A K.K. Roy etc. vs Union of India & Anr., ; , referred to.

The Government of India, in exercise of the powers conferred by r. 75 A(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, issued a notice to the managing agents of various jute mills demanding from them information as to stocks of hessian and acquired under the orders and notices already referred to. The said notice was served on the managing agent of the mills under sub r. (1) of r. 74 A(3) of Defence ofIndia Rules, which provided that if in the suit it was finally decided that the goods were not validly requisitioned or acquired by the Central Government on the 30th September 1946 each of the several previous owners would be entitled to receive as compensation from the Central Govern ment the market price prevailing on the date of institution of the said suit. The notice also stated that the Government had decided to acquire the property under that sub rule. The managing agents were further informed that by virtue of sub r.(3) Of r. 25 A, the said property would vest in the Central government at the beginning of the day on which the notice was so served and that if no such decision was made in the case, the goods would be deemed to have been validly requisitioned and acquired by it on the expiry of the period of requisition. The Government then tried to take possession of the properties requisitioned but the mills and the holders of delivery orders resisted the Government 's attempt on the ground that the orders of requisition and acquisition were invalid. Held, that the notice of acquisition was properly served on all the managing Agents of the Mills as required by r.(1) Of the Defence Of India Rules and was valid and binding on them. The order of requisition was not a contract for the sale of unascertained goods and no property in the goods was transferred to the buyer in view of section 18 of the Indian till the goods are ascertained by appropriation, which in this case took place at the time only of actual delivery. Held further, that as the service on the mills through the managing agency was good service within the meaning of r.(2) Of 0. XXIX, r. 2(a), it was not necessary to serve them with notices under r.75 A(1) for the owners were the mills, and the notice did not speak of an order in writing as contemplated by r . 75 A (2). The service of such an order is necessary on the person who can place the goods in question at the disposal of the requisitioning authority and until that is done there cannot be any valid and effective requisition.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, a notice was issued to the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Apprehending that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, the assessee set apart a sum of Rs. 652,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. Out of this amount an amount of Rs 2,02,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59 with the result that a sum was continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. At the same time the assessee had been contesting the proceedings taken against it under Section23A. Though it failed at the earlier stages, it succeeded ultimately in the Letters Patent Appeal filed by it in the East Punjab High Court. In the said appeal decided on May 24, 1965, it was held that no action can be taken against the assessee u/s 23A. With this order all the orders passed and notices issued under the aforesaid provision prior to the date of the said judgment stood vacated. In its assessment relating to the assessment year 1963 64 under the 112, the asses see contended that the said sum of RS. 4,50,000 is a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken up for hearing, another appeal preferred by the assessee relating to subsequent assessment year (1964 65) was also before the Tribunal. That appeal arose under the provisions of the Companies Sur Profits Tax Act 1964 which replaced the . The Tribunal first disposed of the appeal relating to assessment year 1964 65. In so far as item in question is concerned it held that it was a reserve. Following the said decision, the appeal pertaining to the earlier assessment year 1965 64 was also allowed. (It may be stated that the order of the Tribunal relating to assess ment year 1964 66 was subsequently rectified by an order dated February 15, 1972 and the said item was held to be a provision. But no such order was passed with respect to the assesseee under Section 22A. The assessee contended that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax u/S 23A was made on or before the date relevant to the assess ment Year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a pro ceed. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In Metal Box Company of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen, it is held that the High Court was right in holding it to be an a provision and not a reserve [ 113B] 1.2 The assessee itself called it a provision, and did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve, and hence no order of levying additional Tax under Section 3(1) of the 1922 Act could be passed with regard to the said assessment year. [113C D] 1:3 In Metal box Company of Indian Ltd.v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision & a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L. account, a reserve was in appropriation of profits, the asset or assets by which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business".

The petitioners, who were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) were subjected to competitive written and personality tests and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. On the other hand temporary Assistant Officers, (Officers ' at places), were neither subjected to written nor to a personality test but, as said before, were selected on the basis of interview. Besides the minimum educational qualification, which was the same for both the services three years experience as a Civil Engineer was. The petitioners contended that officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the date of their absorption into the Indian Railways Service of engineers (Class I) (hereafter referred to as 'Engineers '). The respondents contested the writ petitions contending that what is being asked is a virtual review of Katyani Dayal 's case which was not permissible by means of successive writ petitions. It was further contended that principles of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Katyni Dayal ' 's Case, if not the strict principles of res judicata. The respondents also filed counter affidavits. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The distinction and the classification of the temporary Assistant officers and members of the Indian Rail Service of Engi neers ' Class I fell clearly to be identified and marked. The only method of fusion was by means or a phased absorption as noticed in paragraph 9 of the Report detailed above. [1023C] 1.2 In Katyoni Dayal ' case, this court specifically said that relief of equality was being denied to the then petitioners because of the history, origin, and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed however as to the validity of the given weightage of half the length of service to Temporary Assistant Officers. subject to a maximum of five years, because, of its being questioned elsewhere. [ 1024D] 1:3 The rule of weightage also appears to be reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Similarly when the dispute raised between the officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented, in Katakyani 's cases (supra), still it was a dispute raised before this Court which had been decided finally. A dispute now sought to be raised under Article 32 of the Constitution between the Officers in a Representative capacity and Engineer across also in a representatives capacity must be held to be barred by principles of Res judicata as also in the rule of constructive Res judicata. [924E F] 1 :4 The distinction between, the two services was well marked in Kattyani Lal 's ease (supra) and the important question of equality is once for all settled. To find fault with it, at this juncture again on the touch stone of equality would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be counted from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of one half of the length service subject to the maximum of 5 years, it would otherwise be imprerated now, at that point of time to dig up old issues. [936A B] 2:5 The rule is reasonable and it is a scheme which has gone a long way so as to shed the views expressed in KatTyaniII 's ' case justifying demolition of demarcation between the two Services made as it was in Katni Dayal vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors. [1988] Supp. SCC 519 at 691 and Direct Recruit Class II Engineering of officers Association vs State of Maharashtra & Others ; , referred to.

The appellant was tried along with two other persons by the Special Judge, of the Special Court for trial and 1 there expressed the view that it was wrong to think that classification was something that must somehow be discovera ble in every piece of legislation or it would not be legis lation. That way of regarding classification, the State Government referred not certain individual cases but offences of certain kinds committed in certain areas and so the objection as to discriminatory treatment was more easily answered on the line of reasoning indicated in his judgment in the West Bengal case (1) L.R. 476 measure, and the appellant was convicted and sentenced by the High Court. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. Held:(i) The object of section 11 of the Ordinance is to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State. Once this is appreciated it is easy to see that there is something in the Ordinance itself to guide the State Govern ment to apply the special procedure not to any and every case but only to those cases or offences which have a razional relation to, or connection with, the main object and purpose of the Act which for that reason become a class by themselves requiring to be dealt with on a special footing. The clear recital of a definite objective furnishes a tangible and rational basis of classification to the State Govt. for the purpose of applying the provisions of the section is not an un guided discretion; it has to be exercised in conformity with the policy to effectuate which the direction is given and it is in relation to that objective that the propriety of the classification would have to be tested. The words "classes of offences" or "cl classes of cases" make it the duty of the State government to make a proper classification, that is to say, a classification which must fulfil both conditions, namely, that it must be based on some intelligible differentia distinguishing the offences grouped together from other offences and that differentia must have a reasonable relation to the object of the act as recited in the preamble. The Legislature has left it to the Government to classify offences or classes of offences or class of cases for being tried by the special tribunal. If at any time, however, the state Government classifies offences arbitrarily and not on any reasonable basis having a relation to its object, its action will be either an abuse of its power if it is purposeful, or in excess of its powers even if it was done in good faith, and in either case the resulting discrimination will encounter the challenge of the Constitution and the Court will strike down, not the law which is good, but the abuse or misuse or unconstitutional adminis trative of the law creating or resulting in unconstitu tional discrimination. The argument that there has been no discrimination as against the appellant visa vis other persons charged with the same offences is unacceptable. It is no answer to the charge by A of discrim inatory legislation to say that B and C have also been placed in the same category as himself when he finds that D, E and F also liable for the same or kindred offences has been left untouched and are to be tried by ordinary courts under the normal procedure. It may be that all the facts stated by him as regards the frequency and locale of the particular offences are true. But no such grounds for the classifica tion are indicated, much less stated either in the impugned Ordinance or notification.

The appellants were charged with the offence of committing theft and murder. The prosecution case was that on the day of occurrence, the deceased had reported by his brother that the accused persons had committed theft of timber belonging to the village school managed by him. The trial court acquitted nine accused, namely, A 1 to 4,6,12 and 16 to 18 as those who entered the house and attacked her husband and caused injuries to her and carried away the properties from the house.
