The Sessions Judge found that the FIR had been lodged at the Police Station without any inordinate delay and that there was nothing on record to show that there were any oblique motive for concocting a false story of the occurrence itself in that first information report. The High Court, however, acquitted all the nine accused. On appeal by special leave it was contended: (1) that the F.I.R. had been registered at the police station without any delay and therefore there was no reason whatsoever for concocing a false version of the incident itself in this case; (2) that P.W. 2 had modulated her evidence to fit in with the case of the prosecution and that the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 should not be relied upon for basing the conviction of the appellants in this ease; (3) that there is no reason whatever whatsoever for rejecting the evidence Of P. Ws. 1 and 7; (4) that even if P. W.7 who was admittedly one of the residents of the house in which the occurrence had taken place, he would have either fallen down there or returned to his house. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1(a) The F. I.R., Exh. Ka. 1 is not fatal to the prosecution.

The employer, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation created under the State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to the Transport Undertaking. The employer terminated the employment of some of the employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised questioning the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held, overruling the stand of the employer that section 25F had no application to the effect that the discharge was invalid. The employee Corporation came before the High Court challenging the Award. A learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in Section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for noncompliance of section 25 F of the Act. The appellant Corporation challenged the decision of the Single Judge before a Division Bench and the Division Bench upheld the decision. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. When a portion of the staff or labour force is discharged as surplusage in a continuing business, there are (a) termination of the service of a workman; (b) by the employer; (c) for any reason whatsoever; and (d) otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include (a), voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation or absence on account of continued ill health. [793F G] 1. The expression 'termination of service for any reasons whatsoever ' are understood to mean what they plainly say, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of service of workman by an act of the employee. The underlying assumption, of course, is that the undertaking is running as an undertaking and the employer continues as an employer but where either on account or of transfer of the undertaking or on account from the closure of the Undertaking the basic assumption disappears, there can be no question of 'ret retrenchmentrenchment, within the meaning of the definition contained in section 2(0oo). This came to be realised as a result of the decision in L. Robert D 'Souza vs The Executive Engineer, Southern Railway & Anr., [1970] 1 SCR 591 and Mohan Lal vs Management of M/s Bharat Electronics Ltd., ; , referred to. In the instant case, the requirement of section 2 (oo) is fulfilled, it would be wrong to take the definition as destroying the essential meaning of 'the word defined. [788A B] 2.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment under the Act. On 6 June 1959 he made an order rejecting the application. On 7 June 1960 he made another order rejecting his application on 28 January, 1960 on the basis that the dispose of the unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act, and accordingly liable to assess ment under that Act. The assessee then proceeded in further revision before the Board of Revenue, West Bengal. The Board of Re spondent No. 780 referred the following question to the High Court at Calcutta for its opinion: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Controller of Stores, Eastern Railways is a dealer engaged in the business of selling scrap and unserviceable material within the meaning of cl. (c) read with C1 (g) of section 2 of the Bengal Re stitution Finance ( Sales Tax) Rules, 1941?" The High Court answered the other two questions referred to the Tribunal for its conclu sion: " Whether on the findings and circum stances in the case out of which Civil Appeal No. 1069 of 1975 arises are substantially similar to those narrated in the earlier case, except that the assessee here is the Eastern Railway and it is engaged in selling scrap scrap and waste unserviceable materials lying with it. The case was covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In these appeals the question is whether the assessee Railway in each case is a " dealer" for the purpose of as sessment under the Indian Railways Act, 194 1 and therefore liable to assessed assessment under that act. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the Goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway.

The appellants were convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. The prosecution case was that to provide funds for the payment of these losses at the due time, the accused persons entered into the conspiracy for the diversion of the funds of the Insurance Company to the Union Agencies and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 409 I.P.C., and all of them except Vishnu Prasad, were also convicted of various offences arising from the overt act committed by the appellants. The High Court dismissed their appeals holding that Dalmia and Chokhani were entrusted with the dominion over the funds in the Insurance Co. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of Dalmia that he had obtained control over the moneys of the insurance Company by cheating Raghunath Rai inasmuch as he got blank cheques signed by the latter on the representation that they would be used for the legitimate purpose of the company but later used them for not connected with the affairs of the said Bharat Insurance Co., and that therefore, he could not commit the offence of criminal breach of trust. Held: (i) The evidence showed that Dalmia had the necessary criminal intent as what Chokhani did was known to him and was under his instructions, that of Raghunath Rai, Secretary cum Account of the Bharat Insurance Company Ltd., in the name of 'Bhagwati Trading Company, deliberately told Dalmia that it was necessary for the purpose of withdrawal of the securities for which he had given instructions. (ii) The opening expression in the letter did not necessarily mean that Gurha was being informed for the first time that the temporary loans arranged by him for the Union agencies Ltd., were to be utilised in the fictitious purchase of securities. (iii) The fact that the account of the Asia Udyog Udyog Ltd., was in the same building and being looked after by Gurha, could not be a ground for holding that he should report such transactions on the part of Dalmia to the Chairman, if not necessarily for his approval at least for his information, as Chokhani had no authority to purchase and sell securities. The fact, if true, that the Insurance company suffered no monetary loss on account of its purchase and sale transactions and the passing of its money to the union Agencies, did not suffice to make the transaction an honest one. (iv) The statement made by Dalmia in his letter dated September 17, 1955, was not a case of the security missing securities but a case for the prosecution not getting those securities at all.

The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the former State of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1956. The newly constituted State of Gujrat found a dearth of experienced officers in the Secretariat transferred them and posted in various districts in Saurashtra and Kutch. Under section 115 of the it was provided that every person who immediately before the appointed day was serving in connection, with the administration of any of the existing States specified therein shall, as from that day be deemed to have been allotted to him serve in connec tion with the activities of the successor State to that existing State. By virtue of section 116 power was conferred upon the Central Government to give directions to the States. Those provisions were substantially similar to those of sections 115, 116 and 117 of the . The appellants were given notice of their appointment by the State Government under article 309 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that r. 138 only dealt with the existing servants and did not prevent any additional members from being amalgamated in the ministerial staff in the subordinate offices. The High Court held that since the impugned order purported to amalgamate the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States personnel with the Gujarat Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r. 139 of the Recruitment Rules, 1957, it altered the conditions of service of the applicants; and that it violated the provisions of the Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules,1957. The appellants contended that the order violated r.138 of the recruitment rules framed by the Government of Bombay in 1957; that the transfer of the latter Saurashtra and Gujarat and Kutch States Secretariat personnel to the Gujarat secretariat per se was not open to objection. HELD : (i) The expression "absorption" has not been used in the order but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former and Kutch states personnel in the secretariat.

The petitioners of the second category purchase oil seeds for use in manufacture of edible oils. The surplus oil seeds were sold to other dealers, registered or unregistered, inside and outside the State. Both these commodities were essential commodities to which the Central Sales Tax Act applied. Certain provisions of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 were challenged on the ground that they offend section 15 of the Central Act and were also unconstitutional being in violation of Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the Act was not within the competence of the State Legislature to pass such an Act retrospectively. HELD:(i) Under those circumstances there is always a possibility, or even a certainty, of more persons than one having paid tax or being made liable to pay tax in respect of the same goods at different stages. That is quite opposed to the provisions of section 15 (a) of the Act. Even otherwise it is pointed out that if a person has purchased cotton and sells it after the period provided for in section 5(2)(a)(vi), that party is liable to payment of tax and would have also paid the same. Another purchaser from the said party will also be liable to make payment of the tax till he is the dealer liable to Pay the tax. [550 E] (ii) The object of the Haryana Amendment Act was to enable the State by a law "to impose on goods imported (1) [1969] S.C.R. 557, followed. (iii) Section 15(1) of that Act provides an adequate relief, by way of refund, even if tax is collected at an earlier stage. The amendment Acts which are now challenged set about removing these difficulties are again challenged on different lines.

The appellants, who were the representatives of three original plaintiffs, instituted a suit against the present respondent for enforcement of a mortgage against the appel lant. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No. 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte and there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which a sum of RS. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant No 1 and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties and the suit was dismissed against defendant No 2. Against this decree two appeals were taken to the Madras High Court, one by defendant Nos. 3 to 6 being Appeal No. 48 of 1938 who contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to he paid by them under the decree. The High Court accepted the finding of the trial judge and held that defendant No., 2 was entitled to have the debt scaled down in favour of defendants 2 to 7 only and the amended decree directs that the said defendants do pay into court the sum of Rs. 49,255 with certain interest and costs on payment thereof from the decretal amount. The appellants came up on appeal by special leave. Held: (i) The High Courts ' approach to the case has not been a proper one and the conclusion it has reached cannot be supported in law. Arunachalam Pillai vs Seetharam, [1940] 2 M. 39 300 decisions referred to. (ii) In the working of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act alongside the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act several curious and novel situations had arisen for which it was not possible always to find logical solu tions. They then proceeded to discuss the various decisions of the High Court which had a bearing on this point and the conclusions which they reached may be summed up in their words as follows: "It is no doubt somewhat odd that when a person is declared liable to pay a larger amount he should on payment or tender of a smaller amount get his property exonerated from liability but this is inherent in and arises out of the proposition established by the decisions already dealt with, namely, that by the application of the principle of unity and omnisibility of a mort gagor decree a non agriculturist can indirectly get relief which he cannot directly get. " (iii) The Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act is a special statute which aims at giving relief not to debtors in general but only to a specified class of debtors, viz., those who are agriculturists as defined in the Act. To this extent it trenches upon the general law and section 7 of the Act expressly provides that notwithstanding any law, custom, contract or decree of court to the contrary, all debts payable by an agriculturist at the commencement of this Act shall be scaled up in accordance with the provisions Of this chapter".

The City Civil Court, Bombay, had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit filed by the appellants in the City Civil court. The City Civil Judge held that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful sub tenants of the first plaintiff and were entitled to possession, use and occupation of the premises as subtenants thereof. On appeal, the High Court disagreed with the view of the City civil Court that he had jurisdiction to try the suit but did not record any decision on merits of the appellants ' case. The question which requires consideration in this appeal is whether the High court correctly decided that the City Court had no juris diction to entertain a suit filed in the city Civil Court. Held, further, that the suit was essentially a suit between a landlord and a tenant within the meaning of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and the suit related to possession of the Premises and the right of the landlord to evict any of the plaintiffs was denied on the ground that the first appellant was a tenant of the said premises within the mean ing of the Act. The suit was therefore a denial of the right to the defendants as tenants. The claim of the defendants was one which arose out of the act or any of its provisions and only the courts specified in section 28 and no other could deal with it and decide the issue. The suits related to the possession of premises and the rights of the landlords to evict anyone of the plaintiff was denied by the plaintiffs on the grounds that the latter were tenants of tho premises within their meaning of section 29A of the , and the premises had been lawfully sublet by them to the second appellant and third appellants.

The respondent was a director of the appellant company. The appellant was appointed the managing director of a private company for life and was given the power "by deed inter vivos or by will or codicil to appoint any person to be a managing director in his place and stead". Regulation 109 of the articles of the company reproduced these provisions. The shareholders of the Company were Dadoba, his brother, the respondent Bhaskar, and his two sons, the appellant Govind and the respondent Harish. The respondent was the managing directors of the private company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his business to the appellant and had now no interest in the company or the appeal. No one appeared to contest the appeal in this Court, the respondents filed a suit against the appellants for declaration and for an injunction restraining the appellants from appointing their successor, as managing director. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court granted a certificate under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution and the present appeal was filed by the company. Held: (i) that section 312 of the , does not prevent a director from appointing his successor, which is what has been described as "per petual management". The word "assignment" in the section included "appointment", and so, such an appointment would also be void under the section. (ii)that the proviso to section 86B of the 1913 Act does not help the argument that in section 312 the word "resign" in it, can mean "appointment". The rule of construction on which the High court relied in arriving at the view that it did was put in these words, is that if the words "assignatures" included " appointment", the object of the Act would be defeated. It is intended that a certain number of directors would be the chosen representatives of the shareholders. If a director appointed (1) [1960] S.C.R. 969, followed.

The appellants are the tenants against the respondent landlady. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellant firm and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the respondent M/S. Adi sation Mart, and were liable to be evicted forwil ful subletting under the provisions of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Trial Court held that the ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respondent. The appel lants preferred an appeal against this decision to the Appellate Authority under Section 23 of the said Rent Act being the Court of Small Causes at Madras. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The appellants then filed a Civil Revision Petition in the High Court against the aforesaid decision. This Revision Petition was dismissed by the then Chief Justice of the Madras High Court. It is against the decision of the High court that the present appeal is directed. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In an eviction suit under clause 13(3)(iv) and (vii) of tho Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, the appellant has raised a preliminary objection that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. [420C] 1.2 In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. This contention must, therefore, be negatived. [421D] Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership Firm and others vs Shikharchand, , relied upon by Mr. Nayar, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised at the earliest stage and was wrongly negatived by the Trial Court.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act 1 of 1973 was enacted by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature on January 1, 1973. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted with retrospective effect from January 1 1975 and by this amending Act certain amendments were made which included inter alia the introduction of section 41A. In the course of the hearing of the petitions, the Court made it clear to the parties that the question whether a particular land is an urban agglomeration or not would be decided by the Court. The petitioners in CA Nos. 14 to 23 contended that the Andhra Act was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the Andhra State Legislature. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1. A statute intended to strike at concentration of land in the hands of a few and to act as a great equaliser by reducing inequality in holding of land between the haves and the have nots should have practically remained unimplemented for a period of over seven years. The definition of "family unit" in section 2(f) is materially in the same terms as the definition of family unit in the Andhra pradesh Act. Then follow two important definitions which needed to be set out in extenso. The word "person" is defined in section 3(j) to mean "land which A is used or is capable of being used for purposes ancillary thereto, including horticulture, forest land, pasture land, waste land, plantation and tope; and includes land deemed to be agricultural land under this Act". [1155 C E] 1.2. The term "urban agglomeration" in the definition section 2 (f) of the Act is materially different from that defined in the Act. It is not possible to uphold the contention of the landholders that the whole of the State of Andhra Pradesh is concerned. [1156 F G] Union of India vs V.V. Chaudhary, ; , referred to. 1.3. The expression "person", is defined by section 2 of the Central Act but until it is so notified it would not be an urbanisable agglomeration and the Andhra Pradesh Legislature would have legislative competence to provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate within such area.

The workmen of the appellant company were dismissed for alleged disobedience of orders, and on August 18, 1953, a notice was issued by the Company to the workmen calling upon them to resume work between June 5, 1953 and October 2, 1953. The workmen did not join duty but were allowed by the company to resume their duties. On September 23, 1953 the company issued a third notice which stated inter alia that " all employees on the Works rolls of the Company on the 23rd August, 1953 shall be deemed to be discharged with effect from the date of the lock out really meant that the Company refused to employ the workmen during the period when the place of employment was closed. The management of the company thereupon issued a notice to the workman stating inter alia: "All employees on Works rolls on the 3rd August 1953, and who wish to report for duty, must resume work from the dates he is declared fit by the said Company 's Medical authorities. Any worker who has left the vicinity of the Works may resume duty on or before Thursday, the 24th September, 1953." The workmen were not allowed by it to resume his duties. The company thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice and the legality of the action taken against them. The High Court dismissed both the appeals. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the workmen it was contended that (i) the Tribunal had wrongly construed the notices dated August 23,1953, and September 17, 1953 respectively; (ii) the continued illegal stoppages of work, 'slow down tactics and strikes indulged in by the workmen despite the advice of their Union, left the Company no alternative but to discharge the workmen except in some essential departments, with effect on August 24, 1953; and (iii) the notice dated September 17 was not an inflexible rule. Held:(i) The Tribunal had misdirect ed themselves as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Orders of the companies for the period after October 2.1953, the only reasonable construction is the one adopted by the Tribunals, viz., that the employees whose employment had been refused during the lockout were permitted to resume duty without any conditions if they reported for duty by a particular date, and that on fulfilment of a condition if they report for work after that date. The Tribunal found that the charge against the workmen was completely baseless and the enquiry report against the company was not proved even according to the Companies ' own version. (ii)(a) The finding of the two Tribunals on this point is erroneous. On merits, the case against Samar Sen was that as a result of a regular and proper enquiry, he was found guilty of unauthorised absence and insubordination, etc., and therefore, the company dismissed him.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. R.Nathawat retired on 30th September, 1989. Dr, Urea Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list was appointed as Professor in the department of Bot any. Dr Bhikalal, Dr. Shiv Sharma, Dr, Shri Sanjay Mishra and Dr. T.N. Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challeng ing the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant as Professor on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve List exhausted itself. The Division Bench held that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment to Dr. Urea Bhushan from the reserve lists it was held that once the selected person joining the post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve mate list is of no avail and becomes extinct. It was also held that since 1978 not only in the University of Rajasthan but all other universities in the State of Rajasthan reserve lists are prepared and appointments are being made from the re serve list against future vacancies arising on account of resignation, retirement or promotion. A long list of ap pointments made from reserve list in various departments of the University from time to time after joining of the persons from the main list from 1978 to 1990 have been furnished by the appellants before this Court by an additional affidavit. It has also been stated that even out of the petitioners who had filed the writ petition, Dr . T. N. Bhardwaj himself was kept in reserve list and was there after appointed on the post for selection of a teacher in BOTany.

The petitioners were owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay, commonly known as Greater Bombay. They had all similar but separate grievances with respect to the development plan prepared and published under the Act. In Writ Petition No. 228 of 1966 the petitioners challenged the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, on the ground that they had applied through their architect on January 2, 1962 for permission to change the existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose by which they proposed to construct on a portion of the land in section 70, Hissa No. 4 a shed for a factory and other necessary sheds. Along with the said letter they gave a notice under section 33 of the Act to the effect that their lands were needed for the public purpose of a park quashed. The petitioners contended that (i) the notification issued by the first respondent was in proper exercise of the right of rejection of the petitioners ' proposal for construction of two factory buildings and lavatory blocks, which had been earmarked partly for public roads in an industrial area and merely marked by green colour without any specification; (ii) the reservation and re designation of these lands for recreation centre and green belt by the second respondent was invalid as it infringed article 14 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that the power and functions of a local authority for purposes of sections 12 and 13, amongst others, were to be exercised and performed by the Municipal Commis sioner under section 86 of the , and that the decision dated January 27, 1962 was liable to be set aside; (iii) even after the preparation of the draft development plan, the Consulting Engineer heard the parties who had objected to such changes and then framed his proposals in respect of such ward in the development Plan for sanction by the Government. The common complaint in all these petitions was that sections 9 and 10 of the said Act were invalid and unconstitutional in that they empower the local authority and the State Government to modify the development plans without giving opportunity to persons whose interest might be adversely affected by such modification; (iv) even assuming that the State Legislature could pass the Act, nevertheless its provisions regarding the levy of contribution towards the cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the Scheme were unauthorised and unreasonable and that section 19(3) of the impugned Act vested an unguided, unfettered, uncontrolled and uncontrolled power in an executive officer to withhold permission to execute a decree which a landlord had obtained after satisfying the reasonable requirements of law as enacted in the Rent Control Act; (v) even though section 12 did not expressly state the grounds on which the competent authority might grant or withhold permission for execution to execute decrees and the power conferred was therefore arbitrary and violative article 14 Of the Constitution, and (vi) even if it were open to others to make suggestions without any notice to A, the local authori ty was in a position to consider such advis ities and give effect thereto in the Development plan submitted to the State Govern ment. The Court rejected the contentions of the respondents and dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power vested in the competent autho rity at its sweet will and pleasure to refuse permission to execution a decree for eviction violated the right to hold property under article 19(1)(f) of ' the Constitution on the grounds that there were no principles in the Act itself to guide the competent authori ties in the exercise of his discretion. [286 E] (2) The authority was not concerned with considering the advantages or disadvantages which might accrue to a particular person or a group of persons owning lands in different parts of the area concerned, but it had to go by the larger interest of the population at large and the generations to come.

The petitioners who were the Union of India, challenged the validity of the West Pakistan Merged into a Part C State and under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground that it was inconsistent with the provisions of article 31(1) (d), and (e) of the Constitu tion. The contentions raised by them in their writ petitions to the High Court were that the area of Kutch was not a part of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions, that the question whether the land was a part or a part thereof was a matter which could be decided by arbitration, (2) that the dispute related to the boundary between India and Pakistan in the Rann of Kutch and Kutch and therefore the dispute involved some 3,500. square miles of territory; (3) that there was no clear evidence of demarcation of a boundary acceptable to the parties now or in the past, (4) that in any case it was not necessary for the executive authority in India to obtain the approval of Parliament by suitable amendment of the Indian Constitution before effectuating the Award. HELD : The dispute related only to the location of the boundary as delineated by the Tribunal on maps to be annexed to the award. [826 E] (1) The demarcation between the two States was indefinite and by the award of the Tribunal the true boundary of India. But there is no evidence that it is part of the Great Rann or conflicting claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch State authorities before the State merged with the Dominion of India in 1948, and the persistent refusal of the British Authorities, though there were several occasions to demarcate the boundary. [825 C] (2)(a) The question whether a portion of Chilahati is a territory which was administered as if it formed part of West Bengal within the meaning of Entry 13 Part 'A Sch. The Court held that the proposed transfer of a part Of the village of Chilhati which was part of that Indian territory could not be transferred by the Government of India to Pakistan, was not relevant for the purpose of determining whether in implementing the award, the executive Government was ceding territory of India or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maharao of Kutch. [827 D] (b) The evidence on record showed that the disputed sectors were part of tho Kutch State but there was a consistent exercise of sovereign rights and duties by Sind autho rities, and activities of residents of Sind, in one instance, taking the form of a permanent settlement at Shakur. The territory in this sector is contiguous to and in fact is an extension of the mainland of Sind. It is not shown that it has the characteristics of the Ron terrain. There is no reliable evidence about the enjoyment of the benefits of the land in the Sector by the inhabitants of Kutch, nor does it operate as giving rise to, an obligation to cede Indian territory. [828 E F] (c) The contention that the territory in question belonged to the Kutch Kutch State and that claim was supported by survey maps, correspondence between the officials of Kutch State, cannot be accepted. There was no reliable material about the user of the rights of the claimants to relief. Unless there is evidence to show that the inlets were territory over which the Maha Rao of Kutch had sovereign rights, acceptance of the award is not required to be implemented by a constitutional amendment.

The mortgagor had leased 200 bighas of coal bearing land out of his holding in Mauza Bahaldih to certain lessees for an annual royalty of Rs. 2,000 payable in two equal instalments, the first in the month of Aswin of the Vikram year and the second in the months of Chaitra. On June 14, 1922, the mortgagor assigned his interest in Mauza Bansjora to one Mahendra Nath Rai and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his share in Mauza Simitanr Bahaldh to one Moyee Devi. Thereafter in execution of a money decree obtained against the mortgagor, his right title and interest in mauz Bahald Ranchi was sold on January 16, 1937 and after that sale was confirmed possession of Mauza BahaW had taken by auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. By two deeds dated June 18, 1946, Manimala Devi the plaintiff in the suit out of which this appeal arises obtained assignments of the rights of the mortgagees under the two deeds executed by the mortgagor. The plaintiff relied upon certain payments evidenced by these endorsements to extend the period of limitation in respect of the two mortgage claims. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit was within limitation both on account of part payment of principal and interest and upon the cause of action furnished by the dispossession of the lessees in respect Of the Bahaldip property. In appeal by the fourth defendant widow of Mehandra Nath Rai, the High Court reversed the decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the plaintiff 's suit. The High Court held that as the plaintiff had in her plaint not relied upon dispossession as a ground for extension of the period Of limitation, that claim should not have been permitted to be made out by the Trial Court. Held: (i) The terms of the deeds are substantially the same and such differences as there are in the covenants have no bearing on the questions to be decided in this appeal. (ii) A suit for enforcement of the personal covenant to pay the mortgage money when the mortgagor has bound himself to repay the same is governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act from the date of destruction or deprivation of the mortgage security or possession and not from thedate when the mortgage amount is repayable : Unichaman vs Ahmed. [1951] S.C.R. 644, followed. (iii) A mortgagor who has lost all interest in the mortgaged property cannot by payment of interest or principal within the meaning of section 20 bind the person on whom the interest has devolved. But the mortgagor 's interest in a Mauza Bahadldih subsisted on the date when the money sued for becomes due, unless the period prescribed is extended in the manner provided by Part III of the limitation Act.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport facilities which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TILCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month levied for the Transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TULCo factory at Pimgra and back was realised on by the appellant from the employee. Similarly, for the transported facilities provided in the employees 's supervisory grades, they are charged at a rate of RS 5 per day. A show of Rs 2 per mensem was levied for transport of employees of the company from Chinvad Village and back to TLCO factory at Pipri or back. The appellants further averred that these amounts were realised by them only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of arguments, it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman contended that even if a nominalcharge is realised from the appellants, that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. In view of what we have already said, it is not necessary for this Court to go into such meticulous details because the legal position appears to be clear enough. As counsel for the appellants has already undertaken not to charge any amount from the Employees for providing transport facilities and the point has now become more or less academic. The Commissioner appears to have dismissed the appeals of the appellants 5 978 SCI/78 as he felt bound by the judgment of the Bombay High Court which had held that the transport vehicle provided to them by the company would be a public Service vehicle. In these circumstances, therefore, it cannot be said that the Transport vehicle provided by the appel lant could be a Public service vehicle in any sense of the term. The word 'public ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that Company. Thus, qua public the employees employees form a separate class and cannot be so said to be public as contemplated by rule 2(i). On the other hand, the Bombay Motor Vehicles Rules 1959 framed under the Bombay Act defines 'public service vehicles ' as follows: "Private Service Vehicle ' means any omnibus constructed or adapted to carry more than nine persons excluding the driver and ordinarily used by or on behalf of the owner of such vehicle for the purpose of carrying persons for or in connection with his trade or business, or otherwise than for hire or reward; but does not include a motor vehicle used solely for Police purposes". The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition.

The appellants, who were the residents of a locality, applied for grant of a licence for a temporary cinema and the District Magistrate having jurisdiction issued a no objection certificate under his order dated October 10, 1976 for a period of six months. This licence was renewed upto 30th June 1976 and there was a further renewal up to 30th September 1976. A subsequent application for renewal was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate on 29th June 1977 on the ground that Paras Talkies with permanent cinema licence which was closed, had now been functioning in the locality and therefore a renewal of the licence for the temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper. The appellants filed a writ petition under Article 226 questioning the validity of the order dated December 27, 1977 granting a licence to respondent No. 3. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the District Judge was not influenced by the fact that there was mosque and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema license having been re opened in the area locality there was no need for a cinema house with a temporary licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Govt. on being satisfied that there is no impediment to the grant of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and therefore it was not a fit case for interference of the High Court. The appellant contended before this Court that if the grant was granted by an order dated May 10, 1977, the appellants as objectors should have been heard and the decision arrived at by the State government appeal at their back was violative of the principles of natural justice and the order granting licence for quasi permanent cinema by the state Government was invalid. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Rules envisage issuance of a "no objection" certificate relevant to the site on which the cinema house to be built is a sine qua non. The grievance of the appellants is that when their objections were invited before issuance of no objection certificates and they filed the same, the Distt., Magistrate as the licensing authority was persuaded to accept the objections and reject the application for a no. objection certificate and thereafter when under section 5(3) of the Act respondent preferred appeal against the refusal to grant the no objection Certificate, the appeal was decided at the back of those who had not only filed objections but whose objections had prevailed with the licensing authorities and, therefore, the order of the first respondent State Government refusing such a license is violative of principles of Natural justice. [799 C D] 2. The rules envisage issuance or grant of licences for a permanent Cinema and quasi permanent cinemas as well as a touring cinema. Cinema in this context has been defined to mean any place wherein an exhibition by means of cinematograph is given. Rule 3 envisages construction of a cinema building and as a first step, selection of a site where the cinema houses is to be located.

The plaintiff instituted a suit against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated September 2, 1957 the defendant agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekan Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and claiming specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no concluded contract between the parties. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there could be no con cluded contract. HELD: (i) Under section 2(6), a plaint in a suit for specific performance should allege a concluded contract, see the Code of Civil Procedure 1st Schedule Appendix A, Form No. 48. The offer as well as the acceptance should Pr=& the institution of the suit was not an acceptance of the offer, not being it intended to be an acceptance. [ 584 C] (ii) Under the old chancery practice the mere filing of a bill in a Suit to enforce specific performance was regarded as sufficient acceptance of 'the defendant 's offer unless the offer had been withdrawn before, the filing of the plaint, see Boys vs Ayerst, , Fry on Specific Performance, 8th ed., article 306, Pomeroyon vs Biden, , referred to. (iii) The plaintiff was at liberty to revoke the offer at any tune beforeits acceptance by the plaintiffs. [585 C] In re: Pellatt 's Case, , followed.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K. Sugar, Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of Rule 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order 1955 read with section 7 of the , on the ground that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The appellants contended that the investigation on various grounds was not being carried on against the appellants under sub r. (3 ) of rule 3 of Sugarcane (Regulation of Production) Order, 1955. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the regulation of the price was expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 and therefore there could be no cognizance taken of the offence alleged. HELD: 1. The power conferred on the Government under section 3 of ' the Act cannot be challenged as invalid. There is no substance in the contention that the impugned order contravenes the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19 (1) ). No fundamental right is conferred on a buyer not to pay the price Of the goods purchased by him or to pay it whenever he pleases. The contention that in view of section 11 of the Act no cognizance could have been taken of offence alleged was premature. [677 E F] 2. The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section 2(a) of the is a specific mandate. If the Bihar Act provides anything to the contrary the same must be held to have been altered in view Of article 372 of the Constitution which provides that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [678 G H] 3. The authority altered or amended that law is a competent one. The next contention of the appellant was that the Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order was issued on 11th August, 1975 which recited that the Government of Mysore was committed to a policy of rapid industrialization and that, in pursuance thereof, the Government had on 30th November 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The said order dated 12th January, 1977 inter alia provided as under: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new industrial units in the Bangalore State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first 5 years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concession being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce. " By an order dated 11th January 1977, the procedure was prescribed for obtaining the concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th February, 1977, Government of the Karnataka issued another order which stated that the reasons for making the said order of 12th December, 1977 were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The aforesaid order dated 10th January was challenged before a Single Judge of the High Court who dismissed the writ petition holding that the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the ground that undue advantage was being taken of the same. In appeal, the Division Bench held that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds and that the concession granted by the said Order dated 30th June, 1969 were of no legal effect as there is no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted and the order of 30th May, 1969 was ultra vires and bad in law. In the concluding portion of his judgment, the learned Judge clarified that he had not examined the correctness of the individual claims made by the petitioners and that these claims would have to be examined by the competent authorities. He further clarified that the order dated December 12, 1977 would undoubtedly apply to industries started after that date. The learned Trial Judge allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the footing that the benefit given was called a refund, it could not be said to be an exemption or reduction as permitted by section 8A.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. A 1 to A 6 were however found guilty for the offence punishable under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but convicted them under Section 148 and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 3. The appellants contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 149 and on applying 149 I P. C. cannot be sustained. It was argued that after acquittal of some of the accused persons, by the Courts below the appellants could not have formed an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.p.C.; that the appellants being three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful assembly; that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime; and that the High court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction. On behalf of the respondent it was contended that the appel lants being three In number, could not be convicted under Sections 149 and 302 on applying149 I.I.P., on the ground that they formed an assembly alongwith some unidentified person; that the evidence of PW 1 to the extent it is corroborated by the evidence 6 of P.W.3 in so far as the presence and partic ipation of the appe lants in the attack on the deceased is concerned, and that there was long standing enmity between the parties. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants acted in the furtherance of their common intention of killing the de ceased. [8G] 1.2 There is force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appellants. The appellant being only three in numbers, there were no question o f their forming unlawful assembly into an unlawful com pensation within the meaning of Section 2I. P .C. It is not the prosecution case that apartfrom the seven appellants persons there was some other unnamed persons who are involved in tho crime. The High Court clearly fell in error in confirmed the convic tion and sentence.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam, which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 was completed in the normal course and in this assessment no amount was included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by the assessee at the same price at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the sale. On 4th April 1968 however, the Income Tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for for the year 196667 67 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice. The notice did not state what was the income alleged to have escaped assessment but by his subsequent letter dated 4th March 1969 intimated to the assessee that he proposed to fix the fair market value of the said house sold by him on 25th December 1965 at Rs. 65,000 as against the consideration of Rs 16, 500 for which he was purchased. The Income Tax Officer however issued a show cause notice under s 148 of Act seeking reopen the reassessment of the appellant for the reason that there was admittedly no under statement A of consideration in respect thereof and it was enough to attract the applicability of section 52 sub section (2) and taking the view that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent that there should be under statement of consideration. The assessee thereupon preferred a writ petition in Kerala High Court challenging the validity of the order of reassessment in so far as it brought the sum of Rs 48,500 as capital gains and bringing it to tax. The Full Bench heard the appeal but there was a division of opinion, two Judges took one view and the third Judge taking another. While Raghvan C.J. agreed substantially with the view taken by the Isaacs J., Gopalan Nambiar J. and Vishwanath Iyer J.

The appellant was charged with the offence of committing an offence under section 16(1)(a) (i) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The prosecution case was that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 8(2)(i) read with section 7(ii) of that Act. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him on appeal by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the whole object of the Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human use and that it was part of the prosecution case that the quality of the Til seed at his shop were meant, was more probable because it was supported by what the appellant had written on the cash memo when he sold these Til seeds 'o the Food Inspector. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant must get the benefit of that doubt. As already indicated above, the use of the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. It is quite unsafe to base the appellant 's conviction on such shaky foundations. [331 C] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. 2.1 In order to judge whether the Food inspector 's version or the accused 's explanation was more credible, it must be resolved (i ) A. 1. R. # 1318 331 by evidence in the case. After all, if what is stored or sold was `food '. The charge was that Til seeds sold were unfit to for human habitation as food. [333 D E] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Admn., ; , distinguished. 2:2 It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food and even if this be true, it is not so widely known a fact that we could take judicial notice of it. It was also urged that the appellant must have got the benefit Of that doubt because the appellant did not remember. Even after making every possible allowance for a memory which could fade with lapse of time, his version was extra ordinarily nebulous and noncommittal. The principal witness in the present case was section P. Gayadhani, P.W 2 the prosecuting Food Inspector 's evidence showed that the contents of the tea leaves were full of cocoons, visible to the naked eye, nobody could be expected to purchase them for consumption as food; the appellant was not therefore guilty of any offence under sec.

The plaintiff, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September 1960. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17 6 1969 asking for a declaration that the order of dismiss ment was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed by the Trial Court on 31 8 1966. In the second appeal, the Division Bench of the High Court upheld the dismissal of the plaintiff 's suit on the plea of limita tion. The appellant contended before this Court that Article 113 of the Act of 1963, corresponding to Article 120 of the old Act, is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies. It was further submitted that the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The cause of action shall be taken to arise not from the date of the original adverse order but on the date when the order is made or representation was made, the right to sue accrues. [46C] 2. Article 113 does not apply when the remedy availed of has not been provided by law. Repeated representations not provided by Law are not governed by this principle. It is appropriate to notice the provision regarding limitation under section 21 of the . Sub section (1) has prescribed a period of one year for making of the application and power of condonation of delay of a total period of six months has been vested under sub section (3). The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, as far as Government serv ants are concerned Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation. Yet, suits outside the purview of the shall continue to be gov erned by Article 58. [47D E] 3.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father, several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father as well as the sales held in execution proceedings against his father were not binding on him and so his share in them covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienation did not bind him, upheld all the alienations and dismissed his suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree in respect of alienations which covered items 2, 10 and 14 in Schedule A as well in item 5 in Schedule B. It held that the transactions in respect Of these items were not affected thereby and so a preliminary decree for partition was passed in his favour in respect thereof. The rest of the decree passed by the trial Court was confirmed. On further appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The test prescribed by article 133(1)(a) is an independent additional test and its effect has to be judged by interpreting the words used by the relevant clause. If the said clause refers to the amount of the value of the subject matter still in dispute on appeal quite plainly it would be necessary to take the decree as a whole and enquire whether it is a decree of affirmance or not. In the present case, the test prescribed for determining the value under article 133 (1)(c) is that part of the decision or the grounds given for it but the decision of the suit as a part of it. If that be so, in deter mining the character of the appellate decree it would he necessary to have taken the decree into account only the subject matters in dispute in appeal and nothing more. The words used in this connection are clear and unambiguous but they cannot reasonably control the meaning of the word "decision" in the relevant cl which provides for an additional and independent condition. (ii) If two courts which have judged the dispute between the parties and applied their independent minds to it agree in their conclusions the appellate decision is one of affirmence and unless there is a substantial question of law no further right to appeal should lie. That is the basis of the provision. When, however, a variation is made by the appellate court it tends to show that the two courts have not entirely agreed and so it is not a case of affirmation.

The High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in a case arising out of an original suit of the value of Rs. 20,000 and above, including such suits or other proceedings instituted before 1st August 1978; (ii) The District Court possessed exclusive jurisdiction to deal with cases arising out o the original suits of the values of Rs 20,00 and above and (iii) The High Court possessed concurrent jurisdiction under Section 115 in revision petition filed on and after that date, irrespective of the valuation of the suit out of which the case arose : (a) A revision petition under section 5 of the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1972 was admitted, after preliminary hearing, before 1 2 1977; (b) The trial court had exclusive jurisdic tion under section 151 in a revision petition against an order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act disposing of a revision peti tions ? Dismissing the appeal and the special leave petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 In civil cases the jurisdiction has been entrusted to the highest court of the State, demonstrating that broadly the order under section115 is to be regarded, in the absence of anything else, as a final order within the State judiciary. [35B] 1.2 The scheme would, in large measure, lose its meaning. If a revision Petition is permitted to the High Court against the revisional order of District Court arising out af a suit of a value less than Rs.20,000/ , a fundamental contradiction would be allowed to invade and destroy the division of revisional power between the High court and the District Judge, for 40 the High Courts would then enjoy jurisdictional power in respect of an order arising out Of a suitof a valuation below Rs. 10,000. That was never intended at all. [36C] 1:3 The scheme envisaged by the successive amendments was to divide the work load of revision petitions between the two High Court and the district court and decentralise that jurisdiction.

The respondents were the owners of certain lands situated in village Madrampura on the outskirts of Jaipur city. On June 25, 1975 the Special Officer issued a notice under section 52(2) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 stating that it was proposed by the State Government to acquire the said land admeasuring more or less 44,770 square yards under section52 (1) of that Act for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme viz. Civil Lines Extension Scheme. It was also stated that the said notice was duly served on the respondents and they in compliance therewith appeared before the Special officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur and filed their reply dated September 8, 1975. In the reply, the respondents while denying the existence of a public purposes for acquisition of the lands under section 2 52(1) asserted that they needed the said property to start new businesses in the State , to open a branch office at Jaipur and to construct residential quarters for their Director and other Senior Executives , but at a later stage they alleged that they wanted to construct a Three Star Hotel on the said lands. The Special Officer adjourned the case from time to time and issued several notices to the respondents for personal hearing under section 53(3) of Act. The respondents through their representative appeared at each of these hearings and sought adjournment on one pretext or another. However, despite a series of decisions of this Court starting from Siliguri Municipality vs Amalendu Das (I.L.R. , referred to.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction and arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation pendent lite on the allegation that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises in suit on a monthly rent of Rs. 250 on 7th February, 1972, that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 and that the respondent defaulted in the payment of rent despite notice dated 24th March, 1977. The appellant also challenged the service and the validity of the notice terminating his tenancy. The trial court held that the premises was exempt from the operation of the new Rent Act on two grounds; (i) that the buildings in question were constructed substantially by funds obtained by way of loan or advance from the State Government; and (ii) that rent had been cleared upto 6th April, 1977 and there was no default in the payments of rent. The Judge overruled the other pleas of the appellant and decreed the suit for ejectment as also for recovery of arrears of rents and damages. The High Court confirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about the arrears of the rent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the new Act would be attracted if the building completes ten years during the course of litigation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit of section 39 of the old Rent Act there is a change in the cause of action. [338E] 1.2 In A.K. Gupta & Sons vs Damodar Valley Corporation this Court dealing with the cause for action observed as follows: "The expression "cause of action" in the instant context does not mean every fact which it is material to be proved to entitle the plaintiff to succeed" as was said in Cooks vs Gill, [1978] 2 SCR p. 861 1.3 The question whether the appellant would be entitled to the benefit under section 39 as the building had not become ten years old on the date of their the suit. But during the pendency of the litigation it completed ten years.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and other works at Ranchi. After the above works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948 they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that accordingly it fell within item 12. Held, that the copy of the Award which was sent to the Government would appear to have been insufficiently stamped. If that had not been produced in court, it could have been validated on payment of deficiency and penalty under section 35 of the Stamp Act, 1899. The law is no doubt well settled that the copies of an instrument cannot be validated: That was held in the present case by the arbitrator who sent the copy to the appellant. The copy of an award which was forwarded to the Court would have been sufficiently stamped as required by section 35 Of the Stamp Rules and had it validated. Y. K. Lall, Executive Engineer, Ranchi Division, and by the respondents were duly authorised to execute the agreement dated 2nd February 1948.

The respondent, in Criminal Appeal No. 422/88 was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. On various dates in that year, he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received against the respondent pertaining to the purchase. of the sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In that meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The aforesaid First Information Reports were challenged by the Respondent in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 5837 M/85 on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed sign boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2. The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. 100/ each and the issued and paid up capital was 2,500 ordinary and 3 1,000 ordinary and preference shares. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares with no right in the balance of the profits. The respondent company took over the business conducted by it for Rs. 5,50,0001 paid in the form of 2, 500 ordinary and three,000 shares. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The Tribunal held that for three years ended March 31 and March 1, 1949 the Company had declared every year a "unit" as "unilit". Held, that the Explanation to section 23 A was in reality a clause which defined what a company, in which the public are substantially interested, is not one in which it the public were substantially interested. The Explanation raises a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of the Company carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group. For the purpose of computing twenty five% of the votes power, however rights of holders of shares entitled to fixed dividends have to be excluded. It is now settled law that the distinction between the controlling groups and the public is not along the line which distinguishes directors from the remaining members of the 16 company. If a director does not belong to the controlling com pany group, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation must be construed strictly.

The first appellant, a registered joint stock company, was fined and despatched the goods to the second appellant. But in the meanwhile the first appellant credited Dwarkadas Khetan with the money he had received from Dharsi Khemji on account of the 13 consignments less Dwarkad as Khetan & Company had been entered as the person to whom delivery was made. The second appellant thereafter wrote to the first appel lant that his firm had received payment in advance from Shree Kishan and Company, that the 13th bales should be sent to "our godown ", whether the " refers to Dwarkadash" or to a godown jointly shared between Dwarkadandas Khetan and the first respondent was not clear. The third appellant then wrote to first appellant on 17th February 1947, stating that he had been authorised to take delivery of the goods, (2) as shown above, the property in them had passed and so the first appellants no longer had title to them, (3) Dwarkadassas Khetan & Co. was the sole selling agents and they alone were responsible to the Mills for orders which were placed through them; and (4) Dwarkathiramdas Shah vs The Province of Madras ([1952] S.C.R. 835), held inapplicable. Held, further, that in a penal statute of this kind it is our duty to interpret words of ambiguous meaning in a broad and liberal sense so that they will not become traps for honest, unlearned (in the law) and unwary men. If there is honest and substantial compliance with an array of puzzling directions, that should be enough even if on some hypercritical view of the law other ingenious meanings can be devised. In a penal Act of this type it is the duty to construe words of plain meaning in broad and ordinary sense so as to give them a more than outline them here. The facts are truly and accurately given according to the popular and natural meaning of the words used; nothing was hidden.

The respondents were charged under section 165 A, Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 114 of the Indian Penal code. He imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000/ , in default further rigorous imprisonment for six months.
