The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The following table sets out the amounts of dividend received by the assessee from the Company and the years in respect of which they were received, were: Year of Year of declaration amount of dividend 1951 52 1357 B.S. Rs. 37,125/ 1952 53 1358 B. S. Rs . Rs. 28,125. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669 for the year 1357B, Rs. Rs., 20,469/ for the years 1358 58 B.s.S., Rs. 20,470/ , for the period 1358B and Rs. 21,822/ for 1951 52, Rs,7878/ for 1952 53, Rs 1358 for the assessment year 1359 B. Rs,1357 B, Rs 28,469 for the previous years 1357, Rs 7878 for the earlier years 1359 B. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax Act, was liable to be grosated up. In second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by it for the grant of long term leases was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assesse from "other sources". The High Court also observed that it was agreed between the parties that the answers in the negative on all the questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964 pending in this Court. In these appeals by special leave, the assessee company contended: (i) that distribution to the assessee of the sum attributable to land acquisition compensation received by Ukhaura Estate Zamindary (P) Ltd., after the 31st March, 1948 was a receipt of income in its hands and taxable as the income of assessee from other sources" within the ambit of section2(6 A) of Act, therefore, it was not liable to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable to Tax. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: (1) The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain and whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains. Prima facie, receipt of compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of fixed assets of a Company is of a capital nature: Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Assam, ; , followed. (2) The assumption made by the High Court that the whole amount of compensation was deemed to be capital gain cannot therefore be sustained.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain forest produce, challenged the jurisdiction of the court in C.C. Nos. 145 and 148 of 1988. The jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that Sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under Section 2(f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act '. When proceedings were laid under section 51(1)(or contravention thereof, the jurisdiction was of the Court in C .C. No. 1192 of 1992. The forest produce seized by the respondents was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1)( or contravention thereof. As said earlier, the jurisdictional question raised on behalf of the accused was that technical Dictiontries, Botanical Tax Books and expert opinion would bring out a demonstrable distinction between wood oil and sandalwood oil. The wood oil is a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudation from living trees in the forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees whilechin wood oil was a bye product from bamboos (Santalum Album) by industrial process. Wood oil is produced by making a hole on the trunk of the living tree commonly known as "oil trees" or "wood oil trees". This family of trees are variously known in different parts of South India but they relate to Dipteroocarcoae family. Wood Oil was gathered by heating the hole in the trunk to induce exudations of the oleclec resin from the tree and commercially dealt with as wood oil which is a cheap substance in the commercial world used solely for the purpose of painting planks of wood or wooden vessels floating in the sea. The physio chemical properties of wood oil are distinct and different from other oil. Sandalwood as observed by the High Court was forest produce. Even its roots thereof are also included as forest produce and they are timber within the meaning of Section 2 (k) of Kerala Forest Rules, 1961. The purpose of the Act is to conserve forest wealth which is very dear for preservation to maintain ecology. Forest Produce defined under section 2(1) is an inclusive definition. It is settled law that the word 'include ' is generally used as a word of extension. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning Of the words or pharases occuring in the body of the Statute. Craies on Statute Law, Seventh Edition at p. 64 stated the construction to be adopted to the meanings of the words and pharries that 'the cardinal rule for the construction of Acts of Parliament is that they should be construed according to the intention expressed in the Acts themselves. If the words of the statute are themselves precise and unambiguous, then no more can be necessary than to expound those words in their ordinary and natural sense. The words themselves alone do in such a case best declare the intention of the law giver", but rather as declaring what may be comprehended within the term where the circumstances require that it should be so construed. This Court in Babu Manmohan Das Shah & Ors. vs Bishun Das [ ; , followed the ordinary rule of construction stated that "the provisions of a statute must be construed in accordance with the language used therein unless there are compelling reasons such as where the literal construction would reduce the Act to absurdity or prevent manifest legislative purpose from being carried out".

The prosecution alleged that the canal after a temporary closure restarted flowing on May 5, 1953. The accused were tried by the Sessions Judge for an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code but were acquitted. On appeal to the High Court, the order of acquittal was reversed and they were convicted under section302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. Held, that the evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn. The second point on which the judgment of the High court is assailed was the lack of compelling reasons for setting aside the judgment Of acquittal. This Court has held that the High Courts should not set aside an order of conviction unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons" for doing so. In the present ease, however, it cannot be said that the opinions of these authors were given in regard to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before this Court nor was this a satisfactory way of disposing of the evidence of an expert unless, the passages which are sought to discredit his opinion are put to him. This court in Emperor vs The King (A.I.R. , referred to. Held further, that where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused was guilty this Court would set aside the conviction. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Stephen Seneviratne vs The State of Madhya Pradesh ([1954] S.C. 28), relied on.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it had two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and had depots at Patna and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at Dhanbad, the com pany and the said workmen represented by their union that the Indoxco Labour Union was not materially affected by the dispute raised by the union was in respect of the employees of the Company wherever they may be stationed. The Tribunal after observing that the company 's wage scales were satisfactory compared the rates of overtime paid by other industrial concerns in Jamshedpur and awarded 1/4 times the ordinary wages for overtime work exceeding 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours per week. On appeal, the Industrial Tribunal held that the constitution of the said Indox Co Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and Indox co Labour Union does not materially affect the position that the dispute raising by the Union is in respect Of the employees workmen of the appellant 's factory at Ranchi who alone had made the aforesaid demands and disputes arising from those demands only were agreed to be referred and were actually referred to the Tribunal by the said notification. The award was, however, modified by a resolution passed thereat by changing the name of the union to Indian Oxygen Workers Union and making the workmen of all the establishments of the appel lant company in Bihar eligible for its membership. The appellant company challenged the validity of the award on the ground that it had amended its constitution on January 6 1963 and therefore as the workmen 's demands were not referred to them, they could not be asked to pay more than their ordinary rate of wages payable to workmen if they were asked to work beyond 39 hours and not exceeding 54 hours. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the demand for special leave with pay to attend the law courts. But it awarded that the union 's representatives should be given special leave to attend (1) meetings of its executive commit, tee, (2) meetings by the annual convention of the I.N.T.U.C., if held at Jamshedpur; (3) a letter dated January 25, 1964 by the General Secretary of the Golmuri Tinplate Workers ' Union, (4) meetings and the annual conventions of the Indian Company could be attended by the companys delegates by availing themselves of their earned leave. The tribunal also awarded that of the workmen should be paid special leave for attending the meetings of the executive committee of the company. On a reference made to it under section 10(2) of the , the Tribunal held in favour of the Union and allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1 ) Under the conditions of service of the respondent company, the total hours of work per week are 39 hours. Any workman asked to do work beyond these hours would obviously be working overtime and the company in fairness would be expected to pay him compensation for such overtime work. The Bihar Shops & Establishments Act has no relevance to this question as that Act fixes the maximum number of hours of workers allowable thereunder, i. e. 48 hours a week and provides for double the rate of ordinary wages payable for work done over and above 48 hours. It is not, therefore, as if the provisions of that Act govern overtime payment payable by an employer where maximum hours of duty are governed by the conditions prevailing in his establishment.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In 1939 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership to carry on the business in the name of R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Hakam Mal Tani Mal Tiani Mal, the business which was originally carried on by the undivided family. Accounts of this firm were settled till March 31, 1939 and the firm was dissolved. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/s Hakam mal TaniMal was dissolved on March 31., 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1, 1939 was in March 1943 when the assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee 's income from the business was taken over by the assessee. The departmental authorities held that the assessee firm alone was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. On appeal the High Court disagreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Income Tax (Amendment), Act 7 Of 1939 was brought into force on April 1 1939 and was on that count entitled to the benefit of section 25 (4) which was not admissible. HELD : The assessee was constituted to carry On the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1. 1939.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. Among the rival candidates, Prakash Vir Shastri secured 149,943 votes while the appellant secured 1,01875 votes. The Swatantra candidate Sri Naseem secured 34,274 votes. Respondent No. 1 challenged the election on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. At the hearing of the appeal the appellant appeared in person after counsel on his behalf had obtained leave of this Court to withdraw and to allow the appellant to appear in person. The various corrupt practices on which the appellant relied relate to occurrences at six places. The appellant did not press the other occurrence. The first occurrence relates to a meeting held at Hapur on 7 February, 1967. The second occurrence relates only to a meet held at the Town Hall Maidan at Hapur. The news item in the newspaper 'Hindustan ' Exhibit 28 given by the appellant was that a constable was sent to the Town hall Maidenan to make arrangements in connection with the meeting which was to be 'addressed by one Kailash Prakash. The witnesses on behalf of the respondent stated the name of Kailash Prakash and Smt. Kamla Chaudhury as speakers on behalf Of the Congress candidate. It is highly improbable that two meetings of the two rival candidates were held at a place called Nagola. The evidence on behalf, of the appellant is not acceptable for two reasons. First, if there had been any incident of a voter being prevented from voting 'a complaint would have been made to the polling officer of the polling station. Secondly, there was no investigation. The attack on the office of the Republican Party on 7 2 February,1967 at Hapur Town HallMaidan is not proved by the appellants to have been established by respondent Shastri 's workers and supporters. The High Court rightly came to the conclusion that no meeting was held at Ghaziabad on 7th February, and there was an attack on Shri Prakash Vir Gandhi. The other allegations of the appellants were that respondent Prakash Vir Upadhyaya made communal propaganda against the appellant and also published false statements in relation to the personal character of the appel lant. In support of the case with regard to assault on Age Elahi the appellant relies on the oral evidence of PW 11, P.W. 12, P W. 17, P.,W. 19, P,W. 23, P and P.Ws. 25, D.W 10, D,W 11, D and 33. The oral evidence is in support of respondent Prakashvir Shastri but the newspaper report on which appellant relies contains intrinsic evidence which totally nullifies the appellant 's case.

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of a final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh, since deceased, the predecessor in interest of the appellants filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and by another judgment debtor Mst. Abhey Kanwar. All these objections including the applica tion of Ganpat Singh under Order 21 Rule 90 CPC were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was con firmed by the District Judge on January 2, 1979. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale, was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an appli cation under Order XX Rule 95 of the Civil Procedure Code for setting it aside the auction sale. The said application was opposed by the judgment debtors on the ground that as the application was filed more than two years after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . It was held by the learned District Judge that in view of the provision of Explanation I1 of Section 47 which was inserted in the Code by section 20 of the C.P.C., Article 136 prescribing a period of limitation of 12 years for the execution of the decree and not Article 134 would apply. The judgment debtor filed an applica tions under Order XXII Rule 90 Code of C. P.C. for setting the aside the said sale on grounds other than those mentioned in Rules 89, 90 and 91. All that has been ruled by the High Court is that after the amendment of Section 21 of the , an application for delivery of possession can be made within one year from the date on which the sale became absolute as prescribed by Article 180 of that Act, but under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1953 such an applicatio tion can be filed only after the decree is put into execution within the period of limitations as prescribed in Article 136. The period of Limitation prescribed by Articles 136 and 134 are for two different purposes, the former being for the execu tion of a decree for possession in respect of which decree is passed and the latter for an applicationfor delivery of Possession of immovable property which is purchased in the course of execution of decree. The two articles have nothing in common for their operation and it is not readily understandable how the two articles stand in conflict with each other. An application for deliv ery of possession of immovable properties purchased in execu tution cannot, by any stretch of imagination, be construed as an application to invoke the provision Of Article 136, of the Constitution.

The appellant was the candidate of a political party. The first respondent filed an elec tion petition claiming a declaration that he 's election was void on the ground that the appellant had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court negatived all the said corrupt practices except two, viz., (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987, a day prior to the election, pamphlets containing a news item in daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983 and (ii) publication of a wall poster, both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first respondent. The appellant 's appeal before this Court was that both these acts amounted to corrupt practices under Section 123 (4) and were sufficient to 726 void the election. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is clear from the provisions of Sections 123(2), (3) and (4), that election petition has to contain (i)(a) a concise statement of the material facts on which the petitioner relies and also (ii). give full particulars of any corrupt practice that the petitioner alleges. On these facts, the Court of Appeal held: (1) The words were defamatory as reasonable persons knowing the circumstances would understand the words in defamatory sense (ii), it was not necessary for the plaintiff to prove that one or more persons understood the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's Election. [775D] 1.2 In the instant case, the first Respondent has not shown as to how the said two statements or the rest of the contents of exhibit P1 had projected him as the murderer in the eyes of the elec torate. On the other hand, all his witnesses without exception are unanimous that after reading exhibit P 1 the impression it created on them was that it referred to an incident which had taken place on the previ ous day or to an earlier incident and nothing more. The impression that it created in me was that It referred to a incident that took place on that previous day. [764G H] 1:3 In the present case, however, the appellant has not produced any documentary evidence such as the photographs of the posters on the other walls even near the City Rationing Office, nor has he stated that his workers had done it with the knowledge and consent of the election agent. The evidence of this witness is not only consistent to the fact that he had not seen the act of pasting of exhibit PW 1 but also that he did not know who pasted the wall on the walls in other parts of the City. [774A B] 2.1 In the absence of the statement of material facts in the petition as stated above, the Appellant was not called upon to join issue with them in his written statement.

The respondent No. 5 proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No 5 from its erstwhile owner, by aramji Jeejeebhoy Pvt. Ltd., in 1966 sanctioned Development Plan of Greater Bombay, the said land was shown in the residential zone and a contiguous parcel of land was entered as green belt. With a view to developing the disputed land, the respondent Corporation submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of a five Star hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the Respondent No. 1 filed an appeal before the Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act 1966, which was rejected on the ground that the property was proposed for earmark it under reference. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner of Municipal Corporation rejecting the plan submitted by the Respondent NO. 5 after hearing the petitioners as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the Plan on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order granting sanction of the Planning Authority. The appellants filed a writ petition challenging the legality of the order dated 14.3.1974 and Misc. Petition No. 1406 of 1978 challenging the validity of the resolution dated 14th March, 1974 and Misc., Petition No 1406/1978 challenging the order passed by the Government of Maharashtra dated 25.7.1978 exempting the disputed property under section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the view that even the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors, and that even though the proposed Revision could be considered as one one of relevant factors. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the respondent had misunderstood the provisions of section 46. It was submitted by them that the Municipal Corpo ration Authority was entitled to take into consideration other relevant facts including the contemplated revision of plan, apart from those mentioned in section 46, and in support of their contention, the learned Counsel relied on an unreported decision of a Single Judge of the Bombay High Court in Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another vs Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay and Others, Writ Petition No., 2944 of 1932 disposed of on 6.3, 1984.

The appellant union filed two complaints one against M/s Delta Wires Pvt. Ltd., and second against M /s. Delta Spokes Manufacturing Company, two sisters concerns ( 'employers ' for short) under Section 28 read with Items l(a), l(b), 2, 4(a) and 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The Industrial Court framed an issue whether the employers had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of schedule II of that Act. After hearing the parties, the learned Judge answered the issue in negative and dismissed the complaints. The appellant Union filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Court. Both the applications were dismissed in limine. The Union thereupon filed these appeals by special leave. 66 At the hearing of the appeals, it was contended on behalf of the employers that the industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate had resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed and new hands are being recruited. Dismissing the appeals ^ HELD: 1. The true test is that when it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure of industrial activity, the Industrial court in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practices must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employee at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [68H; 69A] 2. When it is alleged that the employers have resorted to closed closure, bona fide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device and pretence.

The appellant company, which was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company, the objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The assessee company purchased shares of Rs. 1.33,930. during the year ending 30th June, 1929, to 30th July, 1939, no purchases were made with the exception of a few shares of Loyal Mills Ltd., taken over from the staff of E.D. Sassoon & Co. Ltd., who retired from service in the year ended 30th September, 1946. The sales were contained in paragraph 3(b) which states that "In relation to the purchases made by the petitioner company as stated above no appreciable sales of shares were made during the period 29th July 1924 to 30st June, 1942, the sales made in the years ending 30rd June, 1930 of the value of Rs 1.29,333 included shares of the values of Rs . 1.30,357,356 were handed over to the creditors in payment of the loan granted by them. From the year to year ended 31st July, 1945, E. D. Sassoons continued to be interested in the said Group of Mills and they were realised by sale only when E.E. Sasast & Co., started relinquishing the managing agencies of the various mills under their agency and the shares held by the assessee company in the Sassoon Group of Mill were handedover to the respective purchasers. In the year 1930, the appellant company made a claim every year being treated as a dealer in investments and properties but this contention was repelled by the Income Tax authorities and upto the assessment year 1939 40 the appellant Company was assessed on the basis of being an investor but it appears that for the assessment years 1940 41, 1941 42 and 1942 43 the Income tax department accepted the plea of the assessee Company and treated it as a 'dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties and assessed it on that basis. For these years and for the year 1943 44, the assessee made its return in that basis but after the return had been filed for the years 1943 44 and 1942 45, the Income. tax department rejected the plea and treated the investment holding it as an investor. The Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the appellant not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was of the company all along in the past was that it was a dealer dealing in investments, securities, and immovable property and assessed the same on that footing. On appeal by the Commissioner of Income tax, the Tribunal held (i) that the assessee 's claim to be a dealer or an investor according as it incurred losses or made profits and (ii) that because of the objects contained in the memorandum and because of its assertion made in past as being a dealer the assessee could not be held to be an investor and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, security etc. could be taxed as business profits. On reference, the High Court held that the appellant was a ' dealer in shares securities and immoveable properties and therefore, the question whether the profits or losses arising therefrom from the sales of share, securities etc. was answered against the assessee. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD: (i). The questions actually framed by this Court on the last occasion are not appropriate and (2) do not reflect the real controversy between the parties. It is therefore expedient in the interest of justice that the questions should be modified as suggested by the appellant assessee company. [52 C D] G. Venkataswami Naidu & Co, vsC.I.T., ; , referred to. (ii).

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On August 22, 1950 he was placed under suspension until further orders. He filed a writ petition in the High Court for transferring them to some other court on the ground that the appellant was attempting through his brother to obtain bribe from the parties and that the order of suspension made by the High court on January 28, 1954, was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the enquiry as held after October 1, 1953, by the Government with effect from October 1. 1953, was without jurisdiction and (ii) the order in question was void as it was in violation of article 31 of the Constitu tion. Held: (i)(a) The High court had no authority under the rules to suspend a judicial officer pending final orders of the Government. But under r. 13 of the Madras Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953 it is the High 'Court of Judicature at Madras that is constituted as the authority which may impose suspension pending enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e) against the Members of the State Judicial Service. The order passed by the appellant on January 29, 1954 was merely one of suspension pending final proceedings by the Govern ment and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution.[421 D] (b) Rule 4 of the Andhra Civil Services Rules could not apply to enquiries which had been validly initiated previously.

The respondent, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, obtained probate of Gannon 's will in the United Kingdom and appointed the respondent as the attorney to administer the estate in British India. The respondent was a registered shareholder of 2675 shares of the company. In the assessment for the assessment years 1946 47 and 1947 48 the Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed and after processing the amount under section 18(5) included it in the total income of Anderson and levied tax thereon at the appropriate rate. The Income tax officer, however, included dividends as deemed to have been distributed under the order dated March 26, 1953. In appeal by the respondent to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bombay, the High Court answered the first question in the negative and declined to answer the second question. With special leave, the Commissioner of Income tax appealed to this Court. The questions that fell for consideration were : (1) whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the dividends deemed as distributed by virtue of section 211 of the Indian Succession Act, in respect of the shares held by a shareholder when before the date on which the fiction of distribution becomes effective viz. the date of the relevant General Meeting of the Company the registered shareholder has died and his representatives have not been substituted in the register of the Companies; (2) whether the Act contains machinery for assessing dividends deemedto have been sold by virtue Of an order under section 23A in respect thereof of the share held by A shareholder when after the date On which the deeming fiction of distributing becomes effective, viz. ,the date of relevant General meeting of theCompany the registered shareholders has died; and (3) whether where the income was notional as under section 22A the legal personality of the deceased must be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such notional income must be deemed to had been received by the legal representatives of the said deceased. Held, that the expression "assessee" in section 2(2) of the , as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a person by whom income tax or any other tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died".

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. After passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to the Government. The appellant contended that his rights had been recognized and guaranteed under the agreements entered into by him with the Govern ment of India. Held, that the appellant was not only an ex Ruler but a maufidar appears to be clear. The ordinary dictionary meaning of maufi is "Released, exempted, exempt from the payment of rent or tax". In view of the provisions of article 363(1) of the Constitution any dispute arising out of the Merger Agreement or the Instrument of accession was beyond the competence of the courts to enquire into. The High Court rightly held that the expression 'maufidar ' in section 2(m) of Act had not been used in any narrow or technical sense. The question whether the villages in Schedule A and B of the petition under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution fell within the category of Estates or Alienated lands but they did fall within the categories of Mahals. Held further, that in view of section 2 (j) of 1947 Act any dispute arose out of a Merger agreement or the instrument of Accession was beyond its competence. The expression 'Maufidars ' was not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler of a State. A mauffidar could be a person who was the holder of land which was exempted from the Payment of rent and tax.

The respondent was working in Shillong since the year 1979. The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Original Application No. 33 of 1991) questioning the order of his transfer. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying at Shillong and further that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago. He further submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer, and that the Tribunal is not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the authority competent to transfer. In this case the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order dated of transfer on the following reasoning: (1) The guidelines issued by the Government are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later; (2) The Administrative Tribunal is also not an appellate Authority sitting In judgment over and the orders passed by the transfer are quashed. [434D E] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 rendered by a Bench of this Court, one of us (J.S. Verma J.) was a member. On a perusal of the judgment, we do not think it supports the respondent in any manner. It is observed therein: "There can be no doubt that ordinarily and as far as practicable the husband and wife who are both employed should be posted at the same station even if their employers be different. The desirability of such a course is obvious. However, this does not mean that their place of posting should invariably be one of their choice, even though their preference may be taken into account while making the decision in accordance with the administrative needs. [534E F] Bank Of India vs Jagir Singh Mehta, [1992 ] 1 S C.C.[635F] Bank OF India vsRaj Jagjit Singh, [92] 1 SCC 306, Bank of Indian India vs Raj Mehta, ; and Bank of india vs Jagjit singh Mehta, , referred to.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A3 armed with sticks, A3, armed with aruval (bill hook) and A6 armed with axes, A1 armed with deadly weapons, A 3 armed with sharp edged weapon, A 1 armed with an iron rod, A 2 armed with iron rods, A 4 armed with bill hooks, A 6 armed with stick and A 7 armed with spear, A6 with a lathi, A 7 and A 6 with sticks. The third charge related ting to riooting wherein the deceased died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [3B] 2. Keeping in view the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case the offence committed by the appellants came within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., and instead convict them under Section 325, IP. C. [4E F] 3.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs,3.00,000, Rs.7,00, Rs,000 and Rs.80,000 advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. The respondent firm owned certain motor vehicles which were mentioned in A and Schedules to the plaint of the said suit. The firm was carrying on its business at Madras as fleet owners and gasolene carriers. It had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, the father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, who were alienees of the mortgaged properties. In the suit the Bank prayed for the sale of the aforesaid properties for the recovery of the amounts claimed by it on account of the loan together with interest due thereon. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statements denying the creation of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos. 2 & 3 in favour of the Bank. The defendants denied the creation or creation of the mortgages alleged to have been mortgaged to the Bank, and contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank was bound by the alienations and transfers made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The suit was decreed and the bank was directed to pay the same to the Firm and its partner. Being dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the Subordinate Judge, the Bank preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour by the bank and accordingly dismissed the suit instituted by the appellant Bank. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Banking Companies Act is quite legal and valid. No other point has been urged by either party in this appeal. In view of the discussion made above, the provisions of the Act are not applicable to the appellant bank and, therefore, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the bank by the respondents. [968G] 1.2 The Banking companies Act is a special Indian law and the provision of section 4(e) of the is applicable to it Bank.

The Central Government promulgated the Sugar Export Promotion Ordinance, 1958, on June 27, 1958. Clause 5 of the Order gave power to the Central Government to fix the price or the maximum price at which any sugar might be andold or delivered, and different prices might be fixed for different areas or different types of sugar. The Central Government was also authorised by that Ordinance to fix quotas for the wholesale sale of sugar produced in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. In exercise of these powers the Central Govern ment promulgated the sugar Export Promotion ordinance, 1958 on June 28, 1958 and the Sugar (Control) Order, 1955, fixing the ex factory prices of sugar manufactured in Punjab. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it did not fix any price at all stages, the Act required that the price must be fixed at an earlier stage or not. Held, that the impugned notification was not an unreasonable restriction on the petitioners ' right to carry on trade under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The impugned notification merely fixes ex factory price and is bad, firstly, on the grounds that the Act and the Order do not authorise the Central Govt. to fix ex factory rates, and secondly, on a ground that even if ex factory Price prices can be fixed it would be an unreasonable restrictions on the right to carrying on trade. The notification was therefore valid. It was not necessary in law for the Government to determine wholesale or retail prices. In fact there were sugar factories in Punjab and North West Bihar and it was these two areas which were called mainly surplus areas. The price of sugar in India depends upon the price of the factories in Uttar Pradesh, Uttar P., and North East Bihar and that there was no reasonable basis for such clasification factories in other parts of India. The Government had ample power to fix wholesale and retail prices also. But if the purpose was served by merely fixing the Ex factory price, it could not be said that any further safeguard was necessary in the form of an appeal or otherwise.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute between the parties to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , and directed that such dispute shall be adjudicated and disposed of by that Tribunal after the commencement of the Amending Act as if that Act had not been passed. The Company preferred Civil Appeal No. 125 of 1958 against the award in so far it went against the employees. For convenience of reference, the parties will be referred to in the course of the judgment as the Company and the Union. The company preferred Civil Appeals Nos. 125/58 and 164/59 against that award to the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Calcutta which with some modification confirmed the award of the Tribunal on August 30, 1951. The Tribunal after making the necessary inquiry made the award on August 26,1957, and it was duly notified in the Calcutta Gazette on September 26, 1957. As a mistake had crept in, the award was modified by the Tribunal by its Order dated August 30. The effect of this amendment was that section 33B inserted in the Act by the Amending act 18 of 1957, was prospective in operation i.e., it would apply only to proceedings initiated in the tribunal constituted under the amended Act and that proceedings pending before the tribunals constituted under that Act before the commencement Of the Amending Acts would be disposed of as if the AmendingAct had not already been passed, and those prevailing at the time of the present reference as to justify making out a new award. The question raised by the Union was whether section 33 B inserted in section 19 by the amending Act was prospective or nugatory. Held: (i) It is implicit in the discretionary reserve power that it cannot be exhaustively defined. It cannot obviously be so construed as to confer a right to a party where he has none under the law. The is intended to be a self contained one and it seeks to achieve social justice on the basis of collective bargaining, conciliation and arbitration. Awards are given on circumstances peculiar to each dispute and the tribunals are, to a large extent free from the restrictions of technical considerations imposed on courts. A free and liberal exercise of the power under article 136 may materially affect the fundamental basis of such decisions, namely quick solution to such disputes to achieve industrial peace. Though article 136 is couched in widest terms it is necessary for this Court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice, causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation, and final decision by this Court or disclosed such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit the consideration of this Court. The limits to the exercise of power under Article 136 cannot be made to depend upon the appellant obtaining the special leave of this court for two reasons viz., (i), at that stage the Court may not be in full possession of all material circumstances to make up its mind and (ii) the order is only an ex parte one made in the absence of the respondent. The same principle should, therefore, be applied in exercising the power of interference with the awards of tribunals irrespective of the fact that the question arises at the date of granting special leave or at thetime the appeal is disposed of. It would be illogical to apply two different standards at two different stages of the same case. The different view was expressed by this court in Pritam Singh vs The State of Madras, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 271 and Pritam Singh v The State Of Punjab, ; , referred to. (ii).

The appellant, who was the Mahant of a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism, filed a suit challenging the scheme. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal by the respondent, the High Court allowed the respondent 's appeal and directed that the writ petition filed by the appellant should be dismissed. Held, that the scheme was framed in 1939, in essential features it was similar to the pattern of schemes which had been subsequently introduced either by legislation or by judicial decisions in respect of the management of public charitable institutions like the present Mutt, the Mutt, and all its endow ments in the hereditary trustee and two non hereditary trustees appointed by the Board. The scheme was not implemented till 1952, but it was open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the scheme on the ground that they contravened his fundamental right under article 19(1)(f) and as such invalid. Held further, that though the scheme might have been valid when it was framed, since the scheme had not been completely implemented till then, it was not open to him to challenge its validity on the grounds that they contravene the Matadhipati 's fundamental rights under article 14 of the Constitution. The result is the appeal must be dismissed with costs. Held also, further, (i) that though a scheme like the instant, is automatically continued by operation of section 103(d), but is liable to be modified if appropriate steps are taken in that behalf under section 62(3). (ii)that the scheme as a whole, will be deemed to have been settled or modified under the provisions of the latter Act and thus continued modifications in it can be effected by adopting the procedure prescribed by section 62 (3).

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. He was not paid the salary for the period of summer vacations during all these years. Although the period during which the appellant continues to serve, the school to date under orders of the Managing Committee yet his appointment after 1986 has not been approved by the educational authorities. The managing committee even passed a resolution on July 6,1987 requesting the educational Authorities of the State of Orissa to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. In response to the notice issued in the Special Leave Petition, the Managing committee through its Secretary cum Head Master has stated that the appellant is still continuing to serve as Hindi tenant in the school under the orders of managing committee yet his appoint after 1986 had not been approval by the Educational Authorities. The appellant filed a writ petition before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teachers with effect on July 8, 1982 and continued till 18.7.1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the Validation Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validation Act does not arise. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appel lant was not entitled to the benefit of the validating Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on 12.71982 and continued until 18. 7.1986with breaks in both between and petitioner ' 's appoint ment was conditioned By the stipulation, that he will continue until replacement by a candidates from the select list. His cases, therefore would not come under the pre review of the Validity Act and therefore,the question of issuance of any direction directing to regularise the appellant 's service in the substantive vacancy since of the Validating Validation Act does no arise.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The respondent challenged the election of the respondent in an election petition inter alia on the ground (1) that he had been disqualified from becoming a member; (2) that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under rules 3 to 7 was in addition to the payment under r. 3 and payment of two sets of aLlowances must necessarily result in profit to 'the payee, and (3) that in view of the issue of this Ordinance, the appellant was allowed to challenge the validity of the Ordinance without amendment of the election petition. The High Court dismissed the election Petition holding that the allowances paid under rules were not convert the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samiti into an office or of profit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1 ) that the grant of travelling allowances and daily allowances under rules 4 to 7 made the office was in lieu of the payment, under r . 3 to the office, and payment under rule 3 was in addi tion to the pay ment under r, and the payment was in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have incurred for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. HELD: (i) The daily allowance is invariably fixed after estimating what extra expenditure in a day the person concerned would have to incur. A Chairman, it appears, was expected to incur more expenditure per day than a Member and that seems to be the reason why a higher rate of daily allowance was prescribed for him. [427 B] (ii) The appellant had failed to establish that the allowance payable under rules 2 to 7 of the Rules result in any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti, and consequently there was no question of any disqualification arising. [445 C] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 654 at p. 656, followed.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut Cantt. ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later they filed a suit for eviction on a number of grounds including the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The disputed constructions include a partition wall in hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH had been constructed by the appellant with the consent o flied by the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed marked with letters C DGH had not been constructed. The trial court held that the partition wall constituted 'material alteration ' and that the tin sheds marked by letters BGHH had also been constructed without the consent by the appel lant, which materially altered the accommodation and on that findings the trial Court decreed the suit. On second appeal made by the respond ents a learned Single Judge of the High Court set aside the order of the first appellate court on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act 10 of 1952. On a second appeal by the respondent, a learned single Judge of tho High Court held that since two sides of the tin roof were resting on the pucca wall it constituted a material alteration in the accommodation. The High Court also took into consideration the Commissioner 's report filed before the Lower Court and on perusal of the same found that the wail which had been built for the tin shop was kuchha, made of bricks and mud and the bamboo tatters were used for enclosing it. The findings recorded by the trial court and the relevant evidence placed before the parties clearly show that the stantial wall did not actual ly partition the hall converting the property permanently into two rooms. The partition wall was made without digging any foundation of the floor nor it touched the ceiling, instead; it was a temporary wall of 6 feet height converted the big hall into two parts for its convenient use, it could be removed at any time without causing any damage to the building. The appellant ' tenant was liable for eviction. There is no dispute that the demised premises is sub ject to the provisions of the Act. Section 14 of the provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, the landlord has right to file suit for evic tion of a tenant without obtaining permission of the District Magistrate but if the tenant, without the landlords permission made or permitted to make construction which materially alter the accommodation, without permission of tho landlord, the embargo placed on the landlord 's right to filing suit is lifted and he is free to file a suit. The Act does not permit a landlord to file suits for eviction of a tenants without obtaining sanction of the district Magistrate but only if he has made constructions which materially altering or which is likely to diminish its value substantial ly, the land is free from filing suit for tenant 's ejectment without obtaining requisite permission of tile District Magistrate.

The appellant company filed a suit for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Additional District Judge held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of the exparte decree. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Service on managing agents who are a corporation is valid under clause (a). The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summons on natural persons. Sending a summons by post to the registered office of the company, unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on the Company itself. But the first part of clause(b) had got to he understood with reference to the other provisions of Order 5 Rule 17 of the C.P.C. [1031E] 2. The meaning in clause (c) has get to be interpreted in the context of the provision contained in Order5 Rule 17 C. In other words, if the serving peon or bailiff is not able to serve the summons on the Secretary or any Director or any other Principal Officer of the Corporation because either he refuses to sign the summons or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the Company and make a report to that effect. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous Case that the service of the summons as effected in accordance with the first sub part of Clause (b), of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the code. Annexure A to the counter affidavit filed by the respondent is the petition filed by it under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Civil Procedure Code.

The Magistrate passed an order on the 29th July, 1976 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for fresh enquiry. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the final order of Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of peace existed at the time the order was passed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of High Court is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [952B] 2.1 In the instant case, there was an omission on the part of the magistrate to mention in his final order that there was a breach of the peace. Therefore, the Magistrate passed the final orders in favour of the appellants. The Magistrate passed final order in favour thereof. The respondents moved their written statements, they did not state that no dispute existed but whereas one party said that there were no apprehension of breach from their side, the other side took the stand that there is an apprehension of violation of peace. [962C D] 2:2 In the preliminary order there was clear finding by the Magistrate that there Was a breach on the parties. Therefore the final Order was bad and the High court rightly allowed the Petition and remitted it to the magistrate for fresh inquiry.

The appellant, a public company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Agents are the firm of Messrs K. R. Thyagaraja Chettiar and Co., whose partners are Mr. Thoyagarajam Chettiar and his two sons. The company is resident and ordinarily resident in British India its head office being at Madurai in Madras State. It carries on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, and for the purpose of that business it purchases cotton and occasionally sells it. Its profits arise for the most part from the sale of the yarn and to some extent from the re sale of cotton. According to the account books of the company, its profits from business for the account year 1941 42 were Rs. 9,25,364, for 1942 43 Rs. 24,09832 and for 1943 44 Rs. 29,1388 1. In its returns, the appellant showed these amounts as its income chargeable to tax for the respective years. The Department did not accept the correctness of the figures as shown in the accounts. It contended that the company had earned more profits than were disclosed in its accounts and that it had contrived to suppress them by resort to certain devices. According, the Department, the scheme evolved by the appellant for this purpose was that the Suppose the Company sold 25 bales of yarn to X for Rs. 50,000 at the then market rate and received the full amount of the price. The books of account showed neither the sale to X nor its receipt of Rs. 5,000 to him. The sales were fictitious and the appellant had the right under section 66(1) to have the decision of the court on its correctness, and support for this position was sought from certain observations in Edwards (Inspector of Taxes) vs Bairstow ([1942] , Bomford vs Osborne ([1891] 1 K.B. 904), Bomford v Osbornee ([1901] 2 K. Bater ([1939] 4 A.E.R. , referred to. Held, further that the finding on the issue must be an inference to be drawn from facts found on the application of the proper principles of law and it will be correct to say in such cases that an inference from facts is a question of law. The proposition that an inferential finding from facts can be challenged under section 64(1)(c) as erroneous in law only if it is not supported by any evidence or if it was perverse, but that where there is evidence to consider, the decision is final even though the court might not, on the materials, have come to the same conclusion if it had the power to substitute its own judgment. In the present case, the finding of the Tribunal that the intermediaries were benamidars for the appellant could not stand. The question as framed by the Department was a pure question of fact and was open to review by the courts. It was not necessary for the department to bring into its profit and loss account a certain amount which it had earned as commission, and the point for decision was one of pure fact or mixed question of facts and law.

The appellant carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assesse, the entire amount of Rs 75,467 paid to General Manager Shri J.P. Vaish was an amount laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. [510 D] (ii) The question referred by the Tribunal and answered by the High court only deals with the claim of deduction of the amount paid to a employee of the assessee under section 10(2)(Xv). [516 C] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., Bombay, ; Swadeshy Cotton Mills Company Co. Pvt. Ltd., vs C .I. T. Bombay vs Walchand & Co. Private Ltd., , referred to. (iii) The test of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and solely laid out for the purpose of business, reasonableness of the expenditure has to be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not (iv) In the present ease, both the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Tribunal rejected the view of Shri Vaish that the rates of commission were reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amounts claimed by the assssee.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. The appellant filed his application to the Patna High Court on March 13, 1957, praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957 by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union. The High Court dismissed this application summarily. Held, that the appellant was entitled to a representation in spite of the fact that the Union which had espoused his cause was being repre sented by its Secretary, Fateh Singh himself had made the complaint against him which resulted in the order of dismissal. The terms of the compromise of the dispute regarding the appellant 's dismissal were that he would not get reemployment but by way of "humanitarian considerations the company agreed without prejudice to pay an ex gratia amount of Rs. 1,000/ (Rupees one thousand) only to him. There was no material on the record to justify a conclusion that this compromise was not entered in what was considered to be the best interests of the workman himself In assessing the requirements of this principle it is necessary and proper to take note also of the facts that when an individual workman becomes a party to a dispute under the Industrial Disputes Act he is a party, not independently of the union which has espoused its cause. The Union or those (1)[1954] S.C.R. 956, followed.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents on the allegation that defendant No. 1 was the tenant inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No 2. The suit was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent. On appeal by defendant No, 2, the District judge set aside the decree for ejectment against defendant No., 2 and confirmed the rest of the decree against defendant Nos. 1 and 2. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the deceased belonged to a joint Hindu family and other members of the family were already on the record and that it was not necessary to bring on record any other person. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the legal representatives could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in view of the provisions of 0. XLI, r. 4 of O. XLI of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held: (i) It is immaterial that the modification which the court will do is one to which exception can or cannot be taken. No question of the Provisions of r. 3 of O., XXII and those of r . 4 of 0, O.XXII of the C.P.C. They operate at different stages and provide for (1) [1962] 2 S.C R. 636, (ii) that the appellate Court cannot, in any way modify that decree directly or indirectly. The reason is plain. It is that in the absence of the legal representative of the deceased respondent, the appellate court cannot determine anything between the appellant and the legal heirs which may affect the rights of the representatives under the decree. It can also take advantage of this provision, but he may not. Once an appeal has been filed by all the plaintiffs the provisions Of 0. XLII, r . 33 are not applicable to it. State of Punjab vs Nathu Ram (I.L.R. [1953] All Pat. 870, Brij Bhushan Singh vs Babu Satdeo Jha (I L.R.[1954) All. Pat. 8, State of Madras vs Nathuram (A.I.R., 1959 Orissa 148 and State of Bombay vs Nathu Lal ([1962] Supp. 2 S C. R. 634), referred to.

The appellant tenant was the tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument had arisen). At the time of the lease the appellant had not been extended to Delhi although later, later on, on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord filed a petition for eviction under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections. There was no dispute that neither notice to terminate the tenancy under section106 of the Act nor notice to forfeiture of the tenancy had been issued, nor notice or notice of termination of the contractual tenancy under Section 106 was needed and further that the forfeiture of tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(g) because the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not, in terms apply to the present lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience. The Rent Controller ordered eviction and the Appellate Tribunal affirmed it. In appeal to this Court, on the question: whether the provisions of the PG NO 908 PG NO 930 PG NO 906 PG NO 907 PG NO 956 PG NO 993 PG NO 933 PG NO 549 PG NO 545 PG NO 548 PG NO 547 PG NO 543 PG NO 546 PG NO 544 PG NO 541 PG NO 483 PG NO of the Rent Act applied to the lease of 1952 executed in Delhi and, secondly, whether it was merely a procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and was not based on any principle of justice. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The requirement as to written notice provided in the Section is intrinsic evidence of the fact that the formality is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. [910G] 1.2 In the instant case, no notice whatsoever was sent to the tenant for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stood determined either by efflux of time limited thereby in terms of section 111 (g) or outside it, the thrust of the holding is found in these concluding words: "However, as held by the Supreme Court in Narender, Lokmanya Lodhi vs Narmada Bai & Ors. [1962] Supp. 2 SCR 930, the requirement of the notice in writing could not be said to be based on a general rule of justice or canon of commonsense. [936C D] 1:3 The requirement of a written notice in the instant ease is not a rule of law but a technical rule and it canon be inferred that every provision in the and every amendment effected is necessarily based on principles of equity, equity, justice and good justice. [946E F] 2.1 In the present case, the appellant tenant fell back on certain grounds grounded on sections 106 and 111(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. The respondent landlord sought to sustain his case on the basis of section III(g), and the provisions thereof. The Tribunal held that no notices were necessary since the lease was created prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the P. Act.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that the Governor had already formed an opinion that the penalty of dismissal from service should be awarded to him. The Governor made these two orders in terms of article 311(2) as it existed before its amendment by the Fortyteenth Amendment Act, 1963 which came into force on October 6, 1963. The amended Article 311(1)(c) provided that where a person was dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; or (b) where an authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for some reason, to be recorded by that authority in writing it is not reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry. The appellants who joined service in the Secretariat of the Assam Government on 1st November, 1946 in the post of Lower Division Assistant filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of these orders and also the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions and dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the expression "reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken" included an opportunity to show cause against his dismissal from which would be an opportunity for showing cause, and that the satisfaction of the Governor under sub clause (c) of the proviso had the effect of depriving a government servant of a very valuable right ofhaving an opportunityto prove his innocence as well as opportunity to make a representation against the penalty proposed to he imposed on him. HELD: The order of dismissal passed against the appellants was not in violation of article 31(2). [488 F] (a) It is not necessary that consultation with the Public Service Commission in such cases cannot, therefore, be held to vitiate the orders impugned. [488 G] (b)(c)(d) In all cases, other than those mentioned in the principal clause or in rule 9, consultation with Public Service Commis sion is made mandatory. The regulations as indicated above, do not dispense with this requirement of article 320(3)(c). [490 A B] (2) It was not obligatory and that this Article did not confer any rights on a public servant so that the absence of consultation or any irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law. [490 G] The satisfaction recorded by the Governor, therefore related to the third step to be adopted under clause (2). The satisfaction of Governor was recorded in the language in which the provision in article 311 stood prior to its amendment and which was as follows: "It is not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and without giving him a reasonable opportunity of making a representation on the penalty proposal proposed, but only on the basis of the evidence adduced during such inquiry". [490 C] (3) The satisfaction under sub cl.(c) is recorded on two points.
