The assessee company disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10,200 but claimed set off of capital loss of Rs,3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. As no further appeal was carried by the assessee with the first appellate order, the matter had become final. The assessee challenged the rejection of its claim of set off before the Appellate Tribunal and he dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim of loss was not admissible. On a reference under section 256(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the High Court held that the Income tax Officer had rightly disallowed the assessee"s claim of revenue loss by holding (i) that it is a capital loss; (ii) that in view of the provisions of Section 80 of the 1961 Act, the loss claimed for the assessment period 1957 58 could be set off against the income determined for the assess ment year 195758 and ultimately allowed the assessee "s claim. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that (i ) the benefit conferred under Section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 act and notwithstanding the wordings of Section80 of the latter Act, and (ii ) that the benefit confer ed under Section24 of 1922 Acts continued to he given effect from under the 1922 Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court reached the correct conclusion and there was nothing merit in the appeal. [1165B] 1.2 In the order for assessment year 1965 66 to which the Act of 1961 applied, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed: "Section 74(1)(a) Where in respect of any assessment year, the net result of the compu tation under the head "capital gains" is a loss such loss shall. subject to the other provisions of this Chapter.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. Their 22 services were inter changeable and inter transferable be tween the three units, and all the service conditions of the persons working in the three Units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. In the year 1979, the Defence Research Service was trifurcated and reconstituted as Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) was reconstituted as defence Research and development Serv ice (DRDS). The appellant who was working in DTD &P became a member of DAQAS. When the trif ulcation was made, the service rules governing the three branches had a common Rule which was rat ing Rule 12 in DAQS and DQAS, and Rule 13 in Dr.D.D., and Rule 14 in DrDS which provided that other conditions of service were to be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. At the time the present controversy arose, and the respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, he was holding the post of Deputy Chief Scientific Officer. By an Office Memorandum dated 7(3)/85 D(R & D) of the Government, Ministry of Defence, Department of Defence Research & Development dated 24.12.1985, the decision of the President was conveyed whereby Scientific and Technical personnel (gazetted) of D.R. and D.S. in the grade of Scientist 'E ' and above, would retire at the age of 60 years provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the preced ing five years. The Tribunal held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the said age of 58 years his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24th December, 1985 read with Rule 12 quoted above, and held that respondent was not entitled to remain in service upto the superannu ture age of sixty years. It was further held that since the condition of service was not expressly provided for in the Service Rules, the denial of the benefit of the enhanced superannuation age to the members of one 24 unit while the same was granted to the Members of DA QAS, was also available to the member of the other unit amounts to discrimination, violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. In appeal by the Union of India, it was contended that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of serv ice for the members belonging to the different units, but merely because the superannuation age of the members was increased, it could not be held that he belonged to another unit viz. DAQ. QAS and D, and that the government had power to vary the service condition of the employees from time to time. The question involved in the appeal is, however, not whether the Government has such power. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The decision of Tribunal is both proper and valid. There is no substance in the present appeal.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The first of these were to the effect that the appellant had published all the phmphlets mentioned in the petition and distributed the same amongst the voters and the appellant 's cause of action bad arisen on that date. On appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) Under section 21(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 which does not contain a similar provision it has been held by this Court that "although. the trial court should be at arms length and the court should not really enter into the dispute as a third party, but it is not to be understood that the Court never had the power to summon a witness or to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter, particularly of corrupt practice which is alleged and is being sought to be proved. [975 H] (ii) The High Court had jurisdiction to call these two persons as witnesses under the provisions of the Act. [973 A B] R. M. Seshadri vs G. Vasanta Pai ; , followed. R.M. Seshadri v G. Basanta Pai, ; , referred to. (iii) In the instant case, if the two persons had not been examined, the Judge might well have decided the issue the other way. But the Act certainly gave him the power of doing so and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the Judge although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summonses to them in the first instance when asked to do so on the 21st August was hardly justifiable.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State Government imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of this notification by a petition under article 32 of the Constitution contending that notwithstanding the Validation Act, the notification in question continued to be void and inoperative because it had not been validated and because the Act itself was ultra vires. Held, that the impugned notification was intra vires the powers of the State Legislature under entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The power conferred on Parliament by article 286(2) is a legislative power and such a power conferred upon a Sovereign legislature carries with it authority to enact a law either prospectively or retrospectively unless there can be found in the Constitution itself a limitation on that power. The State Legislature derives its authority to legislate with respect to tax on the sales of goods under entry 52 in List I in Schedule VII to the constitution, comprehended the power to impose income tax with retrospective operation even for a period prior to the coming into force of the Act. The position will be the same as regards laws imposing tax on sale of goods. In the present case, the sales sought to be taxed took place between April 1, 1956 and July 31, 1957 whereas the Validation Acts by force of which the tax became payable came into force in 1958. It was therefore not a tax on that occasion of sale. Further a sales tax is an indirect tax which can be passed on by the seller to the purchaser. The Sales Tax Acts passed by the legislatures of several States provide for the seller collecting the tax from the purchaser as a tax from purchasers. The words "in the form in which they were in force immediately before the commencement of this Act" qualify the word "section" and not the word 'section 's sections". That is the view expressed by a Bench of the Allahabad High Court in Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officer, ; , followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to four years R.I. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A Philanderer of 22, appellant overpowered by sex stress in excess, hoisted himself into his cousin 's house next door, and in broad day light, overpowered the temptingly lonely prosecutrix of twenty four, rape her in hurried heat and made an urgent exist having fulfilled his erotic sortie. The screaming victim complained to her mother working in the field; thereafter a first information, prosecution and conviction ensued, a sentence of 4 years R .I. was imposed by the Sessions Court and the High Court upheld it in appeals. [592 C D] 2. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychicaling, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [593 E] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted.

The respondent company, which was a limited company dealing in land, maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Act, certain plots of land measuring about 19 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee, were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952 published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the respondent assessee. The assessee was not satisfied with the amount of compensation and preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator 24 Parganas, Calcutta. The Arbitrator made an award on July 29, 1955 whereby he fixed the amount at Rs.30,10,873 on account of the permanent acquisition of the land, thus enhancing the original amount of compensa tion by Rs.513,624 on which he directed interest at 5 per cent per annum from January 8 1953, the date of acquisition to the date when the payment was till the date the date for the payment. The State Government then appealed to the High Court and during the pendency of the appeal on April 25, 1956 it deposited Rs.736,691 which the assessee was permitted to withdraw on May 9, 1956 on furnishing security. On receipt of the amount credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956 the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum Rs. 7,24,914 in the assessee 's business income. This represented the difference between the sum of RS.737,190 payable to assessee in terms of the award dated July 29. 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum which had already been assessed to tax. The Income Tax officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesseee on the date Of the award. The assessment was confirmed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax on first appeal. In second appeal by the assessee before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, two contentions were raised by it. It was urged that the amount received by the respondent related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of business carried on by the assesee, and therefore, was a trading receipts of the business carried out by the assesses, and consequently a receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax, and that the sum did not accrue to the appellant as its income during the relevant previous year ended in March 31. 1956. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the other contention and held that the compensation received by it related to acquisition of Land which was stock intrade of the asses sees, and was therefore a trading Receipt of the Business carried on for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment 1957 57. It allowed the appeal accordingly by its order dated February 22, 1964. At the instance of the Revenue the Appellate Tribunal referred the question of law set out earlier to the Calcutta High Court for its opinion and by its judgment dated January 9, 1973 answered the question in favour of the assesses and against the Revenue. The question raised in this appeal is limited to the point whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Revenue can claim that the sums of Rs.,7,24 paid to the assesses as compensation can be said to have accrued to it as income during that previous year ending March 31st, 1956 relevant to the assessment years 1956 57. The High Court answered the questions in favour favour of assessee and against it by the Revenue, and against its Revenue.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants ' eviction was sought on the basis of the compromise decree. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Third Additional District Judge Gwalior. They preferred a second miscellaneous appeal before the Madhya Pradesh High Court. A single Judge following the decision of that Court in Smt. Chandan Bai vs Surja, , came to the conclusion that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. Hence this appeal by the tenant judgment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law is reviewed exhaustively by this Court in K. K. Chari vs R. M. Seshadri, ; [882A] 2. In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act, the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions of the Act. When the suit is contested the issue goes to trial. The Court passes a decree for eviction only if it is satisfied on evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance 982 with the requirement of the statute has been established. Even when the trial proceeds ex parte, this is so. If, however, parties choose to enter into a compromise due to any reason such as to avoid the risk of protracted litigation expenses, it is open to them to do so. [883B C] 3. The object of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act is to protect the tenant from eviction merely by agreement without anything more. The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree, for eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decrees under the law. [888C] 4. In the instant case, on the facts and in the circumstance of this case, the compromise was clearly valid and executable. [869E] 5. The order so recorded in the compromise petition was in full compliance with the requirements of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [879G] 6. In view of the fact that there is no express provision in the Bombay Rent Act prohibiting contracting out, such a prohibition would have to be read by implication consistently with the public policy underlying this welfare measure" was approved. [90F G] 7. The expression "there is nothing in Section 12 of the Rent Act or any other provision which prevents the tenant in vacating the accommodation in spite of the facts that none of the grounds mentioned in Section 3 exists. Similarly, there is nothing to prevent the tenant In agreeing to vacate the accommodation" in future. [919E F] 8. The provisions of Order23, Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code cannot apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [89882G] 9. In K.K.

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 46,668/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs, 91,116/ . The Income tax Officer however, again invoked the provisions of section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ 4/ per rupee on the distributable surplus of Rs 60,761/ . In appeal the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he, therefore, cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23 A(1). The High Court answered that question in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court by certificate, HELD : (i) The assessee had suffered a capital gain of Rs 12,00,000/ as a result of the depreciation of the value of the shares of Elphinstone Mills Ltd. The loss was not taken into consideration in the application of section 22A( 1). [85 C] Commissioner of Income tax West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., ; , followed. (ii) Section 23A (1) is not applicable to a case where the Directors unjustifiably refrain from declaring dividend. If the Directors of a company had reasonable grounds for not declaring any dividend, it was open for the Income Tax Officer to constitute himself as a super Director. [86 E F] Commissioner Of Income tax, West Bengal, vs Gangadhardas, , followed and applied.

The appellant filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh. The Civil Judge allowed the objection and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the award. On appeal by special leave: Held, that section 37 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, is inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of the Act to the proceedings under the Act. It is not necessary to rely (1) I.L.R. [1959] 1 All. 66 on ff. 63 and 64 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holding Rules, 1954 but it is not essential to rely on section 12(6) of the . The effect of section 37 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1), of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the consolidation proceedings under Act. Attar Singh vs The State of U. P., [1959]. Supp. 1 All E. R. 66, followed. Atttarar Singh 's case was concerned with the validity of the , Act, and ground No. 2 which was urged before the Court was that section 36 of the is applicable to arbitrations referred to in section 37 Of the Act, because, apart from the question of appointment of the arbitrator, in all other respects the matter referred to, i.e., the question whether section 39 applies to arbitrations as well as to arbitration proceedings under section 12 (4) of U . Further, the effect of s. 46 and section 47 is that the entire provisions of U,.P. consolidation of Holdings Rules, 1953, apply to arbitration proceeding under the Consolidation of holdings Act.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, it was decided by the corporation that the Corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner who was senior to respondent NO. 2 would have been promoted to the post on that date. However, since respondent No.2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to that post on the date. It is this promotion which was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence, the petitioner has filed this petition for special leave against the judgment of the Bombay High Court dismissing the said petition. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. For the purpose of promotion, a valid classification can made among the members holding the same post on their qualification. In State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , relied upon. 2.1 The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [718C D] 2.2 In the absence, of rule, or regulation, the authority cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this has been made without noticing the decision in State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao, ; , referred to Roshan Lal Tandon vs Union of India, ; and distinguished it on the facts by pointing out that it was a case of the direct recruits and promotees integrated into one cadre. Once they were integrated they lost their birth marks, viz., the different sources from which they were recruited. [Emphasis supplied].

The petitioners in the writ petition are an advocate practising in this Court. The relief asked for is one for mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the several High Courts of the country and ancil lary orders of directions in regard to the same. The first petition is by an Advocate practising in the Court; the second by the Supreme court Advocates on Record Association and the last by the Honorary Secretary of the Bombay Bar Association. These applications are in the nature of public interest litiga tion. The reliefs asked for are one for a mandamus to Union of india to fill the vacancies in the Bombay High Court, and the various High Courts in the States are covered by Chapter 4 of Part VI of the Con stitution. Article 124(1) of the Constitution provides that every High Court shall consist of a Chief Justice and such other Judges as the President may from time to time deem it necessary to appoint. The petitioners in their writ petition have also filed applications under Arti cle 32 of the Constitu tion. They are praying for a direction to the State of India, to fillup the vacancies by filling up of vacancies in various High Court Courts of Delhi and an advocate Association. The main grievance of the petitioners is that while the process of filling up vacancies was considerably slow prior to the general election held in November, 1989 there has been an improve ment in the process from January, 1990; that as against the sanctioned strength of 462,368 had been filled up and the vacancies were 94 in all; by 16.8.1980, the sanctioned up strength had gone up to 470 and as against these appointments had been made. The total posts to be filled up were 30 in number 19 being permanent and 11 additional vacancies. The Union of lndia took the stand through the Attorney General that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up Of the vacancies was not a justiciable matter; that the filing of the writ petitions and proceedings of the Court have helped the Union Government to fill upto a considerable extent by making the various constitutional authorities con stitutional of the urgency of problem and of their responses. The Attorney General withdrew the objection regarding this Court 's jurisdiction and made a statement that he was of the view that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union India to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of public Interest and the writ Petitions requiring a direction for the Union o India to filling up the vacancy were maintainable. The Court accepted the stand taken by the AttorneyGeneral and made an observation that it would be the constitutional duty of the State to maintain the sanctioned cadre in the Superior Courts and the failure, if anyone, was aggrieved, should not be over burdened with pressure of work which he finds it physically difficult to undertake. This necessarily suggests that the Judge strength should be adequate to the current requirement and must remain under constant review in order that commensurate Judge strength may be provided. Within a few years of functioning under the aegis of the constitution our people started realising that there was backlog in courts and that the same was on rapid and constant increase; that by now some more appointments have been made and the number of unfilled posts has been reduced to around 22. As a result of monitoring by the Court by interim directions in these petitions, the position has somewhat erased but 22 vacancies still remain to be filling up.

The respondent C. Bernard while serving as a Relieving Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch of the Bank availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. Shri Manju Travels of Bangalore and claimed reimbursement for the same. The said bill was passed by the Bank on May 15, 1978 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/S. Shri Manu Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a Memo dated August 1,1978 by the Divisional office of the bank calling for his expla nation. A letter was also addressed on the same day to M/ s. Manju Travel 's Bangalore requesting them to furnish the details of the persons who traveled and the amounts received by the said firm. No reply was received from the said Firm but the respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found to be satisfactory. Some correspondence ensued between the respondent and the appellant in this connection but finally the respondent 's departmental appeal was also dis missed on June 17, 1980. The respondent did not raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the aforesaid Shri U.B. Menon at any time during the pendency and till the disposal of the departmental appeal preferred by him. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition, quashed the order of punishment and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the said order of the Single Judge. The Division Bench dismissed it by a single line order: "no ground for interfer ence is made out". It was contended on behalf of the appel lant that since the initial appoint ment of Shri UB. Hegde was valid, his actions and decisions could not be invalidated by his subsequent retirement. According to him he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer de facto and hence his actions were saved. The High Court ought not to have permitted the respondent to question the competence or jurisdiction of Shri H.B., Menon to act as an Enquiry Officer as well as a Disciplinary Authority after his superannuation since he had participated in the enquiry throughout without a demur. According ly, by conduct the respondent had been estopped from raising such a contention for the first time in a writ petition more so because he had submitted to the jurisdiction of Mr. U. B. Menon and there was no prejudice caused on him on that account. Lastly, he submitted that even otherwise the appellant could have appointed a non official as an enquiry Officer and therefore his decision could be saved on the de facto doctrine. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The respondent will be paid 50% of the consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned order was bad in law.

The respondents are owners and are in possession of the building bearing municipal door Nos. 3766 to 3776 situated in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. As the building was an old construction and required urgent and extensive repairs, on October 16, 1965, the respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well as alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial". A controversy arose between the appellant and the respondents regarding the construction of the new road. The appellant contended that the order refusing sanction was legal and was justified by the provisions of cl. (a) of sub section 2 of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. The respondents further averred that the Master Plan prepared under the Delhi Development Act, 1957, did not conform to bye laws or the provisions Of section 336(2) or any other provision of the corporation Act or of any other law. The High Court accepted the writ petition filed by the respondents and issued a mandamus directing the appellant to accord sanction for the execution of the work in respect of the said property as per their application of October 16. 1965. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Master Plan is prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act,1957 (Act LXVI of 1957). Under section 336 (2)(a) the Commissioner is entitled to refuse sanction for erection of any building on either side of a new street under the circumstances mentioned therein. [172 E] (2) The word "ROW" used in the order refers to "right of way" which is with reference to the road proposed under the Master plan. The Master plan has been prepared under s.7 of the Act and it has come into operation, under section 11, in the area concerned. [173 E F] (3) Under section 334(2)(b), the Commissioner has to give sanction for construction of any buildings on either sides of a building or in that zone otherwise than in conformity with such plan. Section 336 gives power to the Commissioner to refuse to sanction for any erection of a structure on either of a road under the circumstance mentioned therein, except with the previous sanction of the Commissioner. [174 G] (4) The provisions of section 7 clearly indicate and that is borne out by the various matters mentioned in the Master plans that the master Plan has been preparing up to now.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The period of lease expired on 30th October, 1951 but there was an option reserved to the lessee to have a renewal of the lease for a further period of 15 years from the date of such expiration. There were disputes between the syndicate on the one hand and the Panna Durbar on the other and by his order dated 31st October, 1946, the Political Minister of Panna stopped the mining operations of the sy Syndicate. The appellant No 1 was asked to come in February, 1949, for being sent to Sir Chinubhai at Bombay, but he did not do so. On this date the appellant 's request was turned down and on the 13th January, 1949. The Secretary to Government of India, Ministry of Works, Mines and Power, Government of Rajasthan, issued a notice to the appellant that he should be given an extension for 10 years from 1st April, 1949 to 30th September, 1951, so that the period of the leases would expire on 30rd October, 1952, but there were disputes with regard to the resumption of the mining operation etc. The appellants were charged under sections 120 B, 161 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code and the appellants pleaded not guilty. The Special Judge acquitted both of them. On appeal by the State, the Judicial Commissioner reversed the order of acquittal passed by the Special judge and convicted both the appellants of the several offences with which they were charged. The High Court held that the appeal to the Judicial Com missioner from the acquittal by the special judge was competent and that there was no infringement of the fundamental rights of the appellants under articles 14 and 20 of the Constitution. Held, that the appellant had failed to establish his guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It was not necessary for him to prove that the offence charged was committed by him No. I but for the fact that the notice authorities provided the sum of Rs. 25,000 on their own and was utterly confused when explanation was sought from him by the police authorities in regard to their tallying of the numbers of these Government currency notes, it was not easy to surmise that they were suffering from any lapse of memory. The statements made by the appellant to them being admissible in evidence there was nothing remained so far as the witnesses Nagindas and Pannalal on the One hand and a ostensibly independent witness in the person of Shanti Lal Ahuja, the Additional District Magistrate, were concerned which could bring the guilt home to the appellants No.1 who occupied the position of Minister of industries in the State. They also provided a handy and an ostensibly independent witnesses in the persons of Shanti Lai Ahuja,the Additional District Magis trate, took in this affair. The police authorities thus came to their aid would not have been able to bring the whole Affair to its culmination. Not only did the police officers thus become active parties in the matter of trapping the appellants with the result that the appellants could not be allowed to take advantage of the provisions of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code, they also provided for a handmunity to them when they came to Delhi empty handed. The Police authorities therefore provided the sums of Rs 25,00,000 to the Nagind as were found by the witnesses and given to NagindAS on payment of the said sum of money.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the respondent along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. On appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the other accused constable Kahan singh who was also con victed with the plaintiff, had also filed a separate suit against his dismissal from service, which was decreed with an observation that it was open to the competent authorities to pass fresh order of punishment in accordance with law. The trial court dismissed the respondent 's appeal on 20.4.1976. This order of dismiss al was challenged as illegal in the present suit which was instituted on 6.11.1982. Besides taking several technical objections, the suit was defended on merits, as well as on the ground of limita tion. From the judgment of the trial court it appears that only two questions were pressed by the parties, namely, whether the suit is barred by limitation and whether the order of dismissal was illegal on the grounds that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. Both the issues were decided by the learned 824 Subordinate Judge against the plaintiff and the suit dismissed. The respondent appealed against the decision. It appears that before the Additional District Judge who heard the appeal, held that the impugned orders of dismissal were void on the basis of arbitrariness and, there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. It was further observed that this decision would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment, provided such a punishment has been awarded to the other police officials tried and con viced along with him. The authority was also permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because of his being in jail. The defendant appellants filed a regular second appeal before the High Court against the decree of the first appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage by merely saving the appeal stage itself, by merely maintaining that the order assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The High Court should call for the records and decide the case finally at the motion stage itself as the case is an old one. In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High court shall permit the plaintiff to file relevant rebutting evidence.

The appellant company, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In fact the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The assessment year in question is 1959 60 in the relevant previous year which ended on June 30, 1958, the assessee for the first time in its history entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of corn sacks and B Twill for Rs. 11,48,399. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its Income 's income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; , State of Andhra pradesh vs Kolla Sreeramurthy, (1890) I.T.R. 1, D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, ; D.M. Wadhwani vs Commissioner Of Income tax; , and D. R. M Wadhwana 's case, and Manalal M. Verma & Co. (P) Ltd. vs Commissioner for Income tax [1961] 2 S.C.R., referred to. In reaching this conclusion the Income Tax officer held: (i) that the transaction was not speculative; (ii) that if any transfer of the P.D.Os. is not followed up by actual delivery of the goods to the transferee, that transaction is to be considered as speculative; and (iii) that there being two separate transactions of sale, one between the mills and the original purchasers, and the other between the original purchaser and the third parties, tax was payable at both the points. In coming to this conclusion, the Income tax Officer held that loss would be carried forward and set off against speculation profits in the future. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal by the assessee held that there were no speculation profits and as there were speculation profits, he held that it should be set off only against speculation profit profits and that as there was no speculation profit in that year he held the loss would not be carried out and set aside the order of the Income. On reference, the High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. The correctness of that decision is challenged in this appeal by special leave. HELD: (1) The law on the point was correctly stated in D. P. M., Wadhwana & Co., (P.) Ltd. V. Commissioner of income tax, Calcutta, [1961 2 S .C. R., referred tO(2) In the instant case the question whether certain contracts between the appellant and the respondents could be called contracts involving actual delivery or constructive delivery of possession of the Goods concerned. The explanation does not invalidate speculative according to Explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery to that expressing for purposes of income Tax only. [184 D E] (3) In view of the fact that the property in the goods passed to the ultimate endorsee of the delivery orders, the respondent endorsed the delivery order and these passed through several hands before the ultimate holder of the deliver orders presented them to the mills, and obtained delivery of gunnies on payment. The question whether the transaction is speculative or not is a speculative transaction within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, has been correctly answered by this Court in D, M. M am Wadhwana v Commissioner of Incometax, WestBengal, [1955] 2 section C. R,, referred to and distinguished. (4) The Explanation does not validate speculative transactions according to explanation 2 if it is no real delivery of commodity or the scrips.

The first respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed an election petition challenging the rejection of the nomination papers on the ground that it was not accompanied with the required attestation under section 36(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The Election Tribunal decided in favour of the first respondent but the High Court held that the Returning officer was right in rejecting the appellant 's nomination papers. In appeal to this Court by special leave: Held : (i) The words " signing" whenever a signature is necessary must be in strict accordance with the requirements of the Act and that where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by the Rules. Whether the attestation attaches exaggerated importance to the authorisation is not for us to decide. What is beyond dispute is that this is regarded as a matter of special moment and that special provision has been made to meet such cases. [488 F G] (ii) The word "subscribe" in section 2(2) of 'the Representation of People Act shows that the words " sign " with reference to a person who is unable to write his name, include "mark" and not "subscribing". In the case of illiterate persons unable to speak their names it is necessary to guard against misrepresentation and fraud by requiring that their signatures should be formally authenticated in a particular way. A special statutory cloak of protection is thrown around them just as the ordinary law clothes pardanish in women and illiterate and ignorant persons and others likely to be imposed on, with special protective covering. [490 F G; 491 B] (iii) The Returning Officer rightly rejected the nomination paper.

The appellants were employees of the Company. During the pendency of the reference No. 336 of 1972 before the Second Labour Court, Bombay for adjudication of a dispute, 344 workmen of the company including the appellants went on an indefinite strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given by the Company to the Company by their registered union called 'The Association of Chemical Workers ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Unions who had been dismissed by the company. On September 7, 1972, the Company issued notices to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the Co. The Assistant Commissioner summoned the parties for discussion on July 19, 1973 but his attempts at conciliation did not bear any fruit. Thereafter, the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result that the appellants ' union had abandoned the services of the appellant company and had totally abandoned the Company 's service ' their names had been struck off by the rolls of its Company from that date. Along with its communication, the company sent a cheque to each one of the appellants for the amount due to him on account of gratuity, leave salary and one month 's salary. On October 23, 1972 the appellant wrote to the Labour Commissioner complaining about the arbitrary termination of service of 25 workmen (including the appellants) and emphasising that they had not abandoned service. The Company sent a letter to each of the employees intimating them that since "by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of the CO and had completely abandoned the company 's services" their names have been struck out from the rolls. Alongwith its communication the Company sent two letters to the appellant and 10 other workmen informing them that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off by their union. On July 5, 1973, the appellant made a formal demand calling upon the Company not to refute the averment made by the appellants in their letter dated September 26, 1972 but stating therein that it did not wish to revise its earlier decision under which their names were struck off the rolls and that they should report for worked the moment strike was call off by them from the roll of the coffers. On May 19, 1974, the union wrote a letter on September 7. 1973 to the Assistant Commissioner of Labour, Naupada soliciting his intervention in the dispute concerning the re instatedment of the 16 employees including the appellant. The appellants ' case was that the action of the respondent Company in removing the names of the appel lant from its rolls during the pendency o f the proceedings before the Labour Court in respect of the industrial dispute on the presumption that the workmen had abandoned their service would constitute a change in the conditions of service applicable to them immediately before the commencement of the said proceedings which prejudiciously affected them and could not be countenanced. The Tribunal rejected the aforesaid contentions and held that the appellant had voluntarily abandoned the service of its company and did not have abandoned the CO 's Service, that at any rate the termination of their services could only be in terms of the contract of service, and since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the respondent company ' s action was manifestly illegal and invalid. The High Court dismissed the appeal.

The respondents, who were trustees of a public trust, mortgaged a house belonging to the trust to one Saheba to secure repayment of Rs. 5,000. An action instituted by the mortgagee against the trustees to enforce the mortgage was compromised and it was decreed that the trustees did pay Rs. 3,910 due under the mortgage by monthly instalments of Rs 100 each and in default of three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mortgagee property. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under decree, and in an application for execution by the mortgage( mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs.5,000 by the executing court. The trial Court passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs. 250 out of the amount deposited by the trustees be paid over to the appellant. In appeal against that order by the appellant, the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 89 of 0. 21 Code of Civil Procedure, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the sale held in execution of the decree. The High Court also held that since a Judge or a Division Bench of a High Court makes a reference on a question of law arising in a matter before a single Judge or Division Bench that there are conflicting decisions of the same Court, and that a question whether a sale in exercise of authority derived from the trustees, e.g., a covenant for sale under an English mortgage executed by the trustee or a sale deed in terms of a consent decree attracts the application. of section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act was not complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set it aside on his own view. In the appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Legislature did not intend to put any restriction upon the power of the Civil Court executing a decree for recovery of money due from the trust, by sale of the property of the trust. [459 E] (ii) It was not intended thereby to confer upon the Charity Commissioner an overriding authority upon actions of the civil court in execution proceedings. The section imposes a fetter on the power to act contrary to the provisions of the Act. The Legislature had not intend that to put restriction upon its power of executing a decrees for recovery. [460 G] (iii) It is sufficient to observe that consideration of judicial propriety and decorum require that if a single judge hearing a matter is inclined to take the view that the earlier decisions of this Court are whether of a Division or of a Single Judge need,to be re considered, he should not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a single Bench. [461 F] (iv) The judgment delivered by a Full Bench of the High Court was binding upon the High Courts in India which were strongly persuasive and take a view different from the view which prevailed in his or their High Court.

Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, which permits the Central Government to retire a Government serv ant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service, confers unguided powers in the Govern ment and as such is ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The Government has also the power under Rule 2(1) of pension Rules to retire an officer at anytime after he had completed 30 year of qualifying serv ice. The object of this rule is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 (2) provides that such power can only be exer cised in 'Public Interest ' and as a result thereof, a Government servant who has attained the age of 55 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(j). The object underlying this rule was to chops off the unhoti f wood. The Rule 2 provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government to retiring a Government Servant at any one time after him has completed thirty years of qualify service though he has a right to continue till the age Of superannuation which is 58 years. The government servant also may, after attaining the ageof 55 years voluntarily retire after giving three months ' notice to the appointing authority. These provisions will have effect from the Ist December 1962. A bare reading of the Memorandum shows that there was an obvious fallacy in the argument of Mr. Singh. The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitu tion and as it cannot be statutory. The Memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1). Rule 2 gives unguided discretion to Government to prematurely retire a government servant at any stage after he attains the age. The order of retirement has to be in 'public interest ' and, as such, there is no vice of arbitrariness in the Rule. [800G H] Union of India & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by 1. Phool Chand and the sale of Katocu was effected by M/S BiharilalBalkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee firm did not maintain any books of accounts and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/ s Biharilal, Balkrishnan in the accounts styled " Kalyanmal Lal Phoolchand". The assessee 's firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katech u from October 1940 to September 1941. The sales were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 4th April, 1944, when the business was dis continued. Therefore, while there was manufacturing activity there was no sale during the financial years ending 31st December, 1941 and 31st of March, 1943. The dispute in this case is with regard to the set off of deficiency of profit relating to the periods 20th October 1940, to 17th October, 1941, and 23rd November, 1942 to 31th March, 1945, failing in the financial year ending March 31, 1944 and as such there could be no deficiency of profits. The Excess Profits Tax Officer held that the business carried on during the chargeable accounting period was the same as in 1940 41 and the excess profits were liable to be set off in computing the excess profit for the year under consideration. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner. On further appeal, he held that there was a no profit arising during the accounting period ending on 31st April, 1941. He therefore confirmed that there were no profits and losses during the relevant chargeable accounting periods ending on 30th March 1944 and that as such no part of it was sold. The High Court also held that it was not disputed before them that the assessee was carrying on the same business from 28th October to 4st April 1944 for the purpose of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A manufacturing process may begin in one year and result in sale in another year and also that manufacturing process might take at one place and sale at another place. For the purpose Of computing the profit of certain operation, it is true as the High Court noted, that manufacture and sales might take place in two different years. The question must be answered in the negative and in favour of the revenue. [610E] 1.2 A manufacturing activity may begin with in one ' year and results in sale In another year also, and also, that manufacturing processes may take at One place and sell at another places.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the said Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions were in Civil nature, Mechanical Engineering. Petitioners who were qualified in Civil Engineers had to answer the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had qualified in Mechanical Engineering and answered questions indicated in Category 11 in the question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government of Kerala and the K PSC to prepare "two lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the Service Commission has not yet published the rank list.

The respondent No. 1, a partner of a partnership firm, filed a suit for accounts from the appellant No.1 and defendant Nos. 2 and 3 besides denying the plaint allegations made by the plaintiff, challenged the valuation given by the appellant as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the respondent in the suit. It was further submitted that the respondent No 1 had laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint and it was, therefore, preposterous on his part to suggest in paragraph 19 of the Plaint that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. According to the defence case which is challenged as incorrect by the defendant, the plaintiff requested for and was allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch solely and absolutely '. The respondent No 2 contended that it is manifest that relief can be tentativeally valued at only Rs. 50. According ly the defence that was based on incorrect by defendant, he requested for, and was granted a larger right to put on the plaint any value he wishes to and the court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a suit of accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334, and Shama Pershad Shahi vs Sheopershad Singh XLI, I.C. 95 (Patna). In a Suit for accounts the defendant is not required to state exact amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit.[505D E] Smt. Tara Devi vs Sri Thakur Radha Krishna Maharaj, I .C. 96 (Patnna). 1.2 In a plaint for accounts, the defendant has been ousted from the partnership business.

The respondent assessee in these appeals and the petitioners in the other five Special Leave Petitions are certain concerns in M.P. assess able to sales tax ( compendiously referred as the assesses '). All these matters can be conveniently dis posed of by a common judgment as they raise a common issue. The assesses ' claim for exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question was accepted by the High Court in the case of G.S. Dhall & Flour Mills and, following it, in the earlier case of M. P. State (M.P.). The State submits that C.A. 22 11/87 should be allowed and that the assesses should be dismissed in limine. On the other hand, counsel for the assesses sought to distinguish the Jagadamba Indus tries case by contending that this Court had refused leave against the Full Bench judgment on account of certain special facts which were considered sufficient to dis tentwine the assesses in those cases from claiming the exemption. They contend that, in view of this and the fact that the G. S.D. Dhal & Flour Mill case is in appeal before this Court, it should be granted and that, the assesses be dismissed. On behalf of the asses see, it was contended that, even if the 1983 instructions were rightly held by the Supreme Court to have validly supplemented the terms of the 1981 Notification, they could have no application to the two earli cial cases which had to be decided solely on the terms and conditions set out in the notification and not on the basis of any further requirements not so set out. The State also contended that even if a lenient view is taken and a more liberal construction is sought to be placed on the notification, the best that could be said for the State would be that the notification was ambiguous. One could either say that the previous procedure and requirements prevalent for obtaining an exemption certificate were in tended to be incorporated by the words requiring such a certifi cate (as envisaged for the assessee. The argument overlooks the reference in column (3) to the grant of an eligibility certificate by the Director of Industries because, under some earlier schemes, such certificate was being granted on a restricted basis, does not appear to be sound logic. It is not permissible to restrict the scope of the notification in the manner suggested. If such intention can be gathered from the construction of the words of the Notification or by necessary implication therefrom, the matter is different, but that is not the case here.

The petitioners in both these petitions are promotee Additional District and Sessions Judges in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. They were appointed as Additional District & Sessions Judges on May 15, 1971 with a complement of 12 posts. The Delhi Higher judicial Service was constituted on May 16, 1971. These Rules were framed under Article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 2(b) provides that `Cadre Post ' means any post specified in the Schedule and includes a temporary post carrying the same designation as that of any of the posts specified in Schedule any other temporary post declared as cadre post by Administrator. Rule 17 provides for appointment of promotees to temporary vacancies in the service on a temporary basis. The petitioners were appointed to the Delhi High Court on May 25, 1971 and got her confirmation during the pendency of these petitions. The seniority list which was impugned in these two writ petitions is the same as that in the case of Shri C.D. On June 17, 1978, the Administrator created temporary posts in the Service under Rule 16(1) with a view to fill substantive vacancies in Delhi Higherjudicial Service. The High Court of Delhi and direct recruits to the said Delhi HigherJudicial Judicial Service were challenged by the promotees on the ground that seniority between promotees and direct recruit must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional Distt. & Sessions Judge and that, direct recruits who are appointed as Addl. District & Session Judges after the promotees are so appointed cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. The respondents contended that seniority of promotees and promotee officers should be determined on the basis of their combined seniority list between promotees & direct recruits. Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1. Rule 8(2) which deals with fixation of inter se seniority amongst the members of the Delhi Judicial Service who are promoted to the High Court posts in Delhi High Courts is not really a quota rule and it did not lay down any proportion, all it did was to insist that the number of vacancies to be filled in by promotion should not be less than half of the total number of substantive posts in service. It provides two different sources of recruitment. and without fixing any actual quota, but a ceiling of not more than 1/3 of the substantive posts to be held by direct recruits.[394E F] 1.2. Rule 7(a) provides for recruitment to the State Higher Judicial Services alia by promotion on the recommendation of the High court. The Rules are in the nature of a non obstante provision, providing that not withstanding anything contained in the Rules, the administrator may, in consultation with the High Courts, fill substantive vacancy vacancies in such service by making temporary appointments thereto from amongst the Members of the State Judicial Service either constitutes an exception to the quota rule or in the alternative proceeds on the foundation of relaxation or abrogation of quota rule. If the source of recruitment to temporary posts is one and only namely, the members o.e., the Delhi judicial Service, no question of applying the quota Rule can possibly arise. If temporary appointments to the Service, either in temporary posts or in substantive vacancies, can be made within the framework of the Rules and have to be made, if at all, from amongst promotees and promotees only, the quota of rule contained in proviso to Rule 7 must inevitably break down when such appointments are made. [394F G] 1:3. The contention that seniority inter se between promotees cannot be included in the list of seniority of officers belonging to the service is not correct.

The appellant, who was a partner in a trading venture, conducted in the name of 12 Sup. C 1/70 11 Ambala Flour Mills, Ambala. The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant 's income in the status of an association of persons and assessed it to income tax under section 31(3)(b) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment made by the Income tax officer and directed that the direction for assessing the income be deleted. The Tribunal referred the following three questions at the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax: "Whether L. Debi Parlakishan was a stranger in respect of the income tax proceedings against Ambala Flour Mill ? 2. Whether the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner could give a direction in the case of Ambala Flour mills to the effect that the income should be assessed in the hands of L.P. after annulling the assessment in the ease of Ambala Rice Mills ? 3. Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the appeals were filed by DebiParshad, but in dif ferent capacities. The High Court held that the Income Tax Officer had jurisdiction to direct the income in respect Of the income of the Ambala Flour mill after annuling the assessment of the appellant. Held: (i) Where the income Tax Officer assessed a person of an Association of persons under section31(3), the Appellate Tribunal was competent to set aside such assessment and to direct that the Incometax Officer to assess the members individually. The expression "any person" in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the said sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. Commissioner of lncome tax, U.P., vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed. (ii) Where a person other than the assessee might be affected by orders passed by the Appellate Commis sioner.

The appellant, who was the son of Subbiah Chettiar, filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by the respondent. The appellant claimed to have a share in the joint Hindu family properties, and in the assets of the Joint Family and that was the basis on which a claim for partition and accounts was made by the appellant in his suit. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the plaint filed in the present suit did not attract the provisions of section 7(v) of the Act and that the proper court fee to be paid was determined by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Madras Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The order passed by the trial court on October 18, 1951, is final under section 5 of the , and it cannot be reopened at this stage. It may be that when the Division Bench of the High 'Court considered this matter under reference made by it the Master under section S5, the respondent was not heard. Normally the dispute between the litigant and the Registry in respect Of court fees arises at the initial stage of the presentation of the plaint or the appeal and the defendant or the respondent is usually not interested in such a dispute unless the question of payment of court fee involves also the question whether of jurisdiction of the Court either to try the suit or to entertain the appeal. (ii) The question about the proper Court fees leviable on plaints in which Hindu plaintiffs make claims for partition under varying circumstances has given rise to several conflicting decisions in the High Courts of India. Where the plaintiff seeks to enforce his right to share in any property on the ground that it is joint family property, and the amount of fees payable on plaints filed on the Original Side of the said High Court prior to 1953 there was no need to make any jurisdictional valuation. The plaintiffs failure to state the amount at which he values the relief sought is often due to the fact that in suits for partition the plaintiff attempts to obtain the benefit of article 17B of Schedule 11 in the matter of payment, and where the plaintiff seeking to enforce their right to shares in any properties on the grounds that it was joint family Property. The mere fact that the plaintiff has valued the relief for the purposes of court fees that determines the value for jurisdiction in the suit and not vice versa does not make the claim for possession of the suit properties and as such falls within the provisions Of section 7, sub section (v) Of the Act.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought special leave to appeal to this Court from the order dated 28.4.1989 of the High Court of Delhi in Civil Writ Petition 3090 of 1987, declining to sanction the Revised Plans for construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi of which the first respondent is the lessee. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before 5th May, 1989. The NDMC in exercise of power under Section 193(3) of the Punjab Municipal Act 1911 rejected the plans assigning 28 rea sons for the rejection. On 14.5.1987, the Architect of First Respondent claimed to have subsequently complied with or clarified the points on which the rejection was based, resubmitted the plans. On 26.5 .87, the Architects wrote to NDMC to reconsider its decision dated 18.2. 1987 in the light of the rectifications effected. However no positive response having emanated from the NDMC Respondents 1 and 2 on 27.10.1987 filed the Writ Petition in the High court for an appropriate order directing the DUAC and the NDMC and to "forth with deal with the application for grant of sanction". The architect of First Appellant Respondent claimed that the plans for the multi storeyed high rise buildings, as proposed by Statesman Ltd., did not, in the matter of fire safety requirements, accord ing with the mandatory requirements of the Statutory Building Bye laws promulgated under the Punjab Town and Country Planning Act 1911 in relation to the Union territory of Delhi and that the proposed build ing did not also provide for a "podium/pedestrian walk way" made mandatory by the Zonal Development Plan for Zone D 1 (viz. Connaught Place Area) approved by the Central Government on 30th April 1966 in No. 21023(7)66UD under Section 9(2) of Delhi Urban Art Commission Act, 1957. The sanction was revalidated for a further period of two years. In June 1985, however there was, it would appear, prohibition on high rise structures.

The joint family carried on joint family business of a grocery shop, liquor shops, a motor bus service and also money lending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". The family also Possessed immovable property and movable property. Balkrishna Sontakke was the eldest of the brothers and was the plaintiff respondent in the present appeal. He will be referred to hereafter as the plain tiff. It is common ground that up to 1944 the brothers were living and messing together and the income from the said business used to be kept with the plaintiff. From April 14, 1945, all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The suit was numbered 39 of 1945. It was compromised on March 7, 1946, that the accounts were to be taken up to March 31, 1946 and that account of all family business businesses should be taken upto March 31. 1946. In defence it was pleaded that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that accounts of the motor business and grocery shops should actually have been taken up for March 31 and that accounts should actually be taken on April 14. The plaintiff further alleged that the claim was barred by res judicata. Upon the issues framed in the case the Civil Judge found that the suit was not barred by reason of the decision in the previous suit No 39 of 1946, and that the decision of the trial Court was not obtained by fraud and misrepresentation and that he had abandoned his claim to account for the subsequent period. The High Court on appeal held that though the motor bus business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family, yet as it was carried on by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act he held that the two brothers carrying on the motorbusiness were liable to account. Accordingly he passed a preliminary decree directing the accounts for the motor car business to be carried on from March 31 1946 up to the date on which a final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be made. The appellant came by special leave. Held, that on a fair reading of the compromise arrived at between the parties in the circumstances then existing, the only legitimate conclusion was that the parties had agreed to confine the taking of all accounts upto March 1, 1946. It could not be said that the plaintiff 's conduct in going back upon that arrangement by filing a fresh suit in regard to the motor shop only was anything but honest. The compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, misunderstanding or mistake, the decree passed thereon had the binding force of res judicata and the consent decree following upon it.

The appellant was employed on salt works in the Salt Works and described as " Premises" in a deed. The salt work consisted of an open marshy area, surrounded by mud embankment, the height of which is above the highest tide water mark in that locality to prevent inundation. In this embankment, sluice gates are provided with suitable places to take in and discharge the sea water and the waste water respectively. The inner enclosed area was divided into compartments for the storage of sea brine of different densities. When the salt is formed, it is stored on the platform by the laborers engaged in the manufacture. It is then weighed, bagged and carried to Railway Station or to a port of shipment. For this production the sea Water water is taken into the Reservoirs at high water tide twice during a month. The high tides take place on about nine or ten days in a month, five days during time and four times at night. Some of the labourers are detained for this work but they were not required to be present the whole time, when the evaporation is going on. Once the brine is let into the crystallising beds, its surface is not to be disturbed for four or five days. After this, the labourer has to be careful to see that the density does not exceed a certain limit and that the other kinds of salt contained in the brin are not deposited, thus contaminating the sodium chloride (common salt) already formed. This they learn by experience. Sifting and storing then begins. The labourers work is intermittent and not continuous for any fixed hours. It was therefore contended for the appellant that the various provisions of the Act cannot be applicable to salt works where the process of converting sea water into salt is carried on in the open air, because they are less exposed to the evils incident to manufactures carried on by the process Of treatment and adaptation of sea water from there to the crystallizing pans which are specially prepared by thumping the mud and making the layer of the ground hard and water tight. The appellant relied on certain cases which were referred to in this connection. Held, that even though the workers employed on these salt works, are dealing with the sea waters in a particular manner and but for the dealing with it in that manner, salt as made on these works would not be made.

The respondent was a Instructor in tailoring Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, three occupational Institutes (Polytechnics) at Hassan and Chintamani were started in the State. The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere as Instructor in Tailoring and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. On June 11, 1956, the respondent was again posted on deputation as Instructor. In 1955, for no fault of his would cause a great hardship to him, the Commission were of the opinion that he may be absorbed as tailoring Instructor from the date of his appointment as such as had been ordered in the case of Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him, Sri K Narayanaswamy C. Chetty was absorbed with effect from November 28, 1949, but no order was passed in the cases of the Respondent despite repeated representations made by the latter. In 1953, the State Government set up the Department of Technical Education and the Polytechnics at Devagere became part of that Department. The Respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the Department with effect From November 28. 1949, his services were allotted to the new State of Mysore. In 1956, for a short period, he was again transferred to the Polyechnics and joined duty thereafter. The Government by order dated February 19, 1964 ordered the absorption of the respond ents in the department of Technical Educational Education with effect on the respective dates of their joining duty, after deputation, in the Institutes. Accordingly, the services were also allotted to him. In 1960, the Respondent was again appointed on deputation and he continued to be absorbed with retrospective effect from December 1. 1949 but no orders were passed in his case despite repeated representation made by him. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption should be given effect from the dates of his initial appointment as provided in the order.
