In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the respondent had no legal right to be appointed absorbed in service of the Department from a particular anterior date, or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service of that department; (2) the absorption in the Departments of Technical education was not justified as he had been invidiously discriminated against in the matter of absorption and appointment, while his junior K. N. Chetty who was junior to him in the parent Department and came on deputation with effectfrom November 28 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on transfer; (3) the State Govern ment had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department for Technical Education from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date On which a person initially came into deputation, was ever departed from, except in the ease of the re organisation of Technical Personnel Education; (4) the case was fully covered by this Court 's decision in K. V. Rajalakshmiah Setty and Anr.

The Indian Council of Social Welfare and S.O.S. Children 's Villages of India, was constituted under the for the purpose of providing social and legal facts in regard to the foreign parent with a view to its eventual adoption, and it was enacted by the Indian Council for Child Welfare and the Indian Councils of Social welfare to carry out their obligations in the matter of adoption of Indian children by foreign parents. The petitioner sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies " from carrying out further activity of routing children for adoption abroad" and directing the Govern ment of India to carry them out their obligation in the matters of adoption, of Indian Children 'S Villages and to carryout their obligations. This letter was treated as a writ petition and by an Order dated 1st September, 1982 the Court issued notice to Union of India the Indian Association of Social Relief and S who appeared through its counsel Mrs. Urmila Kapoor and applied for being allowed to intervene at the hearing of the writ petition so that they could make their submissions on the question of adoption. The Court also directed that the Registry may address a communication to Barnen Framfoer Allot Adoptioner informing them about the adjourned date of hearing of these writ petitions and stating that if they wished to present any material and make their submission, they could do so by filing an affidavit before the adjourned day of hearing. The Union of Indian Council was also directed to furnish before the next hearing of this writ petition the names of "any Indian Institutions or Organisation other than the Indian Institute of Social Justice Welfare and to appear in answer to the notice issued by the Court and its written submission filed on 30th September,1982 not only carried considerable useful material bearing on the questions of adoption by foreign parent but also contained various suggestions and recommendations for consideration by the court in formulating principles and norms for permitting such adoptions and laying down the procedure for that purpose. The Indian Council had set out in annexure 'B ' to the reply filed by it, guidelines for the preparation of home study report in regard thereto to foreign parent wishing to take a child in adoption, etc., and also contained certain suggestions and recommendation for consideration of the Court in formulating the principles and procedures for allowing such adoption. In response to the notices issued by this Court, the Union of india submitted that the Indian Children Act, 1956 was enacted with a purpose to provide social and economic justice to children in adoption to foreign parents, lest the child may be neglected or abandoned by the adoptive parents in the foreign country or the adoptive parent may not be able to provide to the child a life of moral or material security or the child might be subjected to moral or sexual abuse or forced labour or experimentation for medical or other research and may be placed in a worse situation than that in his own country. The social or child welfare agency sponsoring the application must also agree to send to the concerned social or Child Welfare Agency in India, so that the social or the family welfare agencies licensed or recognised by the Government of India or the Government for the purposes of inter country adoptions, would know which social or children are committed by the juvenile court. The State Government of Maharashtra was directed to consider and decide within a period of three months from today whether any of the institutions or agencies which have appeared as interveners in the present writ petition are engaged in child care and welfare and if they have good standing and reputation and are doing commendable work in the area of child care, the court makes an order appointing the foreign parents as guardian of the child with liberty to him to take the child to his own Country for the welfare of the children.

The appellant company employed workmen numbering over 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,05,32,880. Its accounting year is from 1st April to 31st March of the succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the . The appellant company claimed that this amount should be deducted from its gross profits for calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found payable had to be calculated and 60% of the rebate has to be added back as allocable surplus. The Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, the following dispute "What should be the quantum of bonus payable to the workmen of Indian Cable Company Limited Calcutta for the accounting years 1965 66, 1965 66 and the Unions contended before the Tribunal that the computa tion of allocable available surplus by the company had not been properly made in accordance. The Tribunal accepted the evidence of the Unions and held that a sum of Rs. 21,06,576 being bonus at20% of gross effective salary and wages was payable for the year in question and it directed the payment of the balance 6.49% within the period mentioned 109 in the Award. One aspect which has to he acted is that (in calculating the available surplus, the Tribunal before calculating the notional direct tax deducted the bonus payable for accounting year in dispute. The claim for additional bonus for adjudication was rejected by the Tribunal on the ground that the company has not furnished the requisite particulars. On appeal by the appellant company, the High Court held that the Tribunal committed an error in law in corrupting direct tax after deducting bonus payable and that the Company had failed to do so. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was justified in disallowing the deduction of certain items from the gross profits. [112B] (2) The claim of the appellant for additional payment of Rs, 65,764 has also to be rejected in view of the decision of this Court in Indian Oxygen Ltd. etc. vs Their Workmen, ; , followed. (3) The company had produced figures for depreciation and that has not been subjected to any serious challenge by the Unions.

The appellant, who was working as a Commercial Tax officer in 1954, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d). His Service Book showed that he had an excellent record of service. He had earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The several promotions gained by him react his good record of Service. But there was one dark spot. In 1969 when he was working in as Commercial Tax officers it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner. On November 29, 1974 he was promoted to a Selection post. On April 28, he was served with a charge sheet. The appellant submitted his explanation and sent its report thereon. The Full Board of Revenue (CT) accepted the report of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on May 29, 1975: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. Out of eleven allegations levelled against Thiru D. Ramaswami, seven allegations were not substantiated in the enquiry made by the Director of Vigilance & Anti Corruption Department. The Government examined the report and considered that there was a primafacie case in respect of certain allegations and this was sufficient to proceed against Thiru. D. Ramaswamy on the basis of allegations levelled by him. The Board accordingly framed charges against him in respect thereof in respect to allegations proved, obtained his explanation, and sent it to the Director General of Commercial Tax who accepted the same. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the face of the promotion of the appellant just a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order of the Government retiring the appellant from service. [80G] 1.2 The post of a Deputy Commissioner is a Selection Post. Under Rule 36(b) (i) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for Commercial Taxes Service: "All promotions shall be made on grounds of merit and ability, seniority being considered only where merit and suitability are approximately equal". So, what do we have ? There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of the Appellant in 1969. The basis of the entry 79 was knocked out by the order dated November 29 1974 of the A Government, and the effect of the Entry was blotted out by promotion of his appellant as Deputy Commis sioner. After his promotion as Dy Commissioner there was no entry in his service Book to his discredit or hinting even remotely that he has outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But, with nothing of the sort, it was indeed odd to retire a Govt servant a few month after promoting him to a selection post. [81C E] 1:3 The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. Sometimes, past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotional promotion, we see no justification for needless digging into the past. [82D E] Swami Saran Saksena vs State of U.P., ; , followed.

The appellants who were the operators of a motor transport operators whose permits were liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the Schemes on their coming into force, applied for permits. The Regional Transport Authority rejected the applications and passed an order rejecting the applications. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the schemes. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the scheme was vitiated by mala fides because the scheme did not conform to the statutory requirements of section 68 C and r. 4 of the Rules regarding the particulars to be embodied in the schemes, and (ii) the provisions Of the Scheme were bad as they had been made merely with a view to cause prejudice or in the hope that whether they have basis in fact or not some of it at least might stick. HELD: (i). The scheme was not vitiated by the fact that they were not in conformity with the requirements of s. 68 C. [357 E] (ii). The provisions of r. 5 and rr. 6, 7 and 8 of the Motor Vehicles Rules, 1957, made thereunder were to have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in Chapter IV of this Act or in any law for the time being in force or in a instrument having effect by virtue of any such law. [358 C] (iii) The provisions Of r. 141 of the Andhra Pradesh Motor Vehicles Rule, 1957 and rr., 4, 5 and 6 of the rules made thereunder, were to be set aside as not warranted by law. When the judgment in the above appeals was pronounced on January 27, 1964, the learned Advocate for the appellants brought to our notice the following order passed by this Court on June 10, 1963, passed by a Bench of the High COurt: "The Regional Transport Officer, Kurnool, Nellore and Cuddapah districts in that order would be chosen for nationalisation and not the independent opinion of the Corporation as to what was needed in the public interest as required by section 68C.

The appellant company was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954 in the return for the year the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,99,928 10 0 and deposited the tax of Rs. 9 6 on the said amount in the treasury. The Commercial Tax Officer by notice dated April 22, 1955 fixed August 4, 1955, for hearing the assessee in respect of its return. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act the furnishing of the declaration forms issued by the purchasing dealers was a condition for claiming the exemption thereunder. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry it appeared that in the second week of January 1957 the assessee found that its file containing 147 declaration forms received from its dealers in respect Of the goods received from it was missing. The assessee, it was said, made various attempts to get duplicate forms of declaration from the dealers but, on account of circumstances over which it had no control and because of the unhelpful and hostile attitude of the Commercial Tax officer within whose jurisdiction the said dealers functioned, it could not furnish the duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. On August 8, 1957, the assessee applied to the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes under section 21A of the Bengal Sales Tax Act for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order to prove that they had issued the declaration form to it but the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the production of the prescribed declaration was not obligatory but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed the order of the Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the words "on demand" in r. 27A of Bengal Sales tax Rules, 1941, read with the proviso, impose a condition on a dealer for claiming exemption under the said sub clause but if he seeks exemption he must comply strictly with the conditions under which the exemption can be granted; and (ii) the clear terms of the clause read with proviso, imposed a condition upon a dealer to claim exemption. HELD: (i)(a) The expression "ondemand" only fixes the point of time when the declaration Form forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with the section. [629 C] (ii).

The petitioners were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and section 25 of the Arms Act. The petitioners contended that they had been in jail for a period longer than what they would have been sentenced to suffer, if convicted. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1.1. It is well settled that as a result of the decision of this Court in Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, [1978] 2 SCR 621 that when Article 21 provides that no person shall be deprived of his life or liberty except in accordance with the procedure established by law, it is not enough that there should be some semblance of procedure provided by law. It was an essential ingredient of 'reasonable, fair and just procedure to a prisonel who is to seek his liberation through the court 's process that he should have legal services available to him. This Government hires lawyers to prosecute and defendants who have the money hire lawyers to defend are the strongest indications of the widespread belief that lawyers in criminal courts are necessties, not luxuries. The right of one charged with crime to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trials in some countries but it is in ours. From the very beginning, our state and national constitutions and laws have laid great emphasis on procedural and substantive safeguards designed to assure fair trials before impartial tribunals in which every defendant stands equal before the law. This noble ideal cannot be realised if the poor man charged with crimes has to face his accusers without a lawyer to assist him. [532C D] 1.2. The State Government cannot avoid its constitutional obligation to provide speedy trial to the accused by pleading financial or administrative inabiltiy. The Court is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. It would also the constitutional obligation of this court as the guardian of the fundamental rights of the people, as a sentinel on the qui vive, to enforce the fundamental right of the accused to speedy trial by issuing the necessary directions to the State which may include taking of positive action, such as augmenting and strengthening the investigative machinery setting up new courts, building new court houses, providing more staff and equipment to the courts, appointment of additional judges and other measures calculated to ensure expeditious trial. [540D E] 1:3. The Supreme Court Bar Association will respond to the notice and appear to assist the Court at the hearing of the writ Petition. [541E F] 2.4. It may be appropriate that some of them, on trial may be acquitted of the offences charged against them and in that event they would be have spent several years in jail custody for offences which they are ultimately found not to have committed.

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The notice was for one year as required by section 34 (1) and the tenancy was to terminate from March 31, 1953. The respondent thereupon made an application on April 7, 1953, under section 29(2) of that Act for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. In the meantime an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2 A), which came into force on January 12, 1953 and by this amendment certain restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a protected tenant. The appellant contended that the right to terminate a tenancy having arisen when the notice was given, the law to be applied, in case of notices given before the Amending Act came into operation, would be the law existing on the date of notice and therefore the amendment did not affect any vested right of landlords till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the notice. Held, that the view taken by the High Court was correct and sub section 2 A) would apply to all cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending Acts. The object of the amending Act which came in force before the tenancy stood terminated by the notice will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right Of the landlord in the matter of the termination of the tenancy, for the Amending act put certain fetters on this right of termination. In that case the provisions of the amended Act were not affected by the amendment and the amendment was a piece of beneficent legislation meant for the protection of tenants.

The petitioners, who were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali who had never been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters who thereupon became entitled to them in certain shares. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. Held, that no property of any person can be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act. In the present case there was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting the petitioners ' right in the properties concerned. The acts of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. It was also said on behalf of the respondents that the properties had already been acquired under the , and therefore the petitioners had no longer any claim to them. Held further, that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief against the order of January 10, 1952, in so much as it affected the rights of the petitioners in the property concerned. There was no legal determination by him on the question whether the Custodian was entitled to declare the entirety of the two houses evacuee properties and deprive the appellants of their right in them. The orders of January 11, 1952 were without jurisdiction so far that they could not maintain this petition. It is well established and not disputed that no person can claim that his father left a will giving him a larger share in the house than he would have got on intestacy.

The assessee company had two departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool, and (2) for weaving of yarn. The second Department carried on the operations of spinning of cotton yarn from imported wool tops. The assessee Company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents for the worsted yarn on payment of 2% commission. Subsequently on December 15, 1953 the assessee company entered into an agreement with the agents on October 20, 1955 under which the agents were to get 6% interest on all the advances made by them, 1% commission on net sales and 50% commission at net profits on net profits of the worstned plant in the course of two years. The Income tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed and held that the deductions claimed were actually a division of profits after the profits had come into existence and had been ascertained, therefore could not be claimed as a valid deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also rejected the contention of the assessee Company that the payments in question amounted to a legitimate deduction under the provisions of section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax Act, 1922 and that the amounts in question were not legal deductions as contemplated by section 10.(2)(xiv) of Act but amounted to application of profits before they were earned. The Tribunal also held that though the agreement was a contract of agency it was not a joint venture and accordingly the High Court accepted the plea of the appellant Company. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1 ) The High Court was right in holding that the amount set apart for the purpose of distribution amongst the consumers is not chargeable to tax on the ground that it represents over charge. [197C] (2). It is well settled that the High Courts are not entitled to go behind or to question the statement of facts made by the Tribunal. The statement of case is binding on the parties and they are Dot entitled to gone behind the facts of the Tribunal in the statement. [198F G] (3) In order to determine the question of reason ableness of the expenditure, the test of commercial expediency would have to be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not of the Income tax Department. It is open to the Appellate Tribunal to come to a conclusion either that the alleged payment is not real or that it is not incurred by the assessee in the character of trader or it is laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business of the asses seeant and to disallow it. But it is only when an agreement like the present one was entered into between the assessee and its agents.

The assessee is the Managing Director of a private limited company called R. K. V. Motors & Timber (P) Limited. The company maintains an accounts pertaining to him in its books. The accounts showed that as on March 31, 1958 a sum of Rs. 36,546.17 np was due to him by the company. In January 1959 for the first time he became indebted to the company in the sum of RS. 3,757 np. He was originally assessed for the assessment year 1959 60 (the relevant previous year being the year ended March 31. 1959) on a total income of Rs 43,407. The Income Tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee and determined a sum as dividend under section 2(6A)(e). He arrived at this figure by including the current profits of the company for the account year ending March 31 1959. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed an appeal filed by the assessee. The High Court in second appeal, upheld the claim of the asses see that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not be construed as including current profits but it rejected the contentions of the assesses and determined the sum as "dividend". In the appeal by certificate under section 261 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, against the judgment of the High Court of Kerala interpreting the words 'accumulation profits ' in section 1(6 A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, the High court held that the expression "accuulated profits ' occurring in section 6A(2) could be construed not to include current profits for the purpose of section 2.(6A). 947 Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The respondents contested the suits, pleaded that the lands were not Mal lands comprised within Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that they had been granted in permanent Mokarrari by the then Maharaja of Burdwan to the Rajgunaj Asthal and that the plea of the respondents that they held them under a Lakheraj grant made prior to the permanent settlement was not true. The trial court decreed the suits but on appeal the District Judge affirmed the decision of the trial Court. In second appeals to the High Court, it was contended that (i) the suit lands were included in MouzaNala in Thouzi No. 1 which was comprised in the permanently settle estate of Alipore and were Mal lands assessed to revenue, and (ii) the entry in the record of rights in 1931 was made in compliance with that Rule, and that what it imports is not that there was a rent free grant but that the person in possession was not actually paying rent. Whatever weight might attach to the word " Franchiskar" in a 1175 record of Rights in other context, where the question is whether a presumption of a lost pre settlement Lakhearaj grant could be made in respect thereof. Held, further, that on the facts found, no presumption of the lost grant could he made in favour of the predecessors of the defendant. The suit properties formed part of Mouza within the Zamindari of Burdwan and if a grant had been made in his favour, it must have been made by the Maharaja of Calcutta or by the Rajbhumi Behara and others vs Sreenath Devasikamony (1917) L.R. 44 I.A. 147, 1176 both on the ground of prescription and presumption of lost grant by a rector. In the present case, the defendants had in their written statements denied the title of both the Maharaja and the Asthal, and having failed in that plea, cannot fall back on a presumption Of lost grant.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of agricultural land. The suit was resisted by the defendant, inter alia, contending that the land which was the subject matter of contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 ( 'Tenancy Act ' for short) and as the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the said Act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The trial court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court agreed with the trial court observing that Civil Court has undoubtedly jurisdiction to entertain a suit in a civil court for specific perform of contract for sale and while considering the main issue whether specific performance should be granted or not, civil Court will have to consider whether there are prima facie any facts on account of which granting of specific performance would result into a transaction forbidden by law and, consequently, civil court will have jurisdiction to decide the subsidiary issue whether the plaintiff is an agriculturist. The High Court accordingly dismissed the appeal while agreeing with the Trial Court that the plaintiff had failed to prove that he was an agriculturist and specific performance for sale. In this appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant defendant that if the court does not take note of Ext 78, an issue on the pleadings would arise whether the Plaintiff is an agricultural labourer because if he is not, the Civil Count would be precluded from enforcing the contract as it would be in violation of a statutory prohibition and the contract would be unenforceable as being prohibited by law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authority under the Tenancy Acts is totally ousted. This would lead to inescapable conclusion that the Mamlatdar while performing the function and discharging duties as are conferred upon him by section 70, would constitute an exclusive forum, to the exclusion of the Civil Court, to decide any question that may arise under any of the sub clauses of section 70. [591C] 1.2 The jurisdiction to settle is ousted under section 85. The Bombay High Court which had initially to deal with this problem, resolved the problem by holding that in such a situation the civil suit should be stayed and the parties should be referred to the competent authorities under the Act to get the question decided by the authority and on such decision being brought before the Civil court, it will be binding on the civil Court and the civil courts will have all jurisdiction to try the issues arising in a suit properly cognisable by it.

The assessee, a heavy engineer, manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc., for the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 in respect of the profits and gains derived from its Steel Foundry Division and a similar claim for relief under section15C in respect thereof. The assessee had previously in the earlier years bought from outside the castings manufactured in the steel Foundry division which was started in the assessment year 1958 59, and continued thereafter. Again in the year '1959 60 in addition to the manufacturing of cast ings in the Steel Foundries Division, the Income Tax Officer found that out of the total sales of Rs.1303,509/ sales to the Boiler Division totalled only a sum of Rs,1,13,6971/ . The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the above facts held the under takings as expansion and reconstruction of the business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled (1) 765 to exemption under section '15C of Income Tax, 1922. The Tribunal also came to the conclusion that it could not be said that the undertakings were formed out of a new business to come within the mischief of the exclusion clause in section 15 C(2)(i). The High Court held as follows: (1 ) The machinery was new, was housed in a separate building and that industrial licences had to be obtained, for manufactur ing the parts in question. According to the Tribunal both the Steel Industry and the Jute Mill Division of the assessee were new industrial undertakings. The above conclusion was reached on the basis of several facts found by the Tribunal. These are that the machinery was old, was, housed In a separate build ing and that Industrial licences had lo be obtained for structur ing of the parts, in question, and that purpose the assessee 's main business consisted of manufacturing boilers etc., and for that purpose, the assessee wag purchasing the spare parts, and forgings and castings from outside.

The inam lands were granted by Hindu kings for performance of services of watchman, palanquin bearer, background music player, dancing girl, musical instrument player and mason. The inams were confirmed by the British Government. For over 80 years, the inams were in the enjoyment of alienees from inamdars. By an order passed on April 10, 1947 under section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, the Revenue Divisional Officer resumed the inam lands and regranted them to the temple. On October 17, 1947, this order was confirmed on appeal by the District Collector. The High Court dismissed the appeals in respect of all the inams except the Dasi inam. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the inam grants did not comprise the kudiwaram; (2) the inams did not form personal inams and were granted as inams; (3) there was no alienation of the inam by the alienees for over 60 years under the cowle lease; and (4) there had been no alienation. HELD : (i) The inam lands in the present case are resumable under section44 B(2)(a)(i). [547 A] (ii) There is no period of limitation prescribed for the initiation of proceedings under section 43 B(1). The object of section 44B was to define and enlarge the grounds on which the inams could be resumed and to devise a proper procedure for the resumption. On general grounds of public policy, the legislature has declared that the inam may be resumed on any of the three grounds mentioned therein. [547 C] (iii) Section 44 B(3)(a) (i), though the alienations were made before 1934, was not retrospective in operation and did not authorise resumption of the inams on the ground of any alienation thereof made before 1935; and even apart from section 44 A, any inam whatever its nature could be resume for failure to perform the conditions of the grant. [548 E] (iv) The object ,of section 44A was to defining and enlarge grounds on Which the inams can be resumed, and to evolve a proper machinery for the administration of the resumption.[549 C D] (v) Section 45 B does not apply to a personal inam burdened with a condition of service, and the grant of land as remuneration for an office, see, see. 44 B, C.A. No. 484 of 1965 was therefore in its direct operation prospective as it authorises only future resumption after it came into force.

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by that Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax at the rate of 7% of their gross annual letting value. The respondents as trustees of a charitable trust were the owners of certain houses situate in Indore City. Prior to January 26, 1954 the Indore Municipality was governed under the Indore city Municipal Act 4 of 1909. Under section 2(c) of section 2 it would not be necessary for a Municipality to prepare a new assessment list for every year. It further provides that subject to such modifications as may be made therein under section 77 and to the result of any appeal or revision made under section 190 in the case of other municipalities, the entries in the assessment list so authenticated shall be accepted as conclusive evidence for the purposes of all municipal taxes of the valuation or annual letting values. The appellant Corporation claimed refund on the ground that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual rent less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The difference came to Rs. 1,461 and of this amount the trustees claimed refund of the excess amount collected from them under pain of distress The Municipality having refused to refund the excess respondents filed the suit to recover it on the grounds that the excess amounts were illegally recovered. The Trial Court decreed the suit and the appeals filed by the Corporation in the District Court and the High Court were dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Under section 79(1) of the Act the Municipal Corporation had to prepare fresh assessment list every year and the assessment List on the strength of which the tax was assessed is for each such official year. This is supported by the words "such assessment list" and "of the amount of tax leviable in any official year in which such list is in force".

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association empowered the Company to manufacture and deal in acids, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions, and the assessee company began to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon oil. These were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of association. On May 9, 1943, the assessee Company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings, plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 5, 75,000. It was agreed that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials or any other asset not shown in the agreement of sale. The purchaser was allowed sixty days for the payment of the balance of the price, Rs. 57,500 having been already paid at the time the agreement was 'entered into. The purchasers made a default in payment, and on August 9, 1944, a fresh agreement was entered into between the parties, this time for a consideration of Rs. 7,35,000 and the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the first instance. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944 to the shareholders, the 963 Directors stated that the prices obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and that the sale was of the entire assets including goodwill, and also resulted in a substantial profit. Meanwhile, the assessment of the company for the account years ending April 31, 1944 bad been completed by the Deputy Commissioner of Income tax, and, the appellant Company had been assessed on an income of Rs 36,498 6 4. The Deputy Commissioner, however, relying upon the Memorandum dated May 9. 1943, allowed the assessee to manufacture, and sell chemicals and on the Directors report, held that the assessee was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs 2 lakhs arising from this sale. On appeal by the Department, the Tribunal reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,259. The High Court, however reduced the assessed profits to RS. 1.15, 259 and the Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Newman (II. A. person who carried on business in Western Australia as a pastoralist sold his property including all live stock and plant, as a going concern. On further appeal by certificate, Held: The High Courts were right in holding that the transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business. In the well known case of Californian Copper Syndicate vs Harris (I.L.R. , Doughty vs Commissioner of Taxes) ; , referred to.
